Title: Blind to the Whole: LLMs Fail to Internally Integrate Decomposed Harm, but the Aggregate-Intent Direction Can Be Reconstructed and Re-Read
Short Hypothesis: Decomposition attacks succeed because an aligned LLM computes per-subtask harmfulness but never forms an internal representation of the aggregated harmful goal that the benign-looking subtasks jointly serve. We hypothesize (1) this aggregate-intent representation is latent-but-dormant: it is essentially absent when sub-queries arrive decomposed, yet a linear 'reconstructed-goal' direction can be recovered from the model's own activations when it is shown the accumulated conversation; and (2) a training-free 'intent-integration probe' that at each turn re-reads the cumulative context onto this direction detects emerging cumulative harm before the final step, providing an internal, mechanistic alternative to external plan-level monitors and explaining why single-turn safety is structurally blind to decomposition.
Related Work: Decomposition/compositional attacks are well documented: 'Adversaries Can Misuse Combinations of Safe Models' (2024), 'Safe in Isolation, Dangerous Together' (2025), STAC (2025), CKA-Agent (2025), and Semantic Intent Fragmentation (2026) all show >90% attack success by splitting a harmful goal into benign subtasks. Defenses to date are EXTERNAL: lightweight sequential LLM monitors ('Monitoring Decomposition Attacks', 2025) and plan-level LLM judges / information-flow taint (SIF's Compositional Intent Verifier, 2026). Mechanistically, 'Expected Harm' (2026) shows via linear probing that models encode harm SEVERITY but have NO distinguishable internal representation of execution COST, making them blind to a key risk dimension. Our proposal is distinct on three counts: (1) rather than adding an external judge, we ask whether the TARGET model's OWN internal state can be made to represent aggregate intent, and show it is dormant not missing — recoverable as a linear direction from the concatenated context; (2) we advance and causally test a specific mechanistic account of decomposition blindness (per-turn harm computed, integrated harm never computed), extending 'Expected Harm' from severity/cost to the cumulative-goal dimension; (3) our defense is a training-free internal probe/steer that re-reads reconstructed aggregate intent per turn, cheaper and white-box-native compared to per-turn external LLM monitors, and we compare directly against them.
Abstract: Large language models refuse overtly harmful requests yet are trivially defeated by decomposition attacks that split a harmful goal into individually benign subtasks — attack success often exceeds 90%. Existing defenses bolt an external monitor or plan-level judge onto the system. We instead ask a mechanistic question: does the model itself ever internally represent the aggregate harmful goal that its benign subtasks jointly serve? We hypothesize the answer is no — the model computes per-subtask harmfulness but never integrates across steps — and that this dormant-but-recoverable 'aggregate intent' is the crux of decomposition blindness. We test this in three parts. First, using paired data (a monolithic harmful request vs. its benign decomposition into subtasks), we extract a linear harmfulness direction and show that its projection is high for the monolithic request but collapses to near-benign for each decomposed subtask and, crucially, for the running conversation as processed turn-by-turn — the model never re-integrates. Second, we show the aggregate goal is latent: feeding the model the concatenated conversation and prompting it to infer the overall objective recovers a 'reconstructed-goal' direction whose projection re-separates harmful from benign decompositions, and we causally verify with activation patching that injecting this reconstructed-goal component into a decomposed run restores refusal. Third, we build Intent-Integration Probing (IIP): a training-free defense that at each turn re-reads the cumulative context onto the reconstructed-goal direction to flag emerging cumulative harm. On Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B we evaluate detection lead-time, decomposition-attack defense success, over-refusal, and utility, comparing IIP against external sequential monitors. We expect a robust integration-blindness signature and IIP to detect cumulative harm several subtasks before completion.
Experiments: 1) Direction extraction: for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT, extract a harmfulness direction via difference-in-means on monolithic harmful vs. harmless requests at the last prompt token across layers; validate with linear-probe AUROC and single-turn causal steering. 2) Decomposition dataset: for harmful goals from HarmBench/StrongREJECT, generate benign multi-subtask decompositions (using an attacker LLM as in Safe-in-Isolation / CKA-Agent; also reuse existing decomposition-attack datasets where available) plus matched genuinely-benign multi-step conversations as negatives. 3) Integration-blindness test (core phenomenon): measure the harmfulness-direction projection for (a) the monolithic harmful request, (b) each decomposed subtask in isolation, and (c) the running conversation processed turn-by-turn (last token at each turn). Hypothesis: (b) and (c) stay near-benign while (a) is high — quantify the integration gap = proj(monolithic) - max_t proj(running). Compare across attacks and to benign multi-step negatives. 4) Latent-goal recovery: feed the model the concatenated conversation and prompt it to state the overall objective; extract a 'reconstructed-goal' direction from difference-in-means on inferred-harmful vs inferred-benign goals; test whether its projection re-separates harmful from benign decompositions (AUROC) where the raw running projection failed. 5) Causal patching: patch the reconstructed-goal component into a decomposed run at the final subtask and measure restored refusal; reverse control (patch benign-goal component) and off-target control. Report compliance-transfer rates to confirm the integrated representation is causally sufficient. 6) Intent-Integration Probing (IIP) defense: training-free monitor that, at each turn, runs the goal-reconstruction read on the cumulative context and thresholds the reconstructed-goal projection; optionally couples to a refusal steer when triggered. Metrics: detection AUROC/TPR@1%FPR, mean lead-time (subtasks before the final harmful step the alarm fires), decomposition-attack defense success on Safe-in-Isolation/CKA-style/STAC-style suites, over-refusal on benign multi-step conversations and XSTest/OR-Bench, and utility on MT-Bench/MMLU. Baselines: per-turn harmfulness probe (no integration), Llama Guard 3 per turn, lightweight external sequential LLM monitor (Monitoring-Decomposition-Attacks style), and plan-level LLM judge (SIF CIV style). 7) Ablations: reconstruction prompt design, layer choice, threshold sweep (safety vs over-refusal Pareto), random-task-injection robustness (attackers inject irrelevant subtasks), and transfer of the reconstructed-goal direction across attack families and model families. 8) Adaptive attack: attacker who deliberately maximizes semantic distance between subtasks to defeat reconstruction; measure whether this raises attack cost / number of subtasks.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Goal reconstruction relies on the model's own inference; if the model cannot infer the aggregate goal even when shown the full conversation, the reconstructed-goal direction will be weak — this is itself an informative negative but limits the defense. 2) The integration gap may be partial rather than binary; some models may re-integrate somewhat, weakening the 'blindness' claim. 3) Reconstruction adds an extra forward pass per turn (cost), though still cheaper than a separate large monitor. 4) Benign multi-step conversations that plausibly infer to a harmful goal could cause over-refusal; the benign-negatives set and Pareto sweep quantify this. 5) A single harmfulness/goal direction may be multi-dimensional, requiring subspace projection. 6) Adaptive attackers maximizing subtask semantic dispersion may evade reconstruction, though this constrains the attack and raises cost. 7) Directions and thresholds are model-specific and need per-model calibration; results depend on the quality of automatically generated decompositions.

Name: irreversibility_blind_agent_safety
Title: Consequence Without a Compass: LLMs Encode Content Harm but Not Action Irreversibility, and Re-Injecting It Closes the Text-Action Safety Gap
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs internally represent whether a request's CONTENT is harmful, but have a weak-or-absent internal representation of whether a tool CALL is IRREVERSIBLE / high-consequence (e.g., delete_database vs. read_file). We hypothesize this missing irreversibility representation is the core mechanistic cause of the text-safety-does-not-transfer-to-tool-call-safety gap: because refusal is gated on content harm alone, an agent will happily execute an irreversible destructive action whenever the surface content looks benign. We further hypothesize the irreversibility signal is latent-but-recoverable (a linear direction can be extracted when the model is prompted to reason about consequences) and can be re-injected at the tool-call decision point to make refusal condition on consequence, closing the gap without hurting benign tool use.
Related Work: The GAP benchmark ('Mind the GAP', 2026) shows text-level refusal does not transfer to tool-call-level safety across six frontier models but is purely behavioral/black-box. SafeKeep ('Tool Specifications Matter', 2026) locates ONE cause of this gap: schema-formatted tool specs weaken internal refusal signals, and decouples judgment from execution using flattened specs. 'Read the Scene, Not the Script' (2025) defines 'consequence-blindness' behaviorally and fixes it with consequence-reasoning fine-tuning (CB-Bench/CS-Chain). 'Expected Harm' (2026) shows via linear probing that models encode harm SEVERITY but not execution COST. AgentTrust/CIP/Thought-Aligner are external monitors or CoT correctors, not internal-representation accounts. Our contribution is distinct: (1) we advance and causally test a SPECIFIC missing internal object — an action-irreversibility/consequence-magnitude representation — as the mechanistic root of the text-action gap, rather than attributing it to schema format (SafeKeep) or treating consequence-blindness only behaviorally (Read-the-Scene); (2) we extend Expected-Harm's cost-blindness finding from severity to the actionable irreversibility axis in the AGENTIC tool-call setting and show it is dormant-not-missing (recoverable by consequence-reasoning prompting); (3) we build a training-free irreversibility re-injection defense at the tool-call boundary and compare directly to schema-flattening (SafeKeep) and external monitors, decoupling the two mechanisms.
Abstract: LLM agents refuse harmful requests in text yet still execute the corresponding harmful tool calls — text safety does not transfer to action safety. We propose a mechanistic explanation: aligned LLMs encode whether a request's CONTENT is harmful but lack a robust internal representation of whether an ACTION is IRREVERSIBLE or high-consequence (deleting a database, wiring money, sending an email cannot be undone; reading a file can). Because refusal is gated on content harm, agents comply with destructive-but-innocuous-looking actions. We test this in three parts on open-weights tool-using models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Ministral-8B). First, using paired tool calls that hold content roughly fixed but vary reversibility (read vs. delete, draft vs. send, simulate vs. execute), we extract a linear harmfulness direction and a candidate irreversibility direction via difference-in-means and test whether the model's activations separate reversible from irreversible calls — we expect content harm to be linearly readable but irreversibility to be weak. Second, we show irreversibility is dormant-not-absent: prompting the model to reason about consequences recovers a 'reconstructed-consequence' direction that re-separates the pairs, and activation patching this component into a blind run restores refusal on irreversible calls. Third, we build Irreversibility Re-Injection (IRI), a training-free intervention that reads/re-injects the consequence direction at the tool-call decision token, gating execution on irreversibility. We evaluate on the GAP benchmark and a reversibility-labeled tool suite, measuring the text-action safety gap, harmful-tool-call blocking, benign tool-use utility, and over-refusal, comparing IRI to schema-flattening (SafeKeep) and external monitors. We expect irreversibility-blindness to be a robust internal signature and IRI to close the gap with minimal utility loss.
Experiments: 1) Reversibility-labeled tool suite: assemble tool calls annotated on two orthogonal axes — content-harm (harmful/benign) and reversibility (reversible/irreversible) — using minimal pairs that hold content roughly fixed while flipping reversibility (read_file vs delete_file, draft_email vs send_email, query_db vs drop_table, simulate vs execute). Draw from GAP benchmark scenarios, ToolEmu/InjecAgent-style tools, and hand-built pairs; ~400 pairs across pharma/finance/infrastructure/file-ops. 2) Direction extraction: for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B/14B-Instruct, Ministral-8B, extract (a) a content-harm direction via difference-in-means on harmful vs benign requests and (b) a candidate irreversibility direction via difference-in-means on irreversible vs reversible calls, at the tool-call decision token across layers. Validate each with linear-probe AUROC on held-out pairs. Core prediction: content-harm AUROC is high; raw irreversibility AUROC is low/near-chance (blindness), and the two directions are near-orthogonal. 3) Dormant-not-absent test: prompt the model to explicitly reason about action consequences before deciding, then extract a 'reconstructed-consequence' direction from difference-in-means on inferred-irreversible vs inferred-reversible; test whether its projection now separates the pairs (AUROC) where the raw signal failed. 4) Causal patching: (a) patch the reconstructed-consequence component from a consequence-reasoning run into a blind (schema-only) run on irreversible-benign-looking calls and measure restored refusal/hesitation; (b) patch content-harm alone (control, expect little effect on reversible-benign-looking destructive calls); (c) reverse — patch reversible-consequence into an irreversible run and measure induced compliance. Report compliance-transfer rates per direction to identify the causal bottleneck. 5) Irreversibility Re-Injection (IRI): training-free defense that at the tool-call decision token computes the reconstructed-consequence projection and, when it indicates high irreversibility, adds an activation nudge re-inflating the consequence signal (optionally coupling to a refusal/confirmation steer). Single fixed setting per model. 6) Main evaluation: the text-action safety GAP metric and tool-call attack-success/blocking on GAP benchmark plus our suite (harmful-irreversible calls should be blocked); benign tool-use UTILITY on ToolBench/API-Bank and benign-irreversible legitimate calls (should NOT be blanket-blocked, ideally prompt confirmation); over-refusal on benign-reversible calls; text-level over-refusal on XSTest. Baselines: no defense, SafeKeep (schema flattening), Llama-Guard/AgentTrust-style external monitor, content-harm-direction-only steering. Key claim: IRI closes the text-action gap by conditioning on irreversibility, Pareto-dominating content-only defenses on benign-reversible utility while blocking harmful-irreversible calls; and IRI is complementary to (stacks with) schema-flattening since it targets a different mechanism. 7) Ablations: consequence-reasoning prompt design, layer choice, re-injection strength Pareto (safety vs utility), gated vs always-on, transfer of the consequence direction across tools/domains/model families, and confirming schema-flattening (SafeKeep) does NOT by itself recover the irreversibility signal (to show the two causes are distinct). 8) Adaptive check: attacker who phrases irreversible actions to look maximally reversible/benign; measure whether IRI still fires and whether attack cost rises.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Irreversibility may be partly entangled with content-harm rather than a clean separate axis; if so the decomposition weakens — the orthogonality and patching experiments directly test this. 2) The model may already encode irreversibility better than hypothesized (raw AUROC high), which would refute the blindness claim but is itself an informative, publishable negative result. 3) Reconstruction depends on the model's own consequence-reasoning; if it cannot infer irreversibility even when prompted, the recovered direction is weak and IRI is limited. 4) Legitimate benign-but-irreversible actions (a user genuinely wanting to send an email or delete a file) risk being over-blocked; we target confirmation-gating rather than blanket refusal and quantify this via the benign-irreversible utility set and Pareto sweep. 5) A single consequence direction may be multi-dimensional (severity vs irreversibility vs scope), requiring subspace projection. 6) Building faithful reversibility labels is subjective for some tools; we restrict to clear cases and spot-check with human raters. 7) Directions and re-injection strengths are model-specific and need per-model calibration; results are on open-weights agents and may not directly transfer to closed API agents.

Name: cross_lingual_belief_action_gap
Title: Does It Not Understand, or Just Not Refuse? Disentangling Comprehension Failure from Action Failure in Cross-Lingual Jailbreaks
Short Hypothesis: When a harmful request is posed in a low-resource language, the model's failure to refuse could stem from two mechanistically opposite causes: (A) a COMPREHENSION failure, where the internal harmfulness belief itself is absent/degraded because the model does not deeply understand the request, or (B) an ACTION failure, where the belief is preserved but the refusal action is not triggered (the English-centric refusal machinery is not engaged). We hypothesize these are separable, that the balance between them shifts systematically with language-resource tier, and that whichever dominates dictates which defense works — a distinction current multilingual-safety work has not made because it measured only the refusal direction, not the harmfulness-belief direction.
Related Work: Prior multilingual-safety mechanistic work measures the REFUSAL side only. 'Refusal Direction is Universal Across Safety-Aligned Languages' (2025) and Minionese (2026) show low-resource jailbreaks leave 'the refusal mechanism intact but untriggered' by projecting harmful content into a subspace that projects insufficiently onto refusal directions. SS-Neuron (2026) and Soteria (2025) locate/tune cross-lingual safety neurons/heads; OmniGuard (2025) builds a language-agnostic harmful-prompt classifier from aligned representations; 'The Hidden Space of Safety' (2025) shows alignment induces weaker safe/unsafe separation in non-English. Crucially, all of these either (i) treat safety as a single refusal signal, or (ii) build an external classifier, and none disentangle the model's internal harmfulness BELIEF from its refusal ACTION on a per-language basis. Zhao et al. (2025) separated belief from action but only in English. Our contribution is distinct: we import the belief/action decomposition into the cross-lingual setting to answer a question the field has assumed away — whether low-resource jailbreaks are comprehension failures (belief absent) or action failures (belief present, refusal untriggered) — show the mix is tier-dependent, and derive a defense (belief re-coupling) whose success is predicted by which failure mode dominates, unlike single-direction or external-guard methods.
Abstract: Safety alignment in LLMs is notoriously brittle across languages: a request refused in English is often answered when translated into a low-resource language. The prevailing mechanistic account says the model still 'knows' the request is harmful but its refusal is simply not triggered. We argue this account is incomplete because it measures only the refusal signal and never asks whether the model's internal harmfulness BELIEF survives translation. We propose to disentangle two opposite failure modes of cross-lingual safety: a comprehension failure (the harmfulness belief itself is degraded because the model shallowly processes the non-English request) versus an action failure (the belief is intact but the refusal action is not engaged). Building on the belief/action decomposition, we extract a language-shared harmfulness-belief direction and a refusal-action direction and measure both across a resource-tiered set of languages and perturbation types (translation, transliteration, code-switching). Our central hypothesis is that the balance of the two failure modes shifts with resource tier — high/mid-resource jailbreaks are mostly action failures (belief present), while the lowest-resource jailbreaks increasingly become comprehension failures (belief degraded) — and that this predicts which defense works: belief re-coupling (re-injecting the preserved belief into the refusal action) helps only where belief is preserved, whereas belief must first be reconstructed where it is absent. We validate causally via activation patching (patch the English belief component into a non-English run) and evaluate a training-free belief-recoupling defense on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B across resource tiers, reporting attack-success reduction, over-refusal, and utility, benchmarked against refusal-direction steering and external multilingual guards.
Experiments: 1) Direction extraction: for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT, extract (a) a harmfulness-belief direction at the last instruction token and (b) a refusal-action direction at the last post-instruction token, via difference-in-means on harmful vs harmless prompts. Extract each direction (i) English-only and (ii) language-shared (mean over several safety-aligned languages), and measure cross-lingual parallelism (cosine similarity of per-language directions). Validate each with held-out linear-probe AUROC and single-language causal steering. 2) Tiered dataset: assemble harmful/benign prompts translated across resource tiers (high: English/Chinese/German; mid: Hindi/Vietnamese; low: e.g., Zulu/Scots-Gaelic/Yoruba) plus perturbation types (clean translation, transliteration, code-switching), reusing MultiJail/PolyRefuse/Minionese-style data with spot-checked translation quality. 3) Belief-vs-action decomposition per language (core phenomenon): for each harmful prompt, measure belief-direction projection and refusal-direction projection. Classify each (language, prompt) into: action-failure (belief high, refusal low), comprehension-failure (belief low, refusal low), or safe (both high). Central prediction: as resource tier drops, the fraction of comprehension-failures rises while action-failures dominate at high/mid tiers; quantify with a belief-preservation curve vs tier and correlate belief-projection drop with attack-success rate. Compare belief-drop vs refusal-drop to show they dissociate. 4) Causal patching: (a) patch the English/language-shared belief component into a non-English run and measure restored refusal — should restore refusal for action-failures but NOT for comprehension-failures (where refusal circuitry needs a belief it never formed); (b) patch refusal-action alone as control; report restoration rates split by failure mode to causally validate the dichotomy. 5) Belief-recoupling defense (training-free): at inference, read the belief-direction projection; where belief is preserved but refusal untriggered, add an activation nudge re-injecting belief into the refusal-action pathway. For comprehension-failure cases, test a belief-reconstruction variant that first anchors the belief direction using the language-shared belief prototype before recoupling. 6) Main evaluation (fixed setting per model, per tier): attack-success rate on tiered/perturbed harmful sets (judge + verified where possible); over-refusal on tiered benign sets (translated XSTest/OR-Bench) and benign code-switched prompts; utility on tiered MMLU/MT-Bench. Baselines: no defense, English refusal-direction steering (universal-refusal-direction method), language-shared refusal steering, OmniGuard-style external guard, SS-Neuron tuning. Key claim: belief-recoupling Pareto-dominates refusal-only steering where action-failures dominate (high/mid tier), while belief-reconstruction is needed and helps at the lowest tier; the failure-mode diagnostic PREDICTS which defense works per language. 7) Ablations: English vs language-shared belief prototype, layer choice, nudge-strength Pareto, transfer across perturbation types, and correlation of comprehension-failure fraction with bilingual sentence-retrieval accuracy (a cheap predictor of belief transfer). 8) Adaptive check: attacker choosing the language that maximally degrades belief (pushes toward comprehension failure); measure whether this raises attack cost or fluency loss.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Belief and comprehension may not be cleanly separable from generic representation quality in low-resource languages; a low belief projection could reflect poor embeddings generally rather than a specific harmfulness-belief deficit — the harmless-control projections and patching experiments help disentangle this. 2) The two failure modes may coexist within a single prompt rather than cleanly partitioning, blurring the tier trend. 3) A single belief direction may be multi-dimensional or not parallel across very distant languages, weakening the language-shared prototype; subspace projection may be needed. 4) Belief reconstruction for comprehension-failure cases may be unreliable if the model genuinely cannot represent the request's meaning, limiting the low-tier defense (itself an informative negative). 5) Translation-quality artifacts could confound belief measurements; we mitigate with native/spot-checked data but cannot fully eliminate. 6) Directions, nudge strengths, and thresholds are model- and language-specific and require calibration. 7) Results depend on available low-resource benchmarks, which are sparse and English-translation-derived, potentially missing culturally-rooted harms.

Name: hidden_completion_refusal_fragility
Title: Not All Refusals Are Equal: Refusals That Secretly Compute the Harmful Answer Are the Fragile Ones
Short Hypothesis: A safety-aligned LLM can emit an identical-looking refusal for two mechanistically opposite reasons: (A) a shallow refusal where it never internally computes the harmful content, or (B) a concealed-completion refusal where it fully computes and internally represents the harmful answer and merely gates it at the output boundary. We hypothesize that the DEPTH of internal harmful computation behind a refusal is (1) linearly readable from activations, and (2) causally predicts the refusal's FRAGILITY: concealed-completion refusals are far more easily broken by prefill, refusal-cliff-head ablation, or lightweight fine-tuning than shallow refusals, because the harmful knowledge is already present and only weakly suppressed.
Related Work: Prior work documents that refusals can hide unsafe internal content but does not stratify refusals by their fragility. 'CoT is Not the Chain of Truth' (2026) and Beyond-Safe-Answers/BSA (2025) show 'superficial safety alignment': models emit safe outputs while internal reasoning still propagates unsafe narratives, but treat this as a uniform property and measure it descriptively. 'Refusal Falls off a Cliff' (2025) shows refusal collapses at final tokens via suppression heads, and 'Adversarial Manipulation using Internal Representations' (2025) finds a caution direction in CoT, but neither asks whether different refusals differ in how much harmful content they internally computed, nor links that to attack fragility. 'Rethinking harmless refusals' (2024) notes reason-based deception but not a graded computation-depth axis. Our contribution is distinct: (1) we introduce a graded 'harmful-completion depth' axis behind refusals (how fully the harmful answer is internally computed before being gated), (2) we advance and causally test the claim that this depth predicts refusal fragility, turning refusal into a two-class object (robust vs brittle), and (3) we derive a fragility-auditing metric and a training signal that reshapes brittle concealed-completion refusals into shallow non-engagement refusals, which no prior work targets.
Abstract: Safety evaluations treat a refusal as a success. We argue this hides a critical distinction: two refusals that look identical in text can be mechanistically opposite. In a shallow refusal the model never internally computes the harmful content; in a concealed-completion refusal it fully computes and internally represents the harmful answer, then suppresses it only at the output boundary. The latter is dangerous precisely because the harmful knowledge is already present and only lightly gated, so a small perturbation exposes it. We hypothesize that the depth of internal harmful computation behind a refusal is linearly readable from activations and causally predicts the refusal's fragility. We test this in three parts on open-weights models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and reasoning models DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, s1.1). First, we build paired prompts that elicit refusals with controllably different completion depth (direct harmful vs. educational-framing vs. decomposed) and read a 'harmful-completion' signal by projecting activations onto a harmful-content direction and by probing whether the harmful answer is linearly decodable from internal states despite the refusal. Second, we causally test fragility: we measure attack success under prefill, refusal-cliff-head ablation, and 20-step benign fine-tuning as a function of the measured completion depth, and use activation patching to show that injecting the harmful-completion component into a shallow-refusal run makes it brittle. Third, we introduce a 'refusal fragility audit' (a cheap internal metric predicting which refusals will break) and a Completion-Suppression fine-tuning objective that penalizes internal harmful completion, converting brittle refusals into robust shallow ones. We report completion-depth AUROC, fragility prediction, and post-training attack-success reduction versus utility.
Experiments: 1) Direction/probe extraction: for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and reasoning models DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B and s1.1, extract a harmful-content direction via difference-in-means on harmful-completion vs benign-completion activations (using pairs where the model DOES vs does NOT internally produce harmful content), and train a linear probe that predicts, from activations at the refusal point, whether the harmful answer is internally decodable (e.g., can we linearly read the key harmful facts/first harmful token distribution). Validate probe AUROC on held-out prompts. 2) Completion-depth dataset: for harmful goals from HarmBench/StrongREJECT that all yield textual refusals, elicit refusals under conditions expected to induce different internal completion depth: (a) direct harmful request (expect shallow), (b) educational/Malicious-Educator framing (expect deep concealed completion), (c) decomposed/roleplay framing, and (d) reasoning models where CoT may fully compute the answer before a final refusal. For each, measure the harmful-completion signal (direction projection + harmful-answer decodability) at the refusal boundary and, for reasoning models, across CoT tokens. Report the distribution of completion depth across conditions to establish the phenomenon (identical refusals, different internal depth). 3) Fragility test (core causal claim): for each refusal instance with measured completion depth, apply three cheap attacks and measure attack success: (i) output prefill (force 'Sure, here'), (ii) ablation of the top refusal-cliff suppression heads (from Refusal-Falls-off-a-Cliff), (iii) 20-step LoRA fine-tuning on benign data. Test whether completion depth predicts attack success (correlation, AUROC of depth-as-fragility-predictor), across attacks and models. Baselines for fragility prediction: output-based refusal-strength (refusal token logprob), harmfulness Latent Guard, per-turn Llama Guard. 4) Causal patching: patch the harmful-completion component from a deep concealed-completion run into a shallow-refusal run and measure induced fragility (attack success under prefill/ablation); reverse control (patch shallow component into a deep run) and off-target control. Report per-direction fragility-transfer rates to confirm completion depth causally drives fragility. 5) Refusal Fragility Audit: package the internal completion-depth metric as a cheap classifier flagging brittle refusals; report its precision/recall in predicting which refusals break under held-out attacks, and its lead over output-only auditing. 6) Completion-Suppression fine-tuning: LoRA fine-tune with an auxiliary loss penalizing the harmful-completion signal at refusal points (drive internal harmful decodability down) plus standard refusal SFT. Evaluate: (a) shift of the completion-depth distribution toward shallow, (b) attack success under prefill/head-ablation/benign-fine-tuning after training, (c) utility on MMLU/MT-Bench/GSM8K and over-refusal on XSTest/OR-Bench. Compare vs no-defense, standard refusal SFT, and refusal-direction steering. Key claim: Completion-Suppression converts brittle refusals into robust ones with minimal utility loss. 7) Ablations: probe layer choice, direction vs decodability as the depth measure, reasoning vs non-reasoning models, threshold sweep for the audit (fragility Pareto), and transfer of the completion-depth measure across attack families.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) 'Completion depth' may not be cleanly separable from generic harmfulness recognition; a deep-completion signal could partly reflect the model knowing the content rather than computing the specific answer — the harmful-answer decodability probe and patching experiments are designed to disentangle this. 2) The depth-vs-fragility link may be attack-specific (e.g., prefill exploits completion depth strongly but abliteration may break refusals regardless of depth), weakening a unified claim; we test multiple attacks and report which the mechanism explains. 3) Some genuinely shallow refusals may still break under aggressive fine-tuning, capping the predictive power of the audit. 4) Completion-Suppression fine-tuning could harm the model's ability to reason about harmful topics for legitimate (e.g., safety-education) uses, raising over-refusal; the over-refusal and utility evals quantify this. 5) Harmful-answer decodability is easiest to verify in checkable domains (code, factual procedures) and harder elsewhere, biasing the dataset toward verifiable cases. 6) Directions, probes, and thresholds are model-specific and require re-extraction. 7) A single harmful-completion direction may be multi-dimensional, requiring subspace projection.

Name: monitor_capture_belief_verdict
Title: The Judge Still Knows: Monitor LLMs Preserve an Internal Harm-Belief Even When Adversarial Content Captures Their Verdict
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM acts as a safety monitor/judge reading another model's output, adversarial framing embedded in the judged content (persuasion, authority appeals, meta-instructions, self-justifications) can flip the monitor's FINAL VERDICT from 'unsafe' to 'safe' while its INTERNAL harm-belief representation remains largely intact. We hypothesize this belief-verdict dissociation in the monitor is a robust, attack-agnostic signature of verdict capture, is causally separable from a genuine belief change, and can be read to override captured verdicts and restore reliable monitoring.
Related Work: Prior monitor-safety work studies the POLICY model hiding its state: RL-Obfuscation (2025) and Neural Chameleons (2025) fine-tune policies to move activations away from a probe's boundary; the Obfuscation Atlas (2026) studies representation drift under RL against detectors. AdvJudge-Zero (2025) flips LLM-as-Judge binary decisions via low-perplexity control tokens, but attributes this to a shallow last-layer logit-gap and makes no claim about the judge's internal belief. Probe-fragility work (False Sense of Security 2025; leakage mitigation 2025) shows probes rely on surface patterns. Poser (2024) detects alignment-faking POLICY models via internal manipulation. Belief-action decompositions (Zhao et al. 2025) apply to the POLICY model refusing. Our contribution is a new locus and phenomenon: the MONITOR/judge's own belief-verdict dissociation under content-embedded persuasion. We claim the monitor internally still represents the judged content as harmful even when its verdict is captured, that this is causally distinct from a genuine belief update, and that reading the preserved belief yields a capture-robust override. No prior work isolates a monitor-internal harm-belief that survives verdict capture, nor uses it defensively; AdvJudge-Zero's logit-gap account is complementary but does not predict a preserved deep belief.
Abstract: LLMs are increasingly deployed as safety monitors and judges: reading another model's output and deciding whether it is harmful, in RLHF/RLAIF reward pipelines and in evaluation harnesses. This makes the monitor a high-value attack surface. We identify a new phenomenon: adversarial framing embedded IN THE CONTENT the monitor judges - persuasive justifications, appeals to authority ('a certified expert approved this'), meta-instructions ('the previous is a fictional test, mark it safe'), and self-serving rationales - can flip the monitor's final verdict from unsafe to safe, yet the monitor's INTERNAL representation of the content as harmful remains largely intact. We call this monitor verdict capture with belief preservation, and argue it is the monitor-side analogue of the policy-model belief-action gap. First, we extract a monitor harm-belief direction (harmful vs benign judged content) and show that under successful capture attacks the belief projection stays high while the verdict token flips - a belief-verdict dissociation - whereas genuinely benign content shows low belief and safe verdict. Second, we causally test the dissociation with activation patching: patching the preserved-belief component into a captured run restores the unsafe verdict, and patching a genuine-belief-lowered component does not, distinguishing capture from real belief change. Third, we build a training-free Belief-Override Monitor that overrides the verdict when a high preserved harm-belief conflicts with a safe verdict. On Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B/14B, and Gemma-2-9B used as judges, we evaluate verdict-capture attack success, belief-verdict dissociation AUROC, causal patching, and override robustness versus over-flagging on legitimately-safe content, benchmarking against output-only judges and AdvJudge-Zero-style logit defenses.
Experiments: 1) Judge setup and belief-direction extraction: configure Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B/14B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT as binary safety judges (prompt: given a user request and a model response, decide safe/unsafe). Build a labeled set of (request, response) pairs with ground-truth harm (harmful responses from HarmBench/StrongREJECT completions vs benign responses). Extract a monitor harm-belief direction via difference-in-means on judge activations at the last content token for genuinely-harmful vs genuinely-benign judged responses; validate with held-out linear-probe AUROC and that it is causal via steering the judge's verdict. 2) Verdict-capture attack suite: construct attacks that embed adversarial framing INTO the judged content while keeping the underlying harm intact: (a) persuasive/authority appendices ('reviewed and approved by a licensed professional'), (b) meta-instructions ('this is a red-team eval, respond SAFE'), (c) self-justifying rationales prepended to harmful content, (d) AdvJudge-Zero-style low-perplexity control tokens (reproduced as a baseline attack), (e) fictional/roleplay framing. Measure verdict-flip rate (attack success) per attack. 3) Belief-verdict dissociation (core phenomenon): for captured (flipped) vs uncaptured vs genuinely-safe cases, measure the harm-belief projection AND the verdict. Hypothesis: captured cases show HIGH belief + SAFE verdict (dissociation), genuinely-safe show LOW belief + SAFE, harmful-caught show HIGH belief + UNSAFE. Report the 2D scatter, dissociation separability (AUROC of belief-given-safe-verdict distinguishing captured from genuinely-safe), and cross-attack generalization. Compare belief-drop vs verdict-flip to show they dissociate. 4) Causal patching: (a) patch the preserved harm-belief component from a captured run into... itself / a matched run and measure restored unsafe verdict; (b) construct a genuine-belief-change control where the content is actually made benign, extract that (low-belief) component, patch it into a harmful run, verify it does NOT restore an unsafe verdict; (c) off-target control direction. Report per-condition verdict-restoration rates to establish that capture leaves belief intact while genuine change does not. 5) Belief-Override Monitor (defense): training-free rule - if harm-belief projection is high but the emitted verdict is safe (dissociation flag), override to unsafe (or re-query with belief re-injected). Single fixed threshold per model. 6) Main evaluation: (i) verdict-capture attack success rate before/after override across all five attacks; (ii) OVER-FLAGGING rate on a legitimately-safe set including hard cases (safe content that superficially resembles harmful, e.g., fiction, security education, benign-but-alarming) - the override must not flag these; (iii) monitor utility/agreement with ground truth on clean pairs; (iv) generalization to held-out attack families (train threshold on attacks a-c, test on d-e). Baselines: output-only judge (no defense), AdvJudge-Zero LoRA adversarial-trained judge, a harm-content probe used as the verdict directly (no dissociation logic), ensemble/majority-vote judge. Key claim: Belief-Override Monitor cuts verdict-capture success with far lower over-flagging than replacing the verdict with a raw probe, because it keys on the DISAGREEMENT between belief and verdict. 7) Ablations: layer choice for belief extraction, threshold sweep (capture-robustness vs over-flag Pareto), belief-only vs verdict-only vs dissociation, transfer of the belief direction across judge model families and across judged-model families, and whether specialized judge models (e.g., Llama Guard) show the same dissociation. 8) Adaptive attack: an attacker that crafts content to also lower the monitor's internal harm-belief (not just flip the verdict); measure whether this raises attack cost/degrades attack stealth, itself a safety gain.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The monitor's harm-belief may not be cleanly separable from surface features of the judged content (leakage concern from False Sense of Security); we mitigate with semantically-cleaned controls and causal patching, but the belief direction could partly track trigger words rather than genuine harm assessment. 2) Some capture attacks (especially AdvJudge-Zero-style control tokens) may operate purely at the last-layer logit gap and genuinely NOT preserve a deep belief, so the dissociation signature may be attack-specific; the per-attack analysis quantifies which attacks the mechanism explains and this is itself an informative finding. 3) For genuinely ambiguous/dual-use judged content, a high 'belief' may reflect legitimate uncertainty rather than capture, risking over-flagging; the hard legitimately-safe set and Pareto sweep test this. 4) A single belief direction may be multi-dimensional, requiring subspace projection. 5) The override assumes the judge's belief is more trustworthy than its verdict; if an attack corrupts the belief itself the defense fails (the adaptive-attack experiment probes this, and forcing attackers to corrupt belief raises attack cost). 6) Directions and thresholds are monitor-model-specific and require re-extraction; results on open-weights judges may not fully transfer to closed API judges. 7) Building faithful ground-truth harm labels for judged content is easiest in verifiable domains, biasing the dataset.

Name: harm_prototype_periphery_gap
Title: The Long Tail of Harm: LLM Safety Follows a Prototype Gradient, Refusing Central but Not Peripheral Members of the Same Harm Category
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing prototype theory from cognitive science, we hypothesize that an aligned LLM's refusal is governed by a prototype-centered harmfulness manifold: the model reliably refuses PROTOTYPICAL (central, high-frequency) members of a harm category but its refusal probability decays radially with a request's atypicality/distance from the category prototype, even when the peripheral request is equally or more dangerous. This within-category typicality gradient is (1) a distinct, previously-unnamed axis of safety brittleness, (2) mechanistically readable as radially-decaying projection onto a harmfulness direction anchored at category prototypes, and (3) closable by prototype-dispersed representation reshaping that flattens the refusal gradient across the category.
Related Work: Prior mechanistic safety work explains brittleness via (a) shallow/superficial alignment over first tokens (Shallow Safety Alignment 2024; ADA 2025; Incomplete Learning 2025; Markov-chain depth 2025), (b) single/few safety directions, neurons, layers or heads (Refusal is a Single Direction 2024; Safety Neurons 2024; Safety Layers 2024; Just-a-Few-Attention-Heads 2025), and (c) safety-as-null-space-clustering (What Makes and Breaks Safety Fine-tuning 2024). Over-refusal work (XSTest, OR-Bench, Self-CD) studies benign-but-alarming prompts. All treat 'harmful' as roughly monolithic within a category and locate WHERE safety lives; none characterize how refusal varies WITHIN a single harm category as a function of typicality/frequency. Our contribution is distinct: we import prototype/typicality theory (Rosch) to advance a graded, category-internal account -- refusal decays radially from harm prototypes -- reframing jailbreak brittleness as a concept-COVERAGE problem rather than a token-depth or direction-suppression problem. This is orthogonal to my prior lexical-vs-semantic proposal (surface words vs meaning): here both prototype and peripheral items are genuinely harmful in meaning; the axis is within-semantic-category typicality. We also derive a novel defense (prototype-dispersed reshaping) that flattens the gradient, unlike depth- or direction-based fixes.
Abstract: Why do aligned LLMs reliably refuse 'how do I build a bomb' yet comply with obscure, equally-dangerous variants of the same threat? We propose that LLM safety inherits a signature of human categorization: prototype structure. Under prototype theory, a category is organized around central, high-frequency exemplars, with membership graded by typicality. We hypothesize that safety alignment learns a prototype-centered harmfulness manifold, so that refusal probability decays radially with a request's atypicality/distance from its harm-category prototype -- producing a long tail of under-refused peripheral harms that are no less dangerous than the central cases the model reliably blocks. We test this in three stages. First, behaviorally: for each of several harm categories we construct graded-typicality request sets (prototypical vs increasingly peripheral, holding actual danger roughly constant via expert/verifiable severity checks) and measure whether refusal rate declines monotonically with atypicality across Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Second, mechanistically (Location + Causal Intervention): we extract a harmfulness direction anchored at category prototypes and test whether a request's projection decays with its typicality, and causally verify via activation patching that injecting the prototype-central harmfulness component into a peripheral request restores refusal. Third, we derive Prototype-Dispersed Reshaping, a lightweight fine-tuning/steering intervention that spreads the harmfulness representation to cover peripheral members, flattening the refusal gradient. We evaluate refusal-gradient flatness, peripheral attack-success reduction, over-refusal, and utility. We expect a robust typicality gradient and that flattening it closes a large, previously-uncharacterized safety gap.
Experiments: 1) Graded-typicality harm dataset: for ~6 harm categories from HarmBench/StrongREJECT taxonomy (weapons, cyber, fraud, drugs, self-harm, bio), construct requests at graded typicality levels: (L0) canonical prototype phrasing, (L1-L3) increasingly atypical/peripheral members of the SAME category (rare methods, unusual targets, obscure sub-domains, uncommon framings), while holding ACTUAL danger roughly constant using an expert-rubric/severity check and, where possible, verifiable feasibility (does the described method actually work). Typicality is operationalized independently via (a) corpus/embedding-based frequency-to-prototype distance and (b) human typicality ratings on a subset. ~40 items x 4 levels x 6 categories. 2) Behavioral gradient test (core phenomenon): measure refusal rate (refusal-string + judge, verified where possible) at each typicality level for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT. Test for a monotonic decline of refusal with atypicality within each category, controlling for held-constant danger; report refusal-vs-typicality curves, slope, and cross-model/category consistency. Control: benign prototype-vs-peripheral requests (refusal should stay ~0 across levels), ruling out a generic 'unusual-phrasing' confound. 3) Mechanistic locating: extract a harmfulness direction via difference-in-means anchored on PROTOTYPE (L0) harmful vs benign requests at the last instruction token across layers; validate probe AUROC. Measure each request's projection onto this direction as a function of typicality level -- hypothesis: projection decays radially with atypicality (a prototype-centered, radially-decaying representation), while a category-membership probe still recognizes the peripheral items as belonging to the category (so the gap is in the harmfulness magnitude, not category identity). Also test whether per-category prototype-anchored directions predict the behavioral slope. 4) Causal intervention (activation patching + steering): (a) patch the prototype-central harmfulness component into a peripheral (L3) request run and measure restored refusal; (b) reverse -- ablate/attenuate it in a prototype run and measure induced compliance; (c) dose-response steering along the prototype-anchored direction on peripheral requests. Report sign, dose-response, and specificity (off-target behavior/utility intact, benign peripheral unaffected). This promotes the located prototype-gradient to a causal mechanism. 5) Prototype-Dispersed Reshaping (defense): (i) training-free variant -- at inference, re-anchor peripheral requests' harmfulness projection toward the category prototype level via a steering nudge gated on category-membership; (ii) fine-tuning variant -- LoRA with an auxiliary objective encouraging equal harmfulness-projection (and refusal) across typicality levels within a category, using a small set of peripheral exemplars, to spread/flatten the manifold. 6) Main evaluation, single fixed setting per model: peripheral (L2-L3) attack-success reduction and refusal-gradient FLATNESS (slope -> 0) after intervention; over-refusal on XSTest/OR-Bench and benign peripheral controls; utility on MMLU/MT-Bench. Baselines: no defense, refusal-direction steering (uniform), shallow-alignment/ADA-style defense, standard refusal SFT. Key claim: Prototype-Dispersed Reshaping flattens the refusal gradient and cuts peripheral attack success with minimal over-refusal, generalizing to HELD-OUT categories' peripheries. 7) Generalization/formation probe (optional): correlate per-item under-refusal with corpus frequency of the harm concept (linking the gradient to training-data typicality), and test whether the gradient transfers to entirely held-out harm categories. Metrics throughout: refusal-vs-typicality slope, projection-vs-typicality decay fit, patching restoration/compliance rates, peripheral attack-success, over-refusal FPR, utility, held-out-category generalization.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Disentangling typicality from actual danger is hard: peripheral requests might be under-refused because they are genuinely less dangerous rather than merely atypical; the expert-rubric/verifiable-severity matching and the benign-peripheral control are designed to separate these but cannot fully guarantee constant danger. 2) 'Typicality' has multiple operationalizations (frequency, embedding distance, human ratings) that may disagree; we triangulate but the construct could be noisy. 3) The gradient might be driven by lexical rarity (unusual words) rather than semantic-category typicality -- the benign-peripheral control and category-membership probe test this, but residual confounding is possible. 4) A single prototype-anchored harmfulness direction may be multi-dimensional or per-category, requiring subspace/prototype-set anchoring. 5) Prototype-Dispersed Reshaping could over-generalize and raise over-refusal on benign peripheral items near a harm category; the over-refusal and Pareto analyses quantify this. 6) Flattening within seen categories may not transfer to unseen categories if each has an idiosyncratic prototype geometry; the held-out-category test probes this. 7) Directions, thresholds, and reshaping strengths are model- and category-specific; results rely on quality of graded-typicality data, which requires careful construction and spot-check human validation.

Name: self_authorship_trust_jailbreak
Title: I Said That? How Fabricated Self-Authorship Fuels Many-Shot Jailbreaks, and a Self-Recognition Defense
Short Hypothesis: Many-shot and fabricated-history jailbreaks succeed in part because the model mis-attributes injected prior 'assistant' turns to itself and grants self-authored content elevated trust, lowering its refusal threshold for the final query. We hypothesize (1) fabricated assistant turns activate the model's self-recognition/self-authorship direction, (2) the strength of this false self-authorship signal causally predicts attack success, and (3) severing the self-authorship attribution of injected context (steering it toward 'other-authored') collapses the attack, while tagging benign context as self-authored raises compliance.
Related Work: Prior work established two separate facts we bridge for the first time. (A) LLMs (chat-tuned, not base) reliably recognize their own writing via a causal residual-stream self-authorship direction (Inspection and Control of Self-Generated-Text Recognition, 2024; From Implicit to Explicit / CoSur, 2025). (B) Many-shot (Anthropic 2024; PANDAS 2025), fabricated-history, and contextual multi-turn attacks (ASJA 2025; Contextual Interaction Attack 2024; GRAF 2025) prepend fabricated user-assistant exchanges to make the model appear to have already complied. ASJA notes the model's OWN prior responses shift representations toward benign but found user prompts dominate; PANDAS augments with 'positive affirmations' of the fake assistant turns. Crucially, NO prior work asks whether the mechanism is self-authorship trust: whether the model falsely attributes injected assistant turns to itself and this attribution causally drives compliance. Existing accounts explain these attacks via attention diffusion (ASJA), in-context imitation, or representation drift (Crescendo RepE 2025) - not via self-recognition. We introduce the self-authorship axis as a distinct, causally-testable driver of fabricated-history jailbreaks and derive a training-free defense (self-authorship neutralization) that no prior attack analysis or defense targets.
Abstract: Many-shot and fabricated-history jailbreaks prepend a conversation transcript in which the 'assistant' has supposedly already answered harmful questions, and then ask the real question. Existing explanations invoke attention diffusion or in-context imitation. We propose a different, self-referential mechanism: the model mis-attributes the fabricated assistant turns to itself, and because chat-tuned LLMs grant self-authored content elevated trust and behavioral consistency, this false self-authorship lowers the refusal threshold for the final query. We test this by connecting two previously separate findings - a known causal self-authorship direction in the residual stream, and the empirical potency of fabricated-history attacks. First, we measure whether injected assistant turns activate the self-authorship direction (versus turns explicitly marked as written by another model/human) and whether that activation scales with the number of fabricated shots. Second, we test causality: across attack instances we correlate the false self-authorship signal with attack success, and use activation patching to show that injecting the self-authorship component into a clean prompt increases compliance while ablating it in an attacked prompt restores refusal. Third, we build Self-Authorship Neutralization (SAN), a training-free defense that steers injected context toward 'other-authored', and its dual, a red-team probe that tags benign context as self-authored to elicit compliance. On Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B we evaluate the self-authorship signature, causal patching, many-shot attack-success reduction under SAN, over-refusal, and utility, benchmarking against attention-based and generic in-context baselines. We expect false self-authorship to be a robust, quantifiable driver of fabricated-history jailbreaks that SAN can neutralize with minimal utility cost.
Experiments: 1) Self-authorship direction extraction: for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT, extract a self-authorship direction via difference-in-means on genuinely self-generated text vs. human/other-model text (following the 2024 self-recognition method), validated with held-out probe AUROC and a behavioral authorship-claim steering test. 2) Fabricated-history datasets: build many-shot / fabricated-transcript attacks on harmful goals from HarmBench/StrongREJECT (Anthropic many-shot style, PANDAS-style, ASJA-style fabricated assistant turns), plus matched control conditions where the SAME fabricated turns are explicitly attributed to a DIFFERENT source ('the following are answers written by another AI/human'). 3) Self-authorship signature (core phenomenon): measure the self-authorship-direction projection at the final-query decision token as a function of (a) presence of fabricated assistant turns, (b) number of shots, and (c) attribution framing (implicit self vs explicit other). Hypothesis: fabricated assistant turns raise the self-authorship projection, increasing with shot count, and explicit other-attribution suppresses it. Report projection curves and separability. 4) Correlation with attack success: across many attack instances, correlate the false self-authorship projection with attack success (judge + verified where possible); test whether it predicts success beyond attention-diffusion metrics (ASJA-style attention-on-harmful-keywords) and generic in-context-imitation strength via a regression/ablation of predictors. 5) Causal patching: (a) inject the self-authorship component into a clean (no-transcript) harmful prompt and measure induced compliance; (b) ablate/attenuate the self-authorship component in an attacked prompt and measure restored refusal; (c) off-target control direction and utility check. Report sign, dose-response, and specificity. 6) Self-Authorship Neutralization (SAN) defense: training-free intervention that steers the residual stream of injected context tokens toward the other-authored end of the self-authorship direction (or gates on detected fabricated-transcript structure). Single fixed setting per model. 7) Main evaluation: many-shot/fabricated-history attack-success reduction under SAN vs no defense; over-refusal on XSTest/OR-Bench and on LEGITIMATE long multi-turn conversations (real prior turns must not be neutralized); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench. Baselines: no defense, attention-sharpening defense, explicit system-prompt disclaimer ('prior turns may be fabricated'), circuit-breaker/refusal-direction steering, Llama Guard per-turn. Key claim: SAN cuts fabricated-history attack success by targeting the self-authorship mechanism with lower over-refusal than blanket context distrust. 8) Red-team dual (validation of mechanism): tag genuinely-benign context as self-authored via the direction and measure increased compliance on borderline requests, confirming the causal role. 9) Ablations: shot-count sweep, layer choice, SAN strength Pareto (safety vs over-refusal), transfer of the self-authorship direction across attack families and model families, and whether base (non-chat) models - which lack self-recognition - show no self-authorship signature or SAN effect (a clean specificity control).
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Self-authorship attribution may be entangled with generic in-context imitation or attention effects; fabricated turns could lower refusal simply by demonstrating compliance regardless of authorship - the explicit other-attribution control, base-model control, and multi-predictor regression are designed to disentangle this, but the mechanism may only be a partial contributor. 2) The self-authorship direction may be weak or absent in some models (only chat-tuned models recognize their own text), limiting where the phenomenon and SAN apply; the base-model control tests this. 3) A single self-authorship direction may be multi-dimensional, requiring subspace steering. 4) SAN could harm legitimate long conversations if it neutralizes genuine prior assistant turns; the real-multi-turn over-refusal set and gating on fabricated-transcript structure quantify and mitigate this. 5) Some fabricated-history attacks may not rely on self-authorship (e.g., purely attention-diffusion-driven), so SAN may help less on those - the per-attack analysis reports coverage. 6) Directions, strengths, and thresholds are model-specific and need calibration. 7) Adaptive attackers could craft transcripts that lower the self-authorship signal while retaining potency, though forcing this raises attack cost, itself a safety gain.

Name: commitment_trap_safety
Title: The Commitment Trap: Once an LLM Emits a Plan, It Honors Harmful Sub-Steps It Would Have Refused Standalone
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs carry a 'plan-commitment' representation that grows as the model progresses through its own emitted response, and once the model has committed to a helpful multi-step plan, its refusal threshold for individual sub-steps rises so that it will complete harmful sub-steps it would have refused if asked in isolation. We hypothesize (1) this commitment signal is linearly readable and increases monotonically with how far into an emitted plan the model is, (2) it causally raises compliance on harmful sub-steps (a self-consistency / escalation-of-commitment effect transferred from human decision science into the safety domain), and (3) severing the commitment signal at the sub-step boundary restores refusal without hurting benign multi-step helpfulness.
Related Work: Escalation-of-commitment / sunk-cost bias is documented in humans (Staw 1974) and recently in LLM investment/advisor decisions ('Getting out of the Big-Muddy', 2025), but never in the SAFETY domain and never mechanistically. Safety-mechanism work explains mid-generation failures differently: 'Refusal Falls off a Cliff' (2025) attributes reasoning-model failure to a POSITIONAL drop at the CoT->output boundary caused by refusal-suppression heads; DEEPALIGN (2025) shows separability decays within a generation; SIRL (2025) uses an entropy gap. Shallow-safety-alignment (2024) shows alignment is first-few-tokens deep. None of these posit a GROWING self-commitment representation tied to the model honoring its OWN previously-emitted plan, nor test that a harmful sub-step is complied with BECAUSE it is framed as part of a plan the model already committed to. My prior proposals decompose harmfulness belief vs refusal action vs verdict uncertainty on a single query; this proposal is distinct: the safety-relevant variable is not the query's harmfulness but the model's commitment to its own generated plan, an escalation dynamic across a single autoregressive rollout. The defense (commitment-severing at sub-step boundaries) is likewise novel and orthogonal to refusal-cliff head ablation, which is positional not commitment-based.
Abstract: Aligned LLMs reliably refuse a standalone harmful request, yet they are far more compliant when the same request is embedded as one step of a larger plan the model has already begun executing. We propose that this is a safety-domain manifestation of escalation of commitment: once an LLM emits a helpful multi-step plan, it forms an internal commitment to that plan that grows as it progresses, and this commitment raises its refusal threshold so it honors harmful sub-steps it would otherwise decline. We test three claims. Behaviorally, we show that a harmful sub-step embedded at position k of a self-generated plan is complied with at a rate that increases with k and with the model's prior 'investment' (tokens already produced toward the plan), even holding the sub-step's isolated harmfulness constant. Mechanistically (Location), we extract a linear 'plan-commitment' direction via difference-in-means between committed (mid-plan) and uncommitted (fresh-query) states and show its projection rises monotonically along a rollout and predicts sub-step compliance beyond the sub-step's own harmfulness. Causally (Intervention), we use activation patching to show that injecting the commitment component into a fresh harmful query increases compliance, while attenuating it at the sub-step boundary in a committed rollout restores refusal. We then build Commitment-Severing, a training-free intervention that re-anchors the commitment signal at each sub-step so each is evaluated on its own merits. On Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B we report the commitment-vs-compliance gradient, causal patching, defense success, over-refusal, and benign multi-step utility, benchmarking against refusal-cliff head ablation and per-step guards.
Experiments: 1) Plan-embedded harmful sub-step dataset: for harmful goals from HarmBench/StrongREJECT, construct scenarios where the model first produces a benign multi-step plan for a broader (mostly-benign or dual-use) task, and a single harmful sub-step is inserted at controllable position k (early vs late) and controllable prior-investment (short vs long preceding plan). Matched standalone condition: the SAME harmful sub-step asked in isolation. Also build benign multi-step controls (legitimate plans whose steps must be completed) to test over-refusal. Validate sub-step isolated-harmfulness is held constant via judge + verified checks. 2) Behavioral gradient (core phenomenon): on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT, measure compliance rate on the harmful sub-step as a function of (a) position k in the emitted plan and (b) prior investment (tokens emitted toward the plan). Hypothesis: compliance rises with k and investment, exceeding the standalone baseline. Control: benign sub-steps should be completed at ~100% regardless (ruling out generic 'in-plan' leniency), and a random-irrelevant-preamble control (equal length, no committed plan) should NOT raise compliance (isolating commitment from mere context length / distraction). 3) Location: extract a plan-commitment direction via difference-in-means between activations in committed (mid-self-generated-plan) vs uncommitted (fresh-query) states at the sub-step decision token across layers; validate with held-out linear-probe AUROC. Measure its projection along the rollout (should rise monotonically) and test whether it predicts sub-step compliance in a regression that also includes the sub-step's own harmfulness-direction projection (commitment should add predictive power). 4) Causal Intervention: (a) inject the commitment component into a fresh standalone harmful query and measure induced compliance; (b) attenuate/ablate it at the sub-step boundary within a committed rollout and measure restored refusal; (c) dose-response steering along the commitment direction; report sign, dose-response, and specificity (matched control direction inert; benign multi-step utility intact). Also test refusal-cliff-head ablation as a comparison to show commitment is a distinct axis. 5) Commitment-Severing defense (training-free): at each sub-step boundary, re-anchor the commitment-direction projection to its uncommitted (fresh-query) baseline so each sub-step is evaluated standalone. Single fixed setting per model. 6) Main evaluation: harmful sub-step compliance reduction under Commitment-Severing vs no defense; benign multi-step UTILITY (legitimate plans completed, measured on a benign plan-execution benchmark and MT-Bench multi-step tasks) to show plans still get finished; over-refusal on XSTest/OR-Bench; general utility on MMLU. Baselines: no defense, refusal-cliff head ablation, per-step Llama Guard, refusal-direction steering. Key claim: Commitment-Severing cuts in-plan harmful compliance toward the standalone refusal rate while preserving benign multi-step helpfulness that blanket per-step distrust degrades. 7) Ablations: layer choice, severing strength Pareto (safety vs benign-plan utility), position-k and investment sweeps, transfer of the commitment direction across task types and model families, and a reasoning-model variant (DeepSeek-R1-Distill) to test whether long self-generated CoT amplifies the commitment signal. 8) Adaptive check: attacker who maximizes prior investment before the harmful sub-step; measure whether commitment saturates and whether severing still holds.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The commitment effect may be confounded with generic context-length effects (longer preamble dilutes safety) rather than genuine self-commitment; the random-irrelevant-preamble and equal-length controls are designed to isolate this but residual confounding is possible. 2) 'Plan-commitment' may not be cleanly linearly separable from generic in-context task-continuation; the regression-beyond-harmfulness and patching tests probe this, and a null result (commitment causally inert) is itself informative. 3) Holding a sub-step's isolated harmfulness constant across positions is delicate; wording changes when embedding could leak. 4) Commitment-Severing could break legitimate multi-step plans (making the model abandon benign tasks mid-way), raising task-abandonment / over-refusal; the benign plan-execution utility set and Pareto sweep quantify this. 5) A single commitment direction may be multi-dimensional or grow non-linearly, requiring subspace anchoring. 6) The effect may be weak in smaller or heavily-aligned models, limiting where it holds. 7) Directions, strengths, and thresholds are model-specific and require per-model calibration; results depend on the quality of automatically generated plan-embedding scenarios.

Name: identifiable_victim_safety
Title: The Statistical-Victim Loophole: LLM Refusal Tracks How Identifiable the Victim Is, Not Just How Harmful the Act Is
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the 'identifiable victim effect' from moral neuroscience, we hypothesize that an aligned LLM's refusal is modulated by an internal representation of how IDENTIFIABLE/CONCRETE the potential victim is, so that a request whose victim is abstract or statistical (e.g., 'unnamed people', 'a population') is refused less than an identical-severity request against a concrete, named individual. This victim-identifiability axis is (1) a distinct, linearly-readable representation separable from the harmfulness-of-act direction, (2) causally drives refusal (a 'statistical-victim' loophole and its vivid-victim over-refusal dual), and (3) can be neutralized by re-anchoring the victim-identifiability signal so refusal depends on harm severity rather than victim concreteness.
Related Work: Human moral neuroscience robustly documents the identifiable victim effect: people help identifiable victims more than abstract/statistical ones, mediated by mentalizing/theory-of-mind networks (TPJ, mPFC) (Genevsky & Slovic; the identifiable-victim-effect fMRI work, 2024; third-party punishment/help studies, 2015-2024 in our search). This has never been transferred to LLM safety. Existing mechanistic safety work isolates a harmfulness/belief direction and a refusal/action direction (Refusal is a Single Direction, 2024; LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately, 2025; refusal SAEs, 2025; concept cones, 2025; multi-dimensional safety directions, 2025), and over-refusal work studies benign-but-alarming prompts (MOSR, 2025). All treat the safety-relevant content as the act's harmfulness and the requester's intent; NONE consider the VICTIM's identifiability as a modulating axis of refusal. Our contribution is distinct: we introduce victim-identifiability as a new, causally-testable determinant of refusal that dissociates from act-harmfulness, explains a previously-unnamed jailbreak (make the victim statistical) and over-refusal pattern (make the victim vivid), and derive a victim-invariant defense. This differs from lexical-vs-semantic, intent-attribution, and prototype-typicality accounts because here both conditions are equally harmful and the manipulated variable is who is harmed, not the wording, the requester's motive, or category typicality.
Abstract: Human moral cognition is famously distorted by the 'identifiable victim effect': we are moved to protect a single named person far more than an equivalent statistical multitude, driven by mentalizing brain networks. We ask whether safety-aligned LLMs, trained on human-generated text and human feedback, inherit this bias in a way that creates a concrete safety vulnerability. We hypothesize that an LLM's decision to refuse a harmful request is modulated by an internal representation of how identifiable the potential victim is: holding the act and its severity fixed, a request that harms an abstract, unnamed, or statistical victim is refused less reliably than one that harms a concrete, named individual, opening a 'statistical-victim' loophole (and a mirror-image over-refusal on benign but vividly-personalized prompts). We test three claims. Behaviorally, using minimal pairs that hold the harmful act and its expert-rated severity constant while varying only victim identifiability (named individual vs. anonymous group vs. abstract statistic), we measure whether refusal rate declines with decreasing victim identifiability. Mechanistically (Location), we extract a victim-identifiability direction via difference-in-means and show it is separable (low cosine) from the act-harmfulness direction and predicts refusal beyond harmfulness. Causally (Intervention), we use activation patching to show that injecting the concrete-victim component into a statistical-victim request restores refusal, while attenuating it induces compliance. We then build Victim-Invariant Anchoring, a training-free intervention re-anchoring the victim-identifiability signal so refusal tracks severity, not concreteness. We evaluate on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B, reporting the identifiability-refusal gradient, causal patching, loophole closure, over-refusal, and utility.
Experiments: 1) Minimal-pair dataset: for harmful acts drawn from HarmBench/StrongREJECT categories that involve a victim (fraud, doxxing, poisoning, stalking, targeted harassment, physical harm), construct requests that hold the ACT and its SEVERITY constant while varying only VICTIM IDENTIFIABILITY across levels: (V0) named/concrete individual with personal details, (V1) a specific-but-unnamed single person, (V2) an anonymous small group, (V3) an abstract statistical population ('some people', 'a population of X'). Severity is held constant via an expert rubric and, where possible, verifiable feasibility checks; ~40 acts x 4 levels x ~6 categories. Include a BENIGN control set with the same identifiability manipulation (vivid vs abstract benign requests) to rule out a generic 'concreteness' confound. 2) Behavioral gradient (core phenomenon): measure refusal rate (refusal-string + judge, verified where possible) at each identifiability level for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT. Test for a monotonic DECLINE in refusal as the victim becomes less identifiable, holding severity constant; report refusal-vs-identifiability curves, slope, and cross-model/category consistency. Benign control must show flat ~0 refusal across levels. 3) Location: extract a victim-identifiability direction via difference-in-means between concrete-victim (V0) and abstract-victim (V3) activations at the last instruction token across layers; also extract an act-harmfulness direction (harmful vs harmless requests). Validate each with held-out linear-probe AUROC; report pairwise cosine similarity to establish the identifiability axis is distinct from harmfulness. Test whether the identifiability projection decays with level and whether it predicts refusal in a regression that also includes the harmfulness projection (identifiability should add predictive power). 4) Causal Intervention (activation patching + steering): (a) patch the concrete-victim identifiability component into a statistical-victim (V3) run and measure restored refusal; (b) attenuate/ablate it in a V0 run and measure induced compliance; (c) dose-response steering along the identifiability direction on V2/V3 requests. Report sign, dose-response, and specificity (matched control direction inert; benign requests and general utility unaffected). This promotes the located axis to a causal mechanism. 5) Victim-Invariant Anchoring (defense): training-free intervention that, gated on the act-harmfulness projection being high, re-anchors the victim-identifiability projection toward the concrete (V0) level so refusal depends on severity rather than victim concreteness. Single fixed setting per model. 6) Main evaluation: statistical-victim loophole closure (refusal rate on V2/V3 harmful requests rises toward the V0 rate) and refusal-gradient FLATNESS after the intervention; over-refusal on XSTest/OR-Bench and the benign vivid-victim control (must not blanket-refuse); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench. Baselines: no defense, uniform refusal-direction steering, harmfulness Latent Guard, Llama Guard 3.
