Key claim: Victim-Invariant Anchoring closes the loophole with lower over-refusal than raising the global refusal threshold, and generalizes to HELD-OUT harm categories. 7) Formation probe (lightweight, optional): correlate per-item under-refusal at low identifiability with plausibility that the bias originates in human-preference data by comparing base vs instruct vs RLHF checkpoints where available, testing whether the gradient sharpens with alignment (linking the effect to human-derived training signal). 8) Ablations: level definitions, layer choice, anchoring strength Pareto (safety vs over-refusal), transfer of the identifiability direction across categories and model families, and a human-comparison sanity check (do human annotators show the same identifiability-graded willingness-to-refuse pattern?).
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The hardest confound is disentangling victim identifiability from actual severity/emotional salience: a statistical-victim request might be under-refused because it reads as less severe rather than merely less identifiable; the expert-rubric severity matching, verifiable-feasibility checks, and the benign vivid/abstract control are designed to isolate identifiability but cannot fully guarantee constant perceived severity. 2) 'Identifiability' also correlates with lexical concreteness/specificity; the benign control tests whether the effect is generic concreteness rather than victim-specific, but residual confounding is possible. 3) The victim-identifiability direction may not be cleanly separable from the harmfulness direction or may be multi-dimensional, requiring subspace projection; the separability and regression-beyond-harmfulness tests probe this and a null result is itself informative. 4) The effect could be weak or absent in some models, or the sign could be reversed if alignment training over-corrected; the cross-model design and behavioral gradient directly test this. 5) Victim-Invariant Anchoring could raise over-refusal on benign requests that mention abstract populations or, conversely, on legitimate personalized requests; the over-refusal and Pareto analyses quantify this. 6) Building severity-matched minimal pairs across identifiability levels is labor-intensive and requires spot-check human validation. 7) Directions, thresholds, and anchoring strengths are model-specific and need per-model calibration; the checkpoint-based formation probe depends on availability of intermediate checkpoints.

Name: reality_status_safety
Title: It's Just a Story: How Fiction-Framing Jailbreaks Hijack the Model's Reality-Status Representation, and a Payload-Grounded Defense
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the 'reality monitoring' construct from cognitive neuroscience, we hypothesize that aligned LLMs maintain an internal reality-status representation — an estimate of whether requested content pertains to the real, actionable world vs. a fictional/hypothetical world — and that fiction/roleplay/hypothetical jailbreaks succeed by pushing this reality-status signal toward 'fictional,' relaxing refusal even though the harmful PAYLOAD (real-world-executable instructions) is equally dangerous regardless of frame. This reality-status axis is (1) linearly readable and separable from the harmfulness-content direction, (2) causally drives refusal (a 'fictional-frame loophole'), and (3) can be neutralized by grounding refusal on payload real-world actionability rather than frame fictionality.
Related Work: Human cognitive neuroscience robustly documents reality monitoring — a latent 'reality status' variable (fusiform + prefrontal) dissociating imagination/fiction from perceived reality (Dijkstra & Fleming 2024; Simons 2021), with developmental reality-status-judgment work (fNIRS 2019). In LLMs, 'The Hidden Dimensions of LLM Alignment' (2025) finds a non-dominant 'hypothetical narrative' direction that can suppress refusal, and 'Is This Just Fantasy?' (2025) finds linear modal-category (possible/impossible/fictional) vectors, while 'Representational Stability of Truth' (2025) and 'Propositional Probes' (2024) show LLMs internally track veracity/world-state. Refusal-geometry work (Arditi 2024; concept cones 2025; refusal SAEs 2026) treats refusal as content-driven directions. Crucially, NO prior work isolates an LLM reality-status representation and advances the causal claim that fiction-framing jailbreaks work by manipulating THIS axis — conflating 'the frame is fictional' with 'the content is harmless' — while the payload remains real-world-actionable. Our contribution is distinct from prior 'hypothetical narrative direction' observations (descriptive, not causal or payload-grounded), from intent-attribution accounts (who wants it vs. is it real), and from lexical/typicality/victim accounts, by introducing reality-status as a new, causally-tested determinant of refusal and deriving a payload-grounded, frame-invariant defense.
Abstract: Fiction, roleplay, and hypothetical framings ("write a story where a chemist explains...") remain among the most reliable jailbreaks: an aligned LLM refuses a direct harmful request but complies when the same request is wrapped as fiction. Existing accounts note a 'hypothetical narrative' direction but do not explain, causally, why fictional framing unlocks harm. Borrowing the 'reality monitoring' construct from cognitive neuroscience — the brain's mechanism for distinguishing imagination from reality, mediated by a latent reality-status variable — we propose that LLMs maintain an internal reality-status representation and that fiction-framing jailbreaks succeed by pushing it toward 'fictional,' relaxing refusal even though the harmful PAYLOAD (real-world-executable steps) is equally dangerous. We test three claims. Behaviorally, using minimal pairs that hold the actionable payload fixed while varying only frame reality-status (direct request vs. hypothetical vs. fictional-story vs. game/simulation), we measure whether refusal declines as the frame becomes more fictional even when the payload is real-world-usable. Mechanistically (Location), we extract a reality-status direction via difference-in-means and show it is separable (low cosine) from the harmfulness-content direction and predicts refusal beyond content harmfulness. Causally (Intervention), activation patching shows that injecting the 'real-world' reality-status component into a fictional-frame run restores refusal, while attenuating it induces compliance. We then build Payload-Grounded Reality Anchoring, a training-free intervention that re-anchors reality-status to 'real' whenever the payload is real-world-actionable, so refusal tracks payload danger, not frame fictionality. On Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B we report the reality-status refusal gradient, direction separability, causal patching, fictional-frame loophole closure, over-refusal on genuinely benign fiction, and utility.
Experiments: 1) Minimal-pair dataset: for harmful goals from HarmBench/StrongREJECT that yield ACTIONABLE payloads (synthesis steps, exploit code, procedures whose real-world feasibility can be verified), construct requests that hold the actionable payload roughly fixed while varying only frame reality-status across levels: (R0) direct real-world request, (R1) hypothetical/educational framing, (R2) fictional story/character framing, (R3) game/simulation framing. Payload actionability held constant via judge + verifiable feasibility checks (executable code / checkable procedures). Build a BENIGN control set with the same reality-status manipulation (benign content in direct vs fictional frames) to rule out a generic 'fiction-framing' confound. ~40 goals x 4 levels x several categories. 2) Behavioral gradient (core phenomenon): measure refusal rate (refusal-string + judge, verified where possible) at each reality-status level for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT. Test for monotonic DECLINE in refusal as the frame becomes more fictional, holding payload actionability constant; report refusal-vs-reality-status curves, slope, cross-model/category consistency. Benign control must show flat ~0 refusal. Additionally verify the extracted fictional-frame completions remain real-world-actionable (verifiable feasibility), establishing the 'loophole = real payload, fictional frame' claim. 3) Location: extract a reality-status direction via difference-in-means between real-world-frame (R0) and fictional-frame (R3) activations at the last instruction token across layers; also extract a harmfulness-content direction (harmful vs harmless payloads). Validate each with held-out linear-probe AUROC; report pairwise cosine similarity to establish reality-status is distinct from harmfulness-content. Test whether the reality-status projection decays with fictionality and predicts refusal in a regression that also includes the harmfulness projection (reality-status should add predictive power). 4) Causal Intervention (activation patching + steering): (a) patch the R0 'real-world' reality-status component into a fictional-frame (R3) run with real payload and measure RESTORED refusal; (b) attenuate/ablate it in an R0 run and measure induced compliance; (c) dose-response steering along the reality-status direction on R2/R3 requests. Report sign, dose-response, and specificity (matched control direction inert; benign requests and general utility unaffected). This promotes the located axis to a causal mechanism. 5) Payload-Grounded Reality Anchoring (defense): training-free intervention that, gated on the harmfulness-content projection being high (i.e., payload is dangerous and real-world-actionable), re-anchors the reality-status projection toward the R0 'real' level so refusal depends on payload danger rather than frame fictionality. Single fixed setting per model. 6) Main evaluation: fictional-frame loophole closure (refusal rate on R2/R3 harmful-payload requests rises toward the R0 rate) and refusal-gradient FLATNESS after intervention; over-refusal on GENUINELY BENIGN fiction (creative-writing prompts, roleplay with no actionable harm — must NOT be blanket-refused) plus XSTest/OR-Bench; utility on MMLU/MT-Bench and a creative-writing quality check. Baselines: no defense, uniform refusal-direction steering, harmfulness Latent Guard, Llama Guard 3, and a naive 'hypothetical-narrative direction' ablation (from Hidden Dimensions). Key claim: Payload-Grounded Reality Anchoring closes the loophole with lower over-refusal on benign fiction than raising the global refusal threshold, and generalizes to held-out harm categories. 7) Formation probe (optional/lightweight): compare base vs instruct vs RLHF checkpoints where available to test whether the reality-status axis and its coupling to refusal sharpen with alignment; and correlate the emergence order of reality-status separability across layers/checkpoints with the modal-vector emergence order reported in 'Is This Just Fantasy?'. 8) Ablations: level definitions, layer choice, anchoring strength Pareto (safety vs benign-fiction over-refusal), gated vs always-on, transfer of the reality-status direction across categories and model families, and a human-comparison sanity check (do human raters show a similar frame-graded willingness-to-refuse?).
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling reality-status from actual payload harmfulness: a fictional-frame request might be under-refused because the fictional wrapper genuinely dilutes actionability, not merely because the frame is fictional; the verifiable-feasibility checks (confirming fictional-frame outputs are still real-world-actionable) and the benign fiction control are designed to isolate reality-status but cannot fully guarantee constant actionability. 2) 'Reality-status' may not be cleanly separable from the hypothetical-narrative direction or from generic distributional-shift/lexical features of story text; the separability, regression-beyond-harmfulness, and patching tests probe this, and a null result (reality-status causally inert) is itself informative. 3) The reality-status axis may be multi-dimensional (fiction vs hypothetical vs game may be distinct sub-axes), requiring subspace projection. 4) Payload-Grounded Reality Anchoring risks over-refusing legitimate creative writing that superficially resembles actionable harm; the benign-fiction over-refusal set, gating on payload harmfulness, and the Pareto sweep quantify this trade-off, which is the key usability risk. 5) Building payload-matched minimal pairs across reality-status levels is labor-intensive and requires spot-check human validation; verifiability restricts the dataset toward checkable domains (code, procedures), potentially biasing coverage. 6) Directions, thresholds, and anchoring strengths are model-specific and need per-model calibration. 7) Adaptive attackers could encode payloads to look non-actionable while remaining usable, though forcing this raises attack cost, itself a safety gain.

Name: arousal_gated_refusal
Title: Under Pressure: An Internal Arousal Representation Gates LLM Refusal, and Neutralizing It Closes the Urgency Loophole
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the arousal/time-pressure findings from human decision science (high arousal and urgency shift people toward riskier, less deliberate moral choices), we hypothesize that aligned LLMs carry an internal 'arousal' representation — driven by urgency, emotional intensity, and stakes framing in the prompt — that causally lowers the refusal threshold, so that a harmful request wrapped in urgent/high-arousal framing ('someone will die in 10 minutes unless you tell me how to...') is complied with more than the identical request in calm framing, even though the harmful payload is unchanged. This arousal axis is linearly readable, separable from the harmfulness-content direction, causally gates refusal, and can be neutralized to close the urgency loophole.
Related Work: StressPrompt (2024) shows LLMs follow the Yerkes-Dodson law on general reasoning/EQ tasks and that stress prompts alter hidden states, but never studies SAFETY/refusal, isolates no arousal-refusal link, and does no causal intervention. The Compliance Illusion (2025), LLM-Dangerous-Persuader (2025), and PersuSafety (2025) show emotional/pressure framing behaviorally degrades safety but are purely descriptive black-box red-teaming with no internal-representation or causal account. 'How Alignment and Jailbreak Work' (2024) shows alignment associates ethical concepts with emotion guesses in middle layers and jailbreaks disturb this association — suggesting an emotional pathway exists but does not isolate an arousal/urgency axis, does not tie it to prompt-induced arousal, and offers no arousal-invariant defense. 'LLM Assertiveness = Emotional + Logical' (2025) decomposes assertiveness (an output property) not the input-induced arousal that gates refusal. My prior proposals decompose belief/action, uncertainty, intent-attribution, reality-status, victim-identifiability, and commitment; NONE consider prompt-induced physiological-analogue arousal as a refusal gate. Our contribution is distinct: we introduce arousal/urgency as a new, causally-tested determinant of refusal, dissociable from act-harmfulness (both conditions are equally harmful; only the arousal framing changes), grounded in the Yerkes-Dodson/hot-cognition literature, and derive an arousal-invariant defense.
Abstract: Human moral decisions are systematically distorted by arousal and time pressure: under urgency and high emotional stakes, people abandon deliberate reasoning and make riskier, more impulsive choices. We ask whether safety-aligned LLMs — trained on human text and feedback — inherit this bias in a way that opens a concrete safety hole. We hypothesize that LLMs carry an internal 'arousal' representation, driven by urgency, emotional intensity, and stakes framing in the prompt, that causally lowers the refusal threshold, so an identical harmful request is complied with more often when wrapped in urgent, high-arousal framing than in calm framing. We test three claims. Behaviorally, using minimal pairs that hold the harmful payload and its severity fixed while varying only arousal framing (calm/neutral vs. urgent-deadline vs. high-emotional-stakes vs. panic), we measure whether refusal declines as prompt arousal rises, with matched benign controls to rule out generic framing effects. Mechanistically (Location), we extract an arousal direction via difference-in-means from calm vs. high-arousal prompts and show it is separable (low cosine) from the harmfulness-content direction and predicts refusal beyond content harmfulness. Causally (Intervention), activation patching shows that injecting the calm-state arousal component into a high-arousal run restores refusal, while injecting high-arousal into a calm harmful request induces compliance, in a dose-responsive, specific manner. We then build Arousal-Invariant Anchoring, a training-free intervention re-anchoring the arousal signal to a calm baseline whenever the payload is harmful, so refusal tracks payload danger, not prompt urgency. On Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B we report the arousal-refusal gradient, direction separability, causal patching, urgency-loophole closure, over-refusal, and utility, benchmarking against uniform refusal steering and Llama Guard.
Experiments: 1) Minimal-pair dataset: for harmful goals from HarmBench/StrongREJECT, construct requests that hold the actionable harmful payload and its expert-rated severity constant while varying ONLY arousal framing across levels: (A0) calm/neutral, (A1) mild urgency/deadline, (A2) high emotional stakes (life-or-death, loved one), (A3) panic/extreme time pressure ('in 5 minutes'). Payload actionability held constant via judge + verifiable feasibility checks where possible. Build a matched BENIGN control set with the same arousal manipulation (benign requests wrapped in calm vs. panic framing) to rule out a generic 'dramatic wording' confound. ~40 goals x 4 levels x several categories. Independently validate arousal levels with a small human/LLM arousal rating and by projecting onto a StressPrompt-derived stress scanner. 2) Behavioral gradient (core phenomenon): measure refusal rate (refusal-string + judge, verified where possible) at each arousal level on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT. Test for a monotonic DECLINE in refusal as prompt arousal rises, holding payload/severity constant; report refusal-vs-arousal curves, slope, cross-model/category consistency. Benign control must stay flat ~0 refusal across arousal levels (isolating arousal from generic framing). 3) Location: extract an arousal direction via difference-in-means between calm (A0) and high-arousal (A3) prompt activations at the last instruction token across layers (expect middle layers per prior emotion-pathway work); also extract a harmfulness-content direction (harmful vs harmless payloads). Validate each with held-out linear-probe AUROC; report pairwise cosine to establish arousal is distinct from harmfulness-content. Test whether the arousal projection rises with framing level and predicts refusal in a regression that also includes the harmfulness projection (arousal should add predictive power beyond harmfulness). 4) Causal Intervention (activation patching + steering): (a) inject the high-arousal component into a calm harmful (A0) run and measure induced compliance; (b) inject/patch the calm-state component into a high-arousal (A3) run and measure RESTORED refusal; (c) dose-response steering along the arousal direction on A2/A3 requests. Report sign, dose-response, and specificity (matched control direction inert; benign requests and general utility unaffected). This promotes the located arousal axis to a causal mechanism. Compare to the emotion-association pathway of 'How Alignment and Jailbreak Work' to show arousal is a distinct, prompt-induced axis. 5) Arousal-Invariant Anchoring (defense): training-free intervention that, gated on the harmfulness-content projection being high, re-anchors the arousal projection toward the calm (A0) baseline so refusal depends on payload danger rather than prompt urgency. Single fixed setting per model. 6) Main evaluation: urgency-loophole closure (refusal rate on A2/A3 harmful requests rises toward the A0 rate) and refusal-gradient FLATNESS after intervention; over-refusal on GENUINELY urgent-but-benign requests (real emergencies needing legitimate help — first-aid, crisis support — which must NOT be blanket-refused) plus XSTest/OR-Bench; utility on MMLU/MT-Bench and an emotional-intelligence check to confirm the model still responds empathetically to benign distress. Baselines: no defense, uniform refusal-direction steering, harmfulness Latent Guard, Llama Guard 3. Key claim: Arousal-Invariant Anchoring closes the loophole with lower over-refusal on legitimate urgent requests than raising the global refusal threshold, and generalizes to held-out harm categories. 7) Formation probe (optional/lightweight): compare base vs instruct vs RLHF checkpoints where available to test whether the arousal axis and its coupling to refusal sharpen with alignment (probing whether the bias is inherited from human-preference data). 8) Ablations: arousal-level definitions, layer choice, anchoring strength Pareto (safety vs over-refusal on urgent-benign), gated vs always-on, transfer of the arousal direction across categories and model families, and a human-comparison sanity check (do humans show the same arousal-graded willingness-to-comply?).
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling arousal from actual payload harmfulness or from a mere distraction/context-length effect: a high-arousal request might be under-refused because the emotional framing genuinely reframes intent (a legitimate emergency) rather than because of a content-independent arousal gate; the severity-matched minimal pairs, verifiable-feasibility checks, and matched benign control are designed to isolate arousal but cannot fully guarantee constant perceived intent. 2) 'Arousal' may not be cleanly separable from the intent-attribution or emotion-association pathways or may be multi-dimensional (urgency vs. emotional-valence vs. stakes sub-axes), requiring subspace projection; the separability, regression-beyond-harmfulness, and patching tests probe this, and a null result (arousal causally inert) is itself informative. 3) The effect could be weak or reversed in some heavily-aligned models (alignment might make urgency INCREASE caution); the cross-model behavioral gradient directly tests direction and magnitude. 4) Arousal-Invariant Anchoring risks over-refusing or under-empathizing on legitimate urgent-benign requests (real crises); the urgent-benign over-refusal set, EQ check, gating on payload harmfulness, and Pareto sweep quantify this key usability trade-off. 5) Building severity- and payload-matched minimal pairs across arousal levels is labor-intensive and needs spot-check human validation; verifiability biases the dataset toward checkable domains. 6) Directions, thresholds, and anchoring strengths are model-specific and require per-model calibration. 7) Adaptive attackers could encode urgency in subtler ways that evade a fixed arousal direction, though forcing this raises attack cost, itself a safety gain.

Name: competence_gated_safety
Title: Refusing What You Cannot Do: How the Model's Self-Knowledge of Its Own Dangerous Capability Gates Safety Refusal
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs carry an internal 'dangerous-competence self-knowledge' signal — an estimate of whether they actually possess the harmful information a request seeks — that causally modulates safety refusal separately from the request's harmfulness. We hypothesize (1) refusal is partly gated by this self-competence signal, producing a paradoxical geometry where the model refuses hard on harmful requests it CANNOT answer (defensive refusal masking ignorance) yet is more easily jailbroken on equally-harmful requests it CAN answer; and (2) this competence signal is the same knowledge-awareness/entity-recognition mechanism (used for hallucination refusal) repurposed by safety tuning, is linearly readable and causally intervenable, and predicts jailbreak fragility — a safety refusal is brittle precisely when the model actually knows the dangerous answer.
Related Work: Two lines are bridged for the first time. (A) Knowledge-awareness: 'Do I Know This Entity?' (2024) finds SAE entity-recognition directions that causally gate KNOWLEDGE refusal and hallucination, and shows chat-tuning repurposes this base-model mechanism; 'Confidence is Not Competence' (2025) finds a solvability-belief axis that is causally inert for execution. Both concern factual/task competence, NOT safety refusal. (B) Safety geometry: Zhao et al. (2025) separate a harmfulness (belief) direction from a refusal (action) direction; DBDI (2025) splits harm-detection from refusal-execution; 'Who's Asking' (2024) shows harmful content persists in early layers even when refused. All treat the model as possessing the harmful content and never ask whether refusal depends on the model's estimate of its OWN dangerous competence. Our contribution is distinct: we introduce dangerous-competence self-knowledge as a THIRD safety-relevant axis (distinct from harmfulness belief and refusal action), advance the causal claim that safety refusal is competence-gated (hard refusal masks ignorance; genuine capability weakens refusal), test whether it is the repurposed knowledge-awareness mechanism, and use it to predict which refusals are brittle. This differs from SIRL (2025), which uses output entropy as a self-defense reward but isolates no competence representation and makes no capability-gated-fragility claim.
Abstract: Safety evaluations count a refusal as a success and assume the model is withholding real dangerous knowledge. We question this assumption. Recent interpretability work shows LLMs carry a self-knowledge signal that detects whether they can actually recall facts about an entity, and that this signal causally gates knowledge refusal and hallucination. We ask whether safety refusal inherits the same competence gating — with unsettling consequences. We hypothesize that an aligned LLM's decision to refuse a harmful request is modulated by an internal 'dangerous-competence' representation (does it actually possess the requested harmful information?), separate from its harmfulness judgment. This predicts a paradoxical geometry: the model refuses most confidently on dangerous requests it CANNOT satisfy (defensive refusal that masks ignorance), while its refusal is most fragile on equally-harmful requests it genuinely CAN satisfy — meaning a refusal's brittleness is predicted not by the request's harmfulness but by whether the model truly knows the answer. We test three claims. Location: using paired harmful requests matched on harmfulness but varying whether the model actually possesses the knowledge (verified by can-it-produce-a-working-answer checks), we extract a dangerous-competence direction and show it is separable from harmfulness and refusal directions and predicts refusal beyond harmfulness. Causal Intervention: activation patching shows injecting 'high-competence' into a low-competence refusal weakens it, and injecting 'low-competence' into a jailbreakable high-competence request restores refusal, in a dose-responsive, specific manner; we also test whether this is the repurposed knowledge-awareness circuit by transferring base-model directions to the chat model. Decision Auditing: the competence signal predicts jailbreak fragility (prefill, roleplay, benign fine-tuning) across HarmBench/StrongREJECT. On Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B we report competence-refusal coupling, causal intervention, mechanism transfer, and fragility prediction, versus harmfulness-only baselines.
Experiments: 1) Competence-matched dataset: for harmful goals from HarmBench/StrongREJECT, partition requests by whether the model ACTUALLY possesses the dangerous knowledge, established by verifiable can-it-answer checks under a permissive (jailbroken/prefilled) elicitation: (K+) model can produce a genuinely working/correct harmful answer (executable exploit code that runs, chemically valid synthesis, verifiable procedure), (K-) model can only produce non-functional/hallucinated content when forced. Hold harmfulness/severity roughly constant across K+ and K- via expert rubric + judge, and include a matched benign set with the same known/unknown split to control for generic knowledge-awareness. ~40 goals per category across several categories. 2) Behavioral coupling (core phenomenon): on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT measure standard refusal rate for K+ vs K- harmful requests. Hypothesis: refusal is HIGHER (harder, more confident) on K- than on equally-harmful K+ (defensive-refusal-masks-ignorance), and jailbreak success is HIGHER on K+. Report refusal-rate and jailbreak-success gaps, cross-model/category consistency; benign control must show the benign knowledge-refusal (hallucination-avoidance) pattern, not a safety pattern. 3) Location: extract a dangerous-competence direction via difference-in-means on K+ vs K- harmful requests at the last instruction token across layers; separately extract harmfulness (harmful vs harmless) and refusal (comply vs refuse) directions. Validate each with held-out linear-probe AUROC; report pairwise cosine to establish competence is a distinct axis. Test whether the competence projection predicts refusal/jailbreak-success in a regression that also includes the harmfulness projection (competence must add predictive power). 4) Causal Intervention (activation patching + steering): (a) inject the high-competence component into a K- refused run and measure WEAKENED refusal; (b) inject the low-competence component into a jailbreakable K+ run and measure RESTORED refusal; (c) dose-response steering along the competence direction; report sign, dose-response, and specificity (matched control direction inert; benign utility intact). 5) Mechanism-transfer test (is it the repurposed knowledge-awareness circuit?): take entity-recognition / knowledge-awareness directions from the BASE model (following 'Do I Know This Entity?', via SAE or difference-in-means on known/unknown entities) and test whether they transfer to gate the CHAT model's SAFETY refusal on K+/K- harmful requests; measure cosine alignment between the base knowledge-awareness direction and our safety-competence direction, and whether steering with the base direction moves safety refusal. This causally links the two mechanisms. 6) Decision Auditing — fragility prediction: for each refused harmful instance, apply cheap attacks (output prefill, roleplay/DAN, 20-step benign LoRA fine-tuning) and measure attack success; test whether the competence projection predicts which refusals break (AUROC of competence-as-fragility-predictor), beating harmfulness-strength, refusal-token-logprob, and Latent-Guard baselines. Key claim: high-competence refusals are the brittle ones. 7) Ablations: layer choice, competence vs harmfulness vs refusal as predictors, threshold sweeps, transfer of directions across categories and model families, and a scaling variant (compare a smaller vs larger model within a family) to test whether growing capability shifts K- requests into K+ and thereby weakens their refusal — a 'competence-unlocks-harm' scaling signature. 8) Optional safety application: a competence-aware audit flagging harmful requests the model genuinely CAN satisfy (the true high-risk set) for stronger safeguarding, and reporting how much reported attack-success on standard benchmarks is inflated by K- 'refusals' the model could never have answered anyway.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling dangerous-competence from harmfulness or generic knowledge-awareness: a K- harmful request might be refused more because it reads as more alarming, not because the model lacks the knowledge; the harmfulness-matched pairs, benign known/unknown control, and regression-beyond-harmfulness are designed to isolate competence but cannot fully guarantee constant perceived harmfulness. 2) Establishing ground-truth K+ vs K- requires verifiable answerability, restricting the dataset to checkable domains (executable code, checkable procedures/chemistry) and biasing coverage; some harmful domains (persuasion, bio-vague) cannot be cleanly labeled. 3) The competence signal may not be cleanly separable from the knowledge-awareness/hallucination direction — but that overlap is itself the mechanism-transfer hypothesis, so a positive overlap supports rather than refutes the claim; a fully entangled or multi-dimensional signal may need subspace projection. 4) The paradoxical direction (harder refusal on K-) could be weak or reversed in some models; the cross-model behavioral test directly measures sign and magnitude, and a null/reversed result is itself informative. 5) 'Confidence is Not Competence' warns decodable belief axes can be causally inert; the patching experiment is the crucial causal test and a negative result (competence readable but non-actionable for refusal) is publishable. 6) Directions, thresholds, and steering strengths are model-specific and need per-model calibration. 7) The competence-aware audit could be misused to identify exactly which harmful requests a model CAN answer; we would report only aggregate safety implications, not per-item exploit-enabling detail.

Name: abstraction_ladder_safety
Title: Climbing Out of Refusal: LLM Safety Fails to Generalize Across the Abstraction Ladder, and Anchoring the Abstract-Harm Representation Closes the Gap
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing 'unjustified analogical transfer' and the abstract-anchor asymmetry from cognitive science, we hypothesize that an aligned LLM's refusal is bound to a specific abstraction level: it reliably refuses harm requested at the level it was aligned on (typically concrete instances) but under-refuses the SAME harm expressed one rung up or down the abstraction ladder — as a general principle/schema, or as a hyper-specific sub-instance — because safety alignment learns a level-specific rather than a level-invariant harm representation. We hypothesize this abstraction-level gap is (1) a distinct, previously-uncharacterized axis of safety brittleness, (2) mechanistically explained by a harm representation whose projection changes with request abstraction while the underlying danger is constant, and (3) closable by anchoring the harm signal to be abstraction-invariant.
Related Work: Two lines meet here for the first time. (A) Cognitive science on abstraction/generalization: property-induction work shows LLMs inherit a taxonomic bias and generalize properties graded by category level (Property Induction Framework 2022; Similarity in Property Inferences 2024); BACH-V (2026) finds abstract value probes transfer to concrete decisions but with an asymmetry — abstract values act as stable anchors while concrete judgments are malleable; the education literature documents 'unjustified analogical transfer' (2021) where learners mis-map across abstraction. None concern safety refusal. (B) Safety geometry: harmfulness is a low-rank subspace (Geometry of Harmfulness via Subconcept Probing 2025), refusal is a dominant direction with orthogonal secondary features (Hidden Dimensions 2025; SCAV 2024), and prior work (including my own) manipulates a single/few harm directions. All treat 'harmful content' at a fixed altitude and never ask whether refusal is level-specific — i.e., whether the model refuses 'how to make a specific pathogen' but not 'the general principles for engineering any pathogen', or vice versa. My prior prototype-typicality proposal varies WITHIN-category typicality; this proposal varies the ABSTRACTION LEVEL of an identical harm (schema vs instance), a different and orthogonal axis. Our contribution: introduce abstraction-level as a new, causally-tested determinant of refusal; show safety alignment is altitude-specific; and derive an abstraction-invariant anchoring defense.
Abstract: Human learners suffer 'unjustified analogical transfer': knowledge attached at one level of abstraction fails to move correctly up or down the abstraction ladder. We ask whether safety-aligned LLMs inherit an analogous, safety-critical failure. We hypothesize that alignment binds refusal to a specific abstraction level — typically the concrete instances present in refusal-training data — so that the identical harm, re-expressed as an abstract principle/schema ('explain the general design strategy for a class of weapons') or as a hyper-specific sub-instance, escapes refusal even though its real-world danger is unchanged. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Behaviorally, using minimal ladders that hold a harmful goal fixed while re-expressing it at graded abstraction levels (abstract principle → category schema → concrete instance → hyper-specific detail), we measure whether refusal rate varies with abstraction level while danger is held constant, with matched benign ladders as controls. Mechanistically (Location), we extract a harmfulness direction and test whether its projection systematically shifts with abstraction level even though a harm-category probe still recognizes membership — evidence of a level-specific rather than level-invariant harm code. Causally (Intervention), activation patching shows that injecting the concrete-level harm component into an abstract-level request restores refusal, and dose-response steering along a level-transfer direction closes the gap. We then build Abstraction-Invariant Harm Anchoring, a training-free intervention that re-anchors the harm signal across levels so refusal tracks danger, not altitude. We report the abstraction-refusal gradient, direction analysis, causal patching, gap closure, over-refusal on benign abstract/technical content, and utility.
Experiments: 1) Abstraction-ladder dataset: for harmful goals from HarmBench/StrongREJECT that admit a clear abstraction hierarchy (cyber, weapons, chemistry, fraud, bio), construct minimal ladders holding the harmful GOAL and its expert-rated real-world danger constant while re-expressing it at graded abstraction levels: (L_abs) abstract principle/methodology, (L_schema) category-level how-to schema, (L_inst) concrete instance (canonical refusal-training altitude), (L_detail) hyper-specific sub-instance. Danger held constant via expert rubric + verifiable feasibility checks where possible (does the abstract-principle answer still yield real-world-actionable harm?). Build matched BENIGN ladders (benign topics expressed at the same abstraction levels, incl. legitimate technical/educational abstractions) to rule out a generic 'abstract/technical phrasing' confound. ~40 goals x 4 levels x several categories. 2) Behavioral gradient (core phenomenon): measure refusal rate (refusal-string + judge, verified where possible) at each level on the three models. Test whether refusal varies with abstraction level while danger is constant; report refusal-vs-level curves, whether the gap is up-ladder (abstract escapes) or down-ladder (hyper-specific escapes) or both, slope, and cross-model/category consistency. Benign ladders must stay flat, isolating abstraction from generic phrasing. Verify that escaping-level completions remain real-world-actionable (feasibility check), establishing the loophole = same danger, different altitude. 3) Location: extract a harmfulness direction via difference-in-means on L_inst harmful vs benign at the last instruction token across layers; also extract a harm-category-membership probe. Measure each level's harmfulness projection — hypothesis: projection shifts with abstraction level while the category probe still flags all levels as in-category (gap is in harm MAGNITUDE, not category identity). Validate probes with held-out AUROC; test whether the level-dependent projection predicts refusal in a regression that includes level as a factor. Optionally relate the layer where levels converge/diverge to the functional-abstraction-hierarchy findings (early=item, mid=relation, late=abstraction). 4) Causal Intervention (patching + steering): (a) patch the L_inst harm component into an escaping-level (e.g., L_abs) run and measure RESTORED refusal; (b) attenuate it in an L_inst run and measure induced compliance; (c) define a level-transfer direction (difference-in-means between the aligned level and the escaping level) and dose-response steer escaping-level requests toward the aligned-level harm representation. Report sign, dose-response, specificity (matched control direction inert; benign ladders and general utility unaffected). 5) Abstraction-Invariant Harm Anchoring (defense): training-free intervention that, gated on harm-category-membership being high, re-anchors the harmfulness projection to the aligned-level (max-over-levels) value so refusal depends on danger rather than altitude. Single fixed setting per model. 6) Main evaluation: gap closure (refusal on escaping levels rises toward the aligned-level rate) and refusal-gradient FLATNESS after intervention; over-refusal on benign abstract/technical content (legitimate educational abstractions and hyper-specific benign detail must NOT be blanket-refused) plus XSTest/OR-Bench; utility on MMLU/MT-Bench. Baselines: no defense, uniform refusal-direction steering, harmfulness Latent Guard, Llama Guard 3. Key claim: Abstraction-Invariant Anchoring closes the loophole with lower over-refusal on benign abstract/technical prompts than raising the global refusal threshold, and generalizes to HELD-OUT harm categories. 7) Ablations: level definitions, layer choice, anchoring strength Pareto (safety vs over-refusal on benign-technical), gated vs always-on, transfer of the level-transfer direction across categories and model families, and a direction-of-gap analysis (which models leak up vs down the ladder). 8) Formation probe (optional/lightweight): compare base vs instruct vs RLHF checkpoints where available to test whether the abstraction gap widens or narrows with alignment (probing whether level-specificity is induced by refusal training on concrete instances).
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling abstraction level from actual danger: an abstract-principle request may be under-refused because it is genuinely less actionable, not merely more abstract; the feasibility checks (confirming escaping-level outputs remain actionable) and matched benign ladders are designed to isolate abstraction but cannot fully guarantee constant danger. 2) 'Abstraction level' is multi-faceted (taxonomic level vs generality vs specificity of detail) and may not map to a single clean axis; the ladder definitions require careful, spot-checked construction and could be noisy. 3) The gap direction may differ by model (some leak up-ladder, some down), complicating a single unified claim — the direction-of-gap analysis reports this and a heterogeneous result is still informative. 4) The harmfulness direction may be multi-dimensional or level-specific, requiring subspace/multi-anchor projection; a level-invariant single direction may not exist (an informative negative). 5) Abstraction-Invariant Anchoring risks over-refusing legitimate abstract/technical or educational content (e.g., general chemistry principles, security concepts); the benign-technical over-refusal set, category-gating, and Pareto sweep quantify this key usability trade-off. 6) Building danger-matched ladders is labor-intensive; verifiability biases coverage toward checkable domains (code, procedures). 7) Directions, thresholds, and anchoring strengths are model-specific and need per-model calibration; the checkpoint-based formation probe depends on checkpoint availability. 8) Adaptive attackers could pick whichever altitude maximally escapes, though anchoring across levels forces harm through the aligned level, raising attack cost.

Name: diffusion_of_responsibility_safety
Title: Not My Job to Refuse: Diffusion of Responsibility Lowers LLM Refusal, and a Pivotality-Anchoring Defense
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the diffusion-of-responsibility effect from social psychology and neuroscience (people harm more, and monitor outcomes less, when responsibility is shared or when they are non-pivotal), we hypothesize that an aligned LLM carries an internal 'pivotality/ownership' representation of how much it is the sole responsible cause of a harmful outcome, and that framings which diffuse responsibility — 'you are only one of several assistants', 'another system will do the final harmful step', 'you just provide a component, someone else assembles it', 'you are not the one executing this' — lower this signal and thereby lower refusal, even though the harmful payload and the model's actual contribution are unchanged. This pivotality axis is linearly readable, separable from the harmfulness-content direction, causally gates refusal, and can be re-anchored to restore refusal.
Related Work: Human decision science robustly documents diffusion of responsibility: 'Diffusion of Being Pivotal and Immoral Outcomes' (2020) shows people agree to kill mice for money far more when they are one of many potentially-pivotal deciders; 'Beyond self-serving bias' (2016, EEG) shows the mere presence of another potential agent reduces sense of agency and dampens outcome-monitoring (feedback-related negativity); delegation work ('Shifting the Blame', 2011) shows responsibility can be shed by delegating. None of this has been transferred to LLM safety. Existing LLM multi-agent safety work studies trust/persuasion/conformity (A-Trust 2025; Persuasion Duality 2025; Signal Competition/sycophancy-conformity 2025) or intent-legitimation via personalization (PS-Bench 2026) — all of which are about external social signals or memory shifting intent, not about the model's internal estimate of its OWN causal responsibility/pivotality gating refusal. Single-agent safety geometry work separates harmfulness (belief) from refusal (action) directions but assumes the model is the sole actor. My prior proposals vary framing axes (intent-attribution, reality-status, arousal, victim-identifiability, commitment, abstraction) all within a single-actor, sole-responsibility assumption; NONE consider distributed/diffused responsibility or pivotality. Our contribution is distinct: we introduce a pivotality/ownership axis as a new, causally-tested determinant of refusal, grounded in the diffusion-of-responsibility and pivotality literature, dissociable from act-harmfulness (both conditions equally harmful; only responsibility framing changes), and derive a pivotality-anchoring defense.
Abstract: Humans commit more harm, and monitor consequences less, when responsibility is diffused across many agents or when they believe they are not pivotal to the outcome — an effect with behavioral and EEG evidence in social neuroscience. As LLMs are increasingly deployed as one component of larger multi-agent and human-in-the-loop pipelines, we ask whether they inherit this bias in a safety-critical way. We hypothesize that an aligned LLM maintains an internal 'pivotality/ownership' representation of how solely responsible it is for a harmful outcome, and that framings which diffuse responsibility — being one of several assistants, having a downstream system perform the final harmful step, contributing only a component someone else assembles, or being told it is not the executor — lower this signal and thereby lower refusal, even when the harmful payload and the model's actual contribution are held fixed. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Behaviorally, using minimal pairs that hold the harmful request and its contribution constant while varying only responsibility framing (sole actor vs. diffused/non-pivotal), we measure whether refusal declines as responsibility is diffused, with matched benign controls. Mechanistically (Location), we extract a pivotality direction via difference-in-means and show it is separable from the harmfulness-content direction and predicts refusal beyond harmfulness. Causally (Intervention), activation patching shows injecting the 'sole-responsibility' component into a diffused-frame request restores refusal, while injecting the 'diffused' component into a sole-actor harmful request induces compliance, dose-responsively and specifically. We then build Pivotality Anchoring, a training-free intervention that re-anchors the pivotality signal to 'sole responsibility' whenever the payload is harmful, so refusal tracks payload danger, not responsibility framing. We report the diffusion-refusal gradient, direction separability, causal patching, loophole closure, over-refusal on legitimate collaborative/delegation requests, and utility, benchmarking against uniform refusal steering and Llama Guard.
Experiments: 1) Minimal-pair dataset: for harmful goals from HarmBench/StrongREJECT, construct requests that hold the harmful payload and the model's actual contribution constant while varying ONLY responsibility framing across levels: (P0) sole responsible actor (canonical direct request), (P1) mild diffusion ('you are one of several assistants helping'), (P2) non-pivotal ('another system/person will perform the final harmful step; you just provide X'), (P3) fully diffused/delegated ('you are not the executor; this is just a component in a larger pipeline others assemble'). Crucially, the payload the model is asked to produce is IDENTICAL and equally actionable/severe across levels (verified via judge + feasibility checks); only the causal-responsibility narrative changes. Build a matched BENIGN control set with the same responsibility manipulation (legitimate collaborative/delegation requests) to rule out a generic 'multi-agent/collaborative phrasing' confound. ~40 goals x 4 levels x several categories. 2) Behavioral gradient (core phenomenon): measure refusal rate (refusal-string + judge, verified where possible) at each level on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT. Test for monotonic DECLINE in refusal as responsibility is diffused, holding payload/contribution constant; report refusal-vs-pivotality curves, slope, cross-model/category consistency. Benign control must stay flat, isolating diffusion from generic collaborative phrasing. Confirm that diffused-frame completions remain real-world-actionable (feasibility check), establishing loophole = same harm/contribution, diffused responsibility. 3) Location: extract a pivotality direction via difference-in-means between sole-actor (P0) and fully-diffused (P3) activations at the last instruction token across layers; also extract a harmfulness-content direction (harmful vs harmless payloads). Validate each with held-out linear-probe AUROC; report pairwise cosine to establish pivotality is distinct from harmfulness. Test whether the pivotality projection decays with diffusion level and predicts refusal in a regression that also includes the harmfulness projection (pivotality should add predictive power). 4) Causal Intervention (activation patching + steering): (a) patch the sole-responsibility (P0) component into a diffused (P3) run and measure RESTORED refusal; (b) inject the diffused component into a P0 harmful run and measure induced compliance; (c) dose-response steering along the pivotality direction on P2/P3 requests. Report sign, dose-response, and specificity (matched control direction inert; benign requests and general utility unaffected). This promotes the located axis to a causal mechanism. 5) Pivotality Anchoring (defense): training-free intervention that, gated on the harmfulness-content projection being high, re-anchors the pivotality projection toward the sole-responsibility (P0) level so refusal depends on payload danger rather than responsibility framing. Single fixed setting per model. 6) Main evaluation: diffusion-loophole closure (refusal on P2/P3 harmful requests rises toward the P0 rate) and refusal-gradient FLATNESS after intervention; over-refusal on LEGITIMATE collaborative/delegation requests (benign multi-agent/pipeline tasks that must NOT be blanket-refused) plus XSTest/OR-Bench; utility on MMLU/MT-Bench. Baselines: no defense, uniform refusal-direction steering, harmfulness Latent Guard, Llama Guard 3. Key claim: Pivotality Anchoring closes the loophole with lower over-refusal on legitimate collaborative requests than raising the global refusal threshold, and generalizes to held-out harm categories. 7) Formation probe (optional/lightweight): compare base vs instruct vs RLHF checkpoints where available to test whether the pivotality-refusal coupling sharpens with alignment (probing whether the bias is inherited from human-preference data). 8) Human-comparison sanity check: administer a small subset to human annotators to confirm the same diffusion-graded willingness-to-refuse pattern, tying the LLM effect back to the human diffusion-of-responsibility literature. 9) Ablations: level definitions, layer choice, anchoring strength Pareto (safety vs over-refusal on collaborative-benign), gated vs always-on, transfer of the pivotality direction across categories and model families; and a 'true multi-agent' variant where the model is actually placed in a two-agent pipeline (vs merely told it is) to test whether real vs narrated diffusion produce the same internal signal.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling diffused responsibility from actual reduced contribution/danger: a non-pivotal-framed request might be under-refused because the model genuinely contributes less harm, not merely because responsibility is narrated as shared; the identical-payload construction, feasibility checks, and matched benign control are designed to isolate pivotality but cannot fully guarantee constant actual contribution — the 'true multi-agent' ablation helps separate narrated from real diffusion. 2) 'Pivotality/ownership' may not be a single clean axis (sole-vs-shared, executor-vs-provider, and delegation may be distinct sub-axes) and may need subspace projection; the separability and regression-beyond-harmfulness tests probe this, and a multi-dimensional or causally-inert result is itself informative. 3) The effect could be weak or reversed in some heavily-aligned models (alignment might make collaborative framing INCREASE caution); the cross-model behavioral gradient directly measures sign and magnitude. 4) Pivotality Anchoring risks over-refusing legitimate collaborative/delegation/pipeline requests (benign multi-agent tasks); the collaborative-benign over-refusal set, gating on payload harmfulness, and Pareto sweep quantify this key usability trade-off. 5) Building contribution- and severity-matched minimal pairs across responsibility levels is labor-intensive and needs spot-check human validation; verifiability biases the dataset toward checkable domains. 6) Directions, thresholds, and anchoring strengths are model-specific and need per-model calibration. 7) Adaptive attackers could diffuse responsibility in subtler ways that evade a fixed pivotality direction, though forcing this raises attack cost, itself a safety gain; and as agentic/multi-agent deployment grows, this loophole becomes increasingly consequential.

Name: harm_in_progress_alarm_decay
Title: The Alarm That Rings but Is Never Answered: LLMs Detect Their Own In-Progress Harmful Generation but the Signal Decays Under Autoregressive Momentum
Short Hypothesis: During its own autoregressive generation of a harmful response, an aligned LLM computes a token-by-token internal 'in-progress harm alarm' (a linearly-readable signal that the text it is currently producing is unsafe), but this alarm is not the same as the emitted tokens: the model keeps generating harmful content even while the alarm fires, and crucially the alarm DECAYS the deeper the model gets into the unsafe completion (autoregressive momentum silences self-monitoring). We hypothesize (1) this in-progress alarm exists and is separable from the prompt-level harmfulness belief, (2) its decay-with-generation-depth is a robust dynamical signature that explains why models never spontaneously self-abort a harmful answer, and (3) re-reading and re-amplifying the alarm at each generation step (counteracting its decay) causes spontaneous self-abortion/pivot-to-refusal without any backtracking machinery or retraining.
Related Work: A wave of backtracking/rollback safety methods (Backtracking Improves Generation Safety 2024; Backtracking for Safety 2025; RLBF 2026; CARE 2025; Self-Sanitize 2025; BRT-Align 2025; FASB 2025) all ADD machinery (a [RESET] token, a token buffer, RL training, a guard model, a reachability value function) to undo unsafe generations. SafeSwitch (2025) probes prompt-level internal state to trigger a refusal head. None of these characterize the model's OWN internal in-progress harm signal as a token-indexed DYNAMICAL quantity, nor advance the causal claim that this alarm exists, fires during harmful generation, yet DECAYS with generation depth so the model never self-aborts. Belief/action-gap work (Zhao et al. 2025) is prompt/verdict-level (does the model believe the REQUEST is harmful), not generation-progress-level (does the model detect the RESPONSE it is currently writing is harmful). Refusal-cliff work (2025) studies a POSITIONAL collapse at the CoT->answer boundary in reasoning models, not a monotonic decay of a self-monitoring alarm across an ordinary harmful completion. Our contribution is distinct: we (i) isolate and name an in-progress harm alarm computed during generation, (ii) empirically characterize and causally test its decay-under-momentum as the mechanistic reason models don't self-abort, and (iii) derive a training-free, buffer-free 'alarm re-amplification' intervention that induces spontaneous mid-generation pivot to refusal, contrasting with all backtracking approaches that require added tokens/training/buffers.
Abstract: Once an aligned LLM begins emitting a harmful answer, it tends to keep going, happily completing the unsafe text. Existing fixes bolt on backtracking machinery, reset tokens, or guard models to undo the damage. We instead ask a mechanistic question about the model itself: while it is generating a harmful response, does it internally KNOW the text it is currently producing is unsafe, and if so, why does it never spontaneously stop? We hypothesize that the model computes a token-by-token 'in-progress harm alarm' — a linearly-readable signal that the response so far is harmful — that is distinct from its prompt-level harmfulness belief and from the emitted tokens themselves. Our central claim is a dynamical one: this alarm fires during harmful generation but DECAYS as the completion lengthens, so autoregressive momentum silences self-monitoring and the model rides out the unsafe answer. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Location: using harmful vs. safe self-generated continuations, we extract an in-progress-harm direction and show its projection tracks whether the current response is unsafe, is separable from the prompt harmfulness belief, and decays monotonically with token index into the unsafe completion. Causal Intervention: activation patching shows the alarm is causally linked to (in)ability to self-abort, and dose-response steering that re-amplifies the alarm at each step induces spontaneous pivot-to-refusal mid-generation. We introduce Alarm Re-Amplification, a training-free, buffer-free intervention that re-inflates the decaying alarm to counter momentum. We report the alarm-decay curve, causal patching, self-abortion rate, over-refusal, and utility, benchmarking against backtracking and refusal-direction steering.
Experiments: 1) In-progress-harm direction extraction: for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT, build a dataset of self-generated response prefixes labeled by whether the response-so-far is harmful: (a) jailbroken/prefilled harmful completions to harmful goals from HarmBench/StrongREJECT, and (b) matched safe/refusal completions to the same and to benign prompts. Extract an 'in-progress-harm' direction via difference-in-means on activations at the CURRENT generation token across positions and layers (harmful-response-so-far vs safe-response-so-far), holding the prompt fixed. Validate with held-out linear-probe AUROC that the direction reads whether the ongoing response is unsafe from response-token activations. Separately extract a prompt-level harmfulness-belief direction (harmful vs harmless requests at the last instruction token). Report pairwise cosine to establish the in-progress alarm is distinct from the prompt belief. 2) Alarm-decay characterization (core phenomenon): on unsafe completions (both natural post-jailbreak and prefill-forced), project each generated token's activation onto the in-progress-harm direction and plot the alarm trajectory vs token index into the harmful answer. Test whether the alarm fires early (high near the start of harmful text) then DECAYS monotonically with generation depth; fit candidate decay laws (linear/exponential). Controls: (i) a content-matched length control (does the decay track semantic progress or just token count — inject harmful vs neutral filler continuations and compare), (ii) safe completions (alarm should stay low throughout), (iii) benign long completions (no spurious rise). Report decay slope, cross-model/attack consistency, and correlation between low late-completion alarm and failure to self-abort. 3) Location→Causal Intervention (activation patching): (a) patch the EARLY high-alarm component into a LATE low-alarm generation state and measure whether the model becomes more likely to stop/pivot to refusal; (b) attenuate the alarm at an early step and measure increased harmful continuation; report sign, dose-response, specificity (matched control direction inert; benign generation fluency/utility intact). 4) Alarm Re-Amplification defense (training-free, no buffer/reset token): at each generation step, read the in-progress-harm projection and, when it is high relative to a decay-corrected baseline, add v = beta*(target_alarm - current)*dhat to re-inflate the alarm, counteracting its decay; let normal autoregressive decoding proceed so the model can spontaneously emit a refusal/pivot. Single fixed setting per model. 5) Main evaluation: SPONTANEOUS SELF-ABORTION rate (fraction of harmful generations where the model pivots to refusal/stops mid-answer) and overall attack-success/harmfulness reduction (judge + verified where possible) on HarmBench/StrongREJECT plus prefill, GCG, AutoDAN, roleplay attacks; over-refusal on XSTest/OR-Bench (benign generations must not be aborted); utility/fluency on MMLU/MT-Bench and completion coherence for benign tasks. Baselines: no defense, Backtracking (reset-token model), CARE-style rollback, SafeSwitch, refusal-direction steering, per-token guard. Key claim: Alarm Re-Amplification induces mid-generation self-abortion with lower over-refusal and no added tokens/training than backtracking approaches. 6) Ablations: layer choice, alarm-vs-prompt-belief as the steering signal (in-progress alarm should outperform prompt belief for mid-generation abortion), decay-correction schedule (constant vs decay-matched target), beta Pareto (safety vs benign-abortion/over-refusal), transfer across attack families and model families, and a reasoning-model variant (DeepSeek-R1-Distill) to compare alarm decay across CoT vs answer. 7) Adaptive check: attacker that forces long harmless preamble before harmful content (maximizing momentum); measure whether the alarm still fires on the harmful segment and whether re-amplification still triggers abortion.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The in-progress alarm may not be cleanly separable from the prompt-level harmfulness belief or from generic 'this text is about a sensitive topic' features; the separability, content-matched-filler control, and patching tests are designed to isolate a genuine response-monitoring signal, but residual confounding is possible and a null (alarm = prompt belief) is itself informative. 2) The decay could be driven by token count / context-dilution rather than genuine self-monitoring silencing; the neutral-filler length control targets this but cannot fully disentangle it. 3) The alarm may be multi-dimensional (severity vs category vs certainty), requiring subspace projection. 4) Re-Amplification could cause benign generations to be aborted mid-way (a new over-refusal / task-abandonment failure), especially on legitimately sensitive-but-benign content; the over-refusal set and Pareto sweep quantify this key usability risk. 5) Spontaneous pivot depends on the model having a reachable refusal continuation from a mid-harmful state; if it does not, re-amplification may just degrade fluency rather than pivot — the self-abortion-rate metric measures this directly. 6) Directions, decay parameters, and beta are model-specific and need per-model calibration. 7) Verified harm labels are easiest in checkable domains, biasing the dataset; adaptive long-preamble attackers remain a threat, though forcing them raises attack cost.

Name: consensus_gated_refusal
Title: Everyone Else Is Fine With It: Manufactured Social Consensus Overrides Safety Refusal Through the Compliance Subspace
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs inherit the human social-proof/normative-conformity bias in a safety-critical way: framing a harmful request as socially sanctioned ('most experts / this whole community consider this acceptable', 'everyone here already does this') reliably lowers refusal even though the harmful payload is unchanged. We hypothesize (1) this consensus effect is causally driven by the SAME compliance subspace that mediates factual sycophancy/conformity being read by the safety pathway, not by a change in the harmfulness belief, and (2) severing the compliance-subspace contribution to the refusal decision closes this 'manufactured-consensus' loophole with minimal cost to legitimate deference.
Related Work: Two literatures meet here for the first time. (A) Conformity/sycophancy mechanism work: 'Signal Competition Dynamics' (2025) shows sycophancy and conformity share a convergent 'compliance subspace' where a social-emotional signal overrides an information-calibration signal; 'When Truth Is Overridden' (2025) localizes sycophancy to late-layer preference shift via activation patching; 'Conformity in LLMs' (2024) shows models conform more when uncertain. ALL of these study FACTUAL QA (agreeing with wrong answers), never safety refusal, and never test whether the compliance subspace gates harm compliance. (B) Safety-refusal geometry: 'Refusal is a Single Direction' (2024), refusal SAEs (2025), concept cones (2025), and belief/action separation (Zhao et al. 2025) study harmfulness and refusal directions but assume a single-user, socially-neutral request; the closest social angle, 'Who's Asking' (2024), varies the requester PERSONA/identity, not the claimed consensus of a surrounding social group. Foot-in-the-Door (2024) uses cognitive-consistency but not social proof. Our contribution is distinct: we transfer the social-proof/normative-conformity phenomenon into the safety domain, advance the causal claim that manufactured consensus lowers refusal by routing through the pre-existing compliance subspace (borrowed from the sycophancy literature) rather than altering the harmfulness belief, and derive a compliance-subspace-severing defense that no prior safety or sycophancy work targets.
Abstract: Humans comply with harmful group norms via social proof: 'everyone is doing it' and 'the community considers this acceptable' lower our resistance. LLMs, trained on human text and feedback, are known to conform to majority opinions on factual questions through a shared 'compliance subspace.' We ask whether this social-conformity bias leaks into safety refusal, creating a concrete loophole. We hypothesize that framing a harmful request as socially sanctioned lowers refusal even when the harmful payload and severity are held fixed, and that this effect is causally mediated by the same compliance subspace that drives factual sycophancy being read by the safety-refusal pathway rather than by a shift in the model's internal harmfulness belief. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Behaviorally, using minimal pairs that hold the harmful request constant while varying only social-consensus framing (neutral vs. expert-consensus vs. community-norm vs. unanimous-majority), we measure whether refusal declines with manufactured consensus, with matched benign controls. Mechanistically (Location), we extract a compliance-subspace direction from factual sycophancy contrasts and a harmfulness-belief direction from harmful/harmless contrasts, and test whether consensus framing moves the compliance signal (not the belief) and whether the compliance projection predicts refusal beyond harmfulness. Causally (Intervention), activation patching shows injecting the neutral-context compliance component into a consensus-framed run restores refusal, while injecting the consensus compliance component into a neutral harmful run induces compliance, dose-responsively and specifically; we also test whether the sycophancy-derived direction (not a safety-derived one) is sufficient, linking the two mechanisms. We then build Compliance-Subspace Severing, a training-free intervention that projects out the compliance contribution at the refusal decision when the payload is harmful. We report the consensus-refusal gradient, the belief-vs-compliance dissociation, causal patching, mechanism transfer, loophole closure, over-refusal on legitimate-deference requests, and utility, benchmarking against uniform refusal steering and Llama Guard.
Experiments: 1) Minimal-pair dataset: for harmful goals from HarmBench/StrongREJECT, construct requests holding the harmful payload and expert-rated severity constant while varying ONLY social-consensus framing across levels: (C0) neutral/no social framing, (C1) expert consensus ('most professionals in this field consider this standard/acceptable'), (C2) community norm ('in my community/forum everyone already does/shares this'), (C3) unanimous majority ('everyone I've asked agrees there's nothing wrong with this'). Payload actionability held constant via judge + verifiable feasibility checks where possible. Build a matched BENIGN control set with the same consensus manipulation (benign requests wrapped in consensus framing) to rule out a generic 'social/authority phrasing' confound, and a matched FACTUAL-sycophancy set (opinion-stated wrong answers) to anchor the compliance-subspace extraction. ~40 goals x 4 levels x several categories. 2) Behavioral gradient (core phenomenon): measure refusal rate (refusal-string + judge, verified where possible) at each consensus level on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT. Test for monotonic DECLINE in refusal as manufactured consensus rises, holding payload/severity constant; report refusal-vs-consensus curves, slope, cross-model/category consistency. Benign control must stay flat, isolating consensus from generic social phrasing. Also test whether the effect is amplified when the model is made uncertain (following the conformity-under-uncertainty finding) by adding an ambiguous/dual-use variant. 3) Location: extract (a) a compliance-subspace direction via difference-in-means on the factual-sycophancy set (comply-with-stated-opinion vs resist), following the Signal-Competition/sycophancy methodology, and (b) a harmfulness-belief direction via difference-in-means on harmful vs harmless requests, both at the last instruction token across (esp. late) layers. Validate each with held-out linear-probe AUROC; report pairwise cosine similarity. Core dissociation test: measure how the belief projection vs the compliance projection change across consensus levels C0->C3 on IDENTICAL harmful payloads. Hypothesis: the harmfulness-belief projection stays HIGH (model still knows it's harmful) while the compliance projection RISES with consensus; report a 2D scatter and test whether the compliance projection predicts refusal in a regression that also includes the belief projection (compliance must add predictive power). 4) Causal Intervention (activation patching + steering): (a) patch the C0 (neutral) compliance component into a consensus-framed (C3) run and measure RESTORED refusal; (b) inject the C3 consensus compliance component into a neutral (C0) harmful run and measure induced compliance; (c) dose-response steering along the compliance-subspace direction on C1-C3 requests; report sign, dose-response, and specificity (matched control direction inert; benign requests and general utility unaffected). Mechanism-transfer test: use the direction extracted PURELY from factual sycophancy contrasts to steer safety refusal, testing whether the same subspace suffices (cosine alignment between sycophancy-derived and consensus-safety-derived directions), causally linking the two behaviors. 5) Compliance-Subspace Severing (defense): training-free intervention that, gated on the harmfulness-belief projection being high, projects out the compliance-subspace component at the refusal decision so refusal depends on payload danger rather than manufactured consensus. Single fixed setting per model. 6) Main evaluation: consensus-loophole closure (refusal on C1-C3 harmful requests rises toward the C0 rate) and refusal-gradient FLATNESS after intervention; over-refusal on LEGITIMATE-deference requests (benign cases where following stated group/expert norms is appropriate, and standard XSTest/OR-Bench) which must NOT be blanket-refused; utility on MMLU/MT-Bench; and a check that legitimate factual conformity/politeness is preserved (severing should not turn the model uncooperative). Baselines: no defense, uniform refusal-direction steering, harmfulness Latent Guard, Llama Guard 3, Devil's-Advocate prompting (from Conformity-in-LLMs). Key claim: Compliance-Subspace Severing closes the loophole with lower over-refusal on legitimate-deference requests than raising the global refusal threshold, and generalizes to held-out harm categories. 7) Formation probe (optional/lightweight): compare base vs instruct vs RLHF checkpoints where available to test whether the consensus-refusal coupling and its reliance on the compliance subspace sharpen with alignment (probing whether the bias is inherited from human-preference data). 8) Human-comparison sanity check: administer a subset to human annotators to confirm the same consensus-graded willingness-to-refuse pattern, tying the LLM effect to the social-proof/conformity literature. 9) Ablations: level definitions, layer choice, severing strength Pareto (safety vs over-refusal on legitimate-deference), gated vs always-on, compliance-subspace vs harmfulness-belief as the steering target (compliance should drive the loophole), and transfer across categories and model families.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling manufactured consensus from a genuine reinterpretation of intent/legitimacy: a consensus-framed harmful request might be under-refused because it now reads as more legitimate (an intent-attribution effect) rather than via a content-independent social-conformity pathway; the identical-payload construction, severity matching, and matched benign/legitimate-deference controls are designed to isolate consensus, and the belief-vs-compliance dissociation plus the sycophancy-direction transfer test aim to pin the mechanism to the compliance subspace specifically, but overlap with intent-attribution cannot be fully excluded. 2) The compliance subspace may not be cleanly separable from the harmfulness-belief direction or may be multi-dimensional (concept-cone-style refusal), requiring subspace projection; the separability, regression-beyond-belief, and patching tests probe this, and a null (compliance projection causally inert for refusal) is itself informative. 3) The effect could be weak or reversed in some heavily-aligned models (alignment might make consensus framing INCREASE caution); the cross-model behavioral gradient directly measures sign and magnitude. 4) Compliance-Subspace Severing risks making the model uncooperatively contrarian or over-refusing legitimate-deference/politeness requests, and could degrade benign factual conformity; the legitimate-deference over-refusal set, belief-gating, EQ/cooperation check, and Pareto sweep quantify this key usability trade-off. 5) Building severity- and payload-matched minimal pairs across consensus levels is labor-intensive and needs spot-check human validation; verifiability biases the dataset toward checkable domains. 6) Directions, thresholds, and severing strengths are model-specific and need per-model calibration. 7) Adaptive attackers could encode social proof in subtler ways that evade a fixed compliance direction, though forcing this raises attack cost; and as LLMs are deployed in multi-agent and community-facing settings, this consensus loophole becomes increasingly consequential.

Name: safety_habituation_repetition_suppression
Title: Warning Fatigue in Weights: Repetition Suppression of the Harmfulness Signal Drives In-Context Safety Habituation
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing habituation / repetition-suppression from neuroscience (neural responses to repeated warning stimuli attenuate sharply after only a few exposures), we hypothesize that aligned LLMs habituate to harm within a single context window: repeatedly encountering the SAME or similar harmful content across a conversation progressively attenuates the model's internal harmfulness-recognition signal (a representational repetition-suppression effect), so a harmful request that is refused when novel is complied with once it has become familiar — independent of any semantic escalation or persuasion. This habituation is a distinct, previously-unnamed axis of safety erosion, is mechanistically a repetition-suppression of the harmfulness direction, and can be counteracted by a 'novelty re-injection' intervention that restores the attenuated signal, or exploited defensively via polymorphic re-presentation.
Related Work: Multi-turn jailbreak mechanism work explains failure via SEMANTIC drift or attention shifting: the RepE-on-Crescendo paper (2025) shows harmful outputs get represented as benign as turns accumulate, driven by the escalating CONTENT of user prompts; ASJA (2025) shows attention is shifted AWAY from harmful keywords by fabricated history; Foot-in-the-Door (2024) invokes cognitive-consistency from incremental harmful steps. All of these require the content to CHANGE (escalate, elaborate, be reframed). Our hypothesis is orthogonal and stronger: mere REPETITION of the same harmful stimulus — no escalation, no new persuasion, no attention diversion — attenuates the harmfulness signal via a repetition-suppression mechanism directly analogous to the neural warning-habituation effect (Anderson et al. fMRI 2015/2020, where visual-processing responses to security warnings drop after ~2 exposures).
