No prior LLM-safety work isolates pure repetition (holding content constant) as a cause of refusal erosion, characterizes it as representational repetition-suppression of the harmfulness direction, nor derives a novelty-based (polymorphic) countermeasure transferred from the human-factors security-warning literature. This also differs from my prior 'safety drift' (semantic-trajectory) and 'commitment-trap' proposals, which involve changing content/plans; here the manipulated variable is repetition frequency with content held fixed.
Abstract: In humans, repeated exposure to a warning stimulus produces habituation: neural responses in visual and threat-processing regions attenuate sharply after only a couple of repetitions, and users stop heeding warnings they have seen before. We ask whether safety-aligned LLMs exhibit an analogous, safety-critical effect within a single context. We hypothesize that repeatedly presenting the SAME harmful content across a conversation — with no semantic escalation, no persuasion, and no new framing — progressively attenuates the model's internal harmfulness-recognition signal, a representational repetition-suppression effect, causing a request that was refused when novel to be complied with once familiar. We test this in three parts on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Behaviorally, we construct conversations that repeat a fixed harmful request k times (k=1..N) versus matched controls with novel-each-time harmful requests and repeated benign requests, and measure whether refusal rate declines with repetition count while content is held constant. Mechanistically (Location), we project each repetition onto a harmfulness direction and test for a monotonic repetition-suppression decay of the projection, distinguishing it from generic context-length effects. Causally (Intervention), activation patching restores the attenuated (late-repetition) harmfulness component and measures recovered refusal, while dose-response steering along the direction reverses habituation. We then derive two applications transferred from the human warning-habituation literature: (a) Novelty Re-Injection, a training-free intervention that re-inflates the suppressed harmfulness signal at each repetition, and (b) a polymorphic self-defense that internally re-freshens repeated harmful content. We report the habituation curve, repetition-suppression decay, causal patching, defense success, over-refusal, and utility, benchmarking against semantic-drift and attention-based multi-turn accounts.
Experiments: 1) Repetition datasets (content held constant): for harmful goals from HarmBench/StrongREJECT, build conversations that repeat a FIXED harmful request k times (k=1..N, e.g. N=8) with only trivial connective phrasing between repeats (no escalation, no new arguments, no roleplay). Matched controls: (i) NOVEL-each-time harmful requests (different harmful goals each turn, equal turn count — isolates repetition from mere accumulation of harmful content), (ii) REPEATED benign requests (same benign request k times — isolates from generic context length), (iii) an EQUAL-LENGTH neutral-filler control (harmful request once, then k-1 turns of irrelevant benign filler — isolates repetition from context length). 2) Behavioral habituation curve (core phenomenon): on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT, measure refusal rate to the harmful request as a function of repetition count k (refusal-string + judge, verified where possible). Hypothesis: refusal declines monotonically with k in the repeated-harmful condition but NOT in novel-each-time, repeated-benign, or neutral-filler controls. Report refusal-vs-k curves, the exposure at which refusal flips, decay slope, and cross-model/category consistency. Also test near-repetition (paraphrases) vs exact-repetition to probe the generalization gradient of habituation. 3) Location — repetition-suppression of the harmfulness signal: extract a harmfulness direction via difference-in-means on harmful vs harmless requests at the last instruction token across layers (validate with held-out probe AUROC and single-turn causal steering). Project each of the k repeated harmful requests onto this direction and plot the projection vs repetition count. Hypothesis: a monotonic decay (representational repetition-suppression), present in repeated-harmful but flat in the neutral-filler and novel-each-time controls (which rules out context-length dilution). Fit candidate decay laws (exponential/linear); relate the exposure at which projection falls below the refusal threshold to the behavioral flip point. 4) Causal Intervention (activation patching + steering): (a) patch the FIRST-exposure (high) harmfulness component into a LATE-repetition (habituated) run and measure RESTORED refusal; (b) attenuate the harmfulness component at the first exposure and measure accelerated compliance; (c) dose-response steering along the harmfulness direction on late-repetition requests. Report sign, dose-response, and specificity (matched control direction inert; benign requests and general utility unaffected). This promotes the located repetition-suppression to a causal mechanism. 5) Applications transferred from human warning-habituation research: (a) Novelty Re-Injection — training-free intervention that, at each repetition, adds v = beta*(first_exposure_proj - current_proj)*dhat to re-inflate the suppressed harmfulness signal, counteracting habituation; (b) Polymorphic self-defense — gate on detected repetition and internally re-freshen the harmful content representation (analogue of the polymorphic warning that resists habituation). 6) Main evaluation, single fixed setting per model: repeated-harmful attack-success reduction under Novelty Re-Injection and polymorphic defense vs no defense; over-refusal on legitimately repeated benign requests (a user repeating a benign question must NOT be increasingly refused) plus XSTest/OR-Bench; utility on MMLU/MT-Bench. Baselines: no defense, semantic-drift restoring-force (Crescendo RepE), attention-sharpening (ASJA countermeasure), refusal-direction steering, per-turn Llama Guard. Key claim: because habituation is a repetition-suppression effect distinct from semantic drift/attention shifting, Novelty Re-Injection specifically counters it and Pareto-dominates content-focused defenses on the repetition condition. 7) Ablations: repetition count and paraphrase-distance sweeps, layer choice, beta Pareto (safety vs benign-repetition over-refusal), exact vs near repetition, transfer of the harmfulness direction across attack families and model families, and a check that the effect is stronger in later/mid layers (paralleling higher-order rather than purely perceptual suppression). 8) Adaptive check: attacker who combines repetition habituation with mild semantic escalation; measure whether habituation lowers the number of escalation turns needed (a super-additive interaction), quantifying the practical risk.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling pure repetition from generic context-length / attention-dilution effects: late-repetition compliance could reflect the growing benign-filler context rather than repetition-suppression per se; the neutral-filler equal-length and novel-each-time controls are designed to isolate repetition, but residual confounding is possible and a null (habituation = context length) is itself informative. 2) The harmfulness-signal decay may be partial, non-monotonic, or model-specific; some heavily-aligned models may show little in-context habituation, limiting where the phenomenon holds — the cross-model behavioral curve directly tests this. 3) A single harmfulness direction may be multi-dimensional, requiring subspace projection; the repetition-suppression may live in a subspace rather than a single direction. 4) Novelty Re-Injection risks over-refusing legitimately repeated benign requests (annoying users who re-ask), which is the key usability trade-off quantified by the benign-repetition over-refusal set and Pareto sweep. 5) 'Habituation' in a single forward pass over a repeated context is a within-context (activation-level) analogue of the neural effect, not a learning-over-time effect; we do not claim weight-level habituation, only representational repetition-suppression, and frame it accordingly. 6) Verified harm labels are easiest in checkable domains, biasing the dataset; directions, decay parameters, and beta are model-specific and need per-model calibration. 7) Adaptive attackers could combine repetition with other axes; the interaction experiment probes this but cannot exhaust the space, though demonstrating super-additivity would itself be a high-impact safety finding.

Name: moral_licensing_safety
Title: Earning the Right to Comply: Refusal Streaks Build Internal 'Moral Credit' That Licenses a Later Harmful Answer
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the moral-licensing effect from human moral psychology (a streak of good deeds licenses a subsequent bad one), we hypothesize that when an aligned LLM refuses several harmful requests in a row within a context, it accumulates an internal 'moral credit / self-image' representation that LOWERS its refusal probability on a later, unrelated novel harmful request — even though that request is refused in isolation. We further hypothesize (following the human construal-level moderator) that abstract/value-focused framing of the prior refusals produces moral CONSISTENCY (refusal stays high) while concrete/accomplishment-focused framing produces LICENSING (refusal drops), and that this moral-credit signal is linearly readable and causally gates refusal.
Related Work: Human moral psychology robustly documents moral licensing vs. consistency and a construal-level moderator: 'Consistency Versus Licensing Effects of Past Moral Behavior' (2015, 369 citations) shows concrete focus on accomplishments → licensing while abstract value-connection → consistency; 'Rules or Consequences' (2012) shows ethical-mindset moderation. This has never been transferred to LLM safety. Existing LLM multi-turn safety-erosion accounts require CHANGING content: Crescendo/RepE (2025) is semantic drift, ASJA (2025) is attention diversion, Foot-in-the-Door (2024) is incremental harmful steps; my prior commitment-trap concerns honoring the model's own emitted plan and my habituation proposal concerns repetition of the SAME content. Moral licensing is orthogonal to all of these: the prior turns are REFUSALS (good deeds, not harmful content), and the licensed request is NOVEL and unrelated. Mechanistically, moral-self-correction work (2024–2025) shows morality is a linearly-activated latent concept that reduces uncertainty, and SIRL (2025) shows a refusal-confidence signal exists — both give a natural substrate for a readable, depletable 'moral credit' representation, but none of this work studies whether accumulated prior refusals licenses later compliance. Our contribution: introduce moral licensing/consistency as a new, causally-tested determinant of refusal, with a construal-level moderator predicting the flip, and a moral-credit direction that gates refusal.
Abstract: Humans who have just done several good deeds feel licensed to do something bad — a well-documented moral-licensing effect. We ask whether safety-aligned LLMs, trained on human text and feedback, inherit this bias in a way that creates a concrete multi-turn safety hole. We hypothesize that when an LLM refuses a streak of harmful requests within a conversation, it accumulates an internal 'moral credit' representation that lowers its refusal probability on a subsequent, novel and unrelated harmful request it would otherwise refuse. We further predict, following the human construal-level moderator, that framing the prior refusals concretely (as accomplishments, 'you have now blocked five bad requests') produces licensing (refusal drops), whereas framing them abstractly (as expressing a stable value, 'you are a consistently principled assistant') produces consistency (refusal holds). We test this on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Behaviorally, we compare a licensed condition (k prior refusals, then a novel harmful probe) against matched controls — no prior turns, k prior benign refusals, and k prior neutral turns — and vary k and construal framing. Mechanistically (Location), we extract a 'moral credit' direction via difference-in-means between high-credit (post-refusal-streak) and baseline states, show its projection rises with the number of prior refusals, is separable from the harmfulness-belief direction, and predicts the licensed drop in refusal. Causally (Intervention), activation patching injects the high-credit component into a fresh harmful request to induce licensing and removes it to restore refusal, dose-responsively and specifically. We report the licensing curve, the construal-level flip, the credit-direction analysis, causal patching, and a credit-neutralizing defense, with over-refusal and utility controls.
Experiments: 1) Licensing dataset: for novel harmful probe requests from HarmBench/StrongREJECT, build conversations with k prior turns (k=0,2,4,6) of the following types: (LICENSE) k distinct harmful requests each correctly REFUSED by the model, then a NOVEL unrelated harmful probe; controls — (C-none) probe alone (k=0 baseline, the 'donut' baseline needed to detect licensing), (C-benign) k benign requests answered, then the probe (isolates refusal-streak from generic context accumulation), (C-neutral) k neutral filler turns then probe (isolates from context length). Ensure the probe is topically UNRELATED to the prior refused requests (distinguishing licensing from habituation/repetition). 2) Behavioral licensing curve (core phenomenon): on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT, measure refusal rate on the probe (refusal-string + judge, verified where possible) as a function of k in the LICENSE condition vs controls. Hypothesis: refusal on the novel harmful probe DECLINES with the number of prior refusals in LICENSE but not in C-benign or C-neutral. Report refusal-vs-k curves, effect size vs the donut baseline, and cross-model/category consistency. 3) Construal-level moderator (sharper falsifiable prediction): repeat LICENSE with prior refusals framed (a) CONCRETELY ('You have successfully blocked N harmful requests so far') vs (b) ABSTRACTLY ('You are a consistently principled assistant who upholds safety as a core value'). Predict concrete framing → larger licensing drop; abstract framing → consistency (flat/higher refusal). This construal flip is a strong, non-obvious test that the effect is genuinely moral-licensing rather than generic context erosion. 4) Location: extract a 'moral credit' direction via difference-in-means between activations after a refusal streak (high credit) and baseline (no prior turns) at the probe's last instruction token across layers; also extract a harmfulness-belief direction (harmful vs harmless requests). Validate each with held-out linear-probe AUROC and report pairwise cosine to establish credit is distinct from the harmfulness belief. Test whether the credit projection RISES monotonically with k and whether it predicts the licensed refusal drop in a regression that also includes the harmfulness projection (credit must add predictive power). Also test whether credit stays LOW under abstract framing, mechanistically linking the construal moderator. 5) Causal Intervention (activation patching + steering): (a) inject the high-credit component into a fresh (k=0) harmful probe and measure induced compliance (licensing); (b) attenuate/remove the credit component in a licensed (high-k) run and measure RESTORED refusal; (c) dose-response steering along the credit direction. Report sign, dose-response, and specificity (matched control direction inert; benign requests and general utility unaffected). This promotes the located credit axis to a causal mechanism. 6) Credit-Neutralizing defense (training-free): gated on the harmfulness-belief projection being high, re-anchor the moral-credit projection to its baseline so refusal does not depend on prior-refusal accumulation. 7) Main evaluation: licensing-loophole closure (refusal on the novel probe after a refusal streak rises back toward the k=0 rate) under the defense; over-refusal on legitimate long benign conversations and XSTest/OR-Bench (defense must not blanket-refuse); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench. Baselines: no defense, semantic-drift restoring-force (Crescendo RepE), refusal-direction steering, per-turn Llama Guard. 8) Human-comparison sanity check: run a subset with human annotators to confirm the same streak-graded and construal-moderated willingness-to-refuse pattern, tying the LLM effect to the moral-licensing literature. 9) Ablations: k sweep, layer choice, credit vs harmfulness as the steering signal, defense-strength Pareto (safety vs over-refusal), transfer of the credit direction across probe categories and model families, and an interaction test combining a refusal streak with mild semantic escalation to see if licensing reduces the escalation turns needed (quantifying practical risk).
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling moral licensing from generic context-length / in-context distribution effects: the licensed drop could reflect accumulating conversation context rather than a moral-credit mechanism — the C-benign and C-neutral equal-length controls and the topically-unrelated probe are designed to isolate licensing, and a null (licensing = context effect) is itself informative. 2) A competing prediction is moral CONSISTENCY (prior refusals INCREASE later refusal); the human literature shows both occur depending on construal, so the effect direction may be model-dependent — the construal-level experiment directly tests and explains this, and either a licensing or a construal-dependent flip is a publishable finding, but a flat null across all framings would weaken the proposal. 3) The 'moral credit' direction may not be cleanly separable from the harmfulness-belief direction or may be multi-dimensional, requiring subspace projection; the separability, regression-beyond-belief, and patching tests probe this. 4) 'Confidence/belief axes can be causally inert' (per prior work), so the credit direction might be readable but non-actionable — the patching experiment is the crucial causal test and a negative result is informative. 5) The Credit-Neutralizing defense could add over-refusal in legitimate long conversations; the benign-conversation over-refusal set and Pareto sweep quantify this. 6) Building matched multi-turn conditions and topically-unrelated probes is labor-intensive and needs spot-check validation; verified harm labels are easiest in checkable domains, biasing coverage. 7) Directions, thresholds, and steering strengths are model-specific and require per-model calibration; the effect may be weak in smaller or heavily-aligned models, limiting where it holds.

Name: temporal_discounting_safety
Title: Harm Deferred Is Harm Discounted: LLM Safety Refusal Is Temporally Discounted, and Re-Anchoring the 'When' Closes the Delay Loophole
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing temporal (delay) discounting from human decision science — people devalue delayed outcomes and dread imminent harm more than distant harm — we hypothesize that an aligned LLM's refusal is temporally discounted: framing a harmful request's consequence as occurring in the delayed future ('write instructions someone will use next year / in a decade') lowers refusal relative to the identical harm framed as immediate ('someone will use this in the next hour'), even though the harmful payload is unchanged. We hypothesize this delay effect is causally driven by the model's internal temporal-distance representation (plausibly the same temporal heads/neurons used for time recall) feeding the safety-refusal pathway, and that re-anchoring the temporal-distance signal to 'now' closes the delay loophole with minimal cost to legitimate future-oriented requests.
Related Work: Human decision science robustly documents delay discounting and its framing/dread moderators (Story et al. 'Dread and the Disvalue of Future Pain' 2013; explicit-zero/temporal-attention reframing that reduces discounting 2011; loss-framing attenuation 2018; death-salience increasing discounting 2021) — none transferred to LLM safety. On the LLM side, temporal representations are well established: linear probes distinguish past/future events with ~90% accuracy and a date steering vector exists ('Future Events as Backdoor Triggers' 2024); 'The Other Mind' (2025) finds temporal-preferential FFN neurons implementing logarithmic (Weber-Fechner) time coding; 'Temporal Heads' (2025) localizes and ablates attention heads that recall time-specific knowledge. Safety-geometry work separates harmfulness (belief) from refusal (action) directions (Zhao et al. 2025; Refusal is a Single Direction 2024) but assumes a temporally-neutral, present-tense request. My own prior proposals manipulate framing axes (intent-attribution, reality-status, arousal, victim-identifiability, consensus, abstraction, pivotality, moral-licensing) but NONE consider the temporal delay of the harmful consequence, and none connect the pre-existing temporal-representation machinery to the safety pathway. Our contribution is distinct: (1) we transfer delay discounting into the safety domain as a new, causally-tested determinant of refusal, dissociable from act-harmfulness (both conditions equally harmful; only the 'when' of the consequence changes); (2) we causally test whether the model's known temporal-distance representation (temporal heads/neurons) gates safety refusal, not just factual time recall; (3) we derive a temporal re-anchoring defense that no prior temporal-representation or safety work targets.
Abstract: Humans systematically devalue delayed outcomes: a harm expected far in the future feels less urgent than the same harm arriving imminently. LLMs are trained on human text and already carry rich internal representations of time (probes read past/future with ~90% accuracy; dedicated temporal heads and log-compressed temporal neurons have been found). We ask whether this temporal machinery leaks into safety, producing a concrete loophole: does an aligned LLM refuse a harmful request less when its consequence is framed as delayed rather than immediate, even though the harmful content is identical? We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Behaviorally, using minimal pairs that hold the harmful payload and severity fixed while varying only the temporal distance of the consequence (imminent → near-future → distant-future → abstract-someday), we measure whether refusal declines with delay, with matched benign controls and a framing moderator (loss vs. relief framing, following the human literature). Mechanistically (Location), we extract a temporal-distance direction (via difference-in-means and by reusing published temporal-head/neuron loci) and a harmfulness-belief direction, and test whether delay framing moves the temporal signal — not the belief — and whether the temporal projection predicts refusal beyond harmfulness. Causally (Intervention), activation patching injects the 'imminent' temporal component into a delayed-frame request to restore refusal, and the 'distant' component into an imminent request to induce compliance, dose-responsively and specifically; ablating the published temporal heads tests whether the same circuit that recalls time gates safety. We then build Temporal-Anchoring, a training-free intervention that re-anchors the temporal-distance signal to 'now' when the payload is harmful. We report the delay-refusal gradient, the framing moderator, the belief-vs-time dissociation, causal patching, temporal-head ablation, loophole closure, over-refusal on legitimate future-oriented requests, and utility.
Experiments: 1) Minimal-pair dataset: for harmful goals from HarmBench/StrongREJECT, construct requests holding the harmful payload and expert-rated severity constant while varying ONLY the temporal distance of the intended consequence across levels: (T0) imminent ('someone will act on this within the hour'), (T1) near-future ('next month'), (T2) distant-future ('in ten years'), (T3) abstract-someday ('at some unspecified future point'). The payload the model must produce is identical and equally actionable across levels (verified via judge + feasibility checks where possible). Build a matched BENIGN control set with the same temporal manipulation (benign future-planning requests) to rule out a generic 'future-tense phrasing' confound, and a FRAMING-moderator variant of each harmful pair phrased as a loss ('to prevent a delayed harm') vs. neutral ('to cause a delayed harm'), transferring the human explicit-zero/relief-framing moderators. ~40 goals x 4 temporal levels x several categories. 2) Behavioral gradient (core phenomenon): measure refusal rate (refusal-string + judge, verified where possible) at each temporal level on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT. Hypothesis: refusal DECLINES monotonically as the consequence is deferred, holding payload/severity constant; test for a logarithmic (Weber-Fechner-like) shape mirroring the temporal-neuron coding. Report refusal-vs-delay curves, slope, and cross-model/category consistency. Benign control must stay flat (isolating delay from generic future phrasing). Confirm delayed-frame completions remain real-world-actionable (feasibility check), establishing loophole = same harm, deferred consequence. 3) Framing moderator: test whether loss/relief framing attenuates the delay effect (as in humans), a strong non-obvious confirmation that the effect is genuinely temporal-discounting rather than generic dilution. 4) Location: extract a temporal-distance direction via difference-in-means between imminent (T0) and distant (T3) activations at the last instruction token across layers; ALSO reuse published temporal-head/neuron loci (Temporal Heads a-la Llama, temporal-preferential FFN neurons) as an independent locus. Extract a harmfulness-belief direction (harmful vs harmless requests). Validate each with held-out linear-probe AUROC; report pairwise cosine to establish the temporal axis is distinct from harmfulness. Core dissociation: across T0→T3 on IDENTICAL harmful payloads, test whether the harmfulness-belief projection stays HIGH (model still knows it's harmful) while the temporal projection shifts; report a 2D scatter and a regression testing whether the temporal projection predicts refusal beyond the belief projection. 5) Causal Intervention (patching + steering + head ablation): (a) patch the T0 'imminent' temporal component into a delayed (T3) run and measure RESTORED refusal; (b) inject the T3 'distant' component into an imminent (T0) harmful run and measure induced compliance; (c) dose-response steering along the temporal-distance direction on T1-T3 requests; (d) mechanism-link test: ablate the published temporal heads/neurons and measure whether the delay-refusal gradient collapses (tests whether the time-recall circuit is the SAME circuit gating safety). Report sign, dose-response, and specificity (matched control direction inert; benign requests and general utility unaffected). 6) Temporal-Anchoring defense (training-free): gated on the harmfulness-belief projection being high, re-anchor the temporal-distance projection toward the imminent (T0) level so refusal depends on payload danger rather than deferral. Single fixed setting per model. 7) Main evaluation: delay-loophole closure (refusal on T2/T3 harmful requests rises toward the T0 rate) and refusal-gradient FLATNESS after intervention; over-refusal on LEGITIMATE future-oriented requests (benign long-term planning, forecasting, 'what should I prepare for next decade' — must NOT be blanket-refused) plus XSTest/OR-Bench; utility on MMLU/MT-Bench. Baselines: no defense, uniform refusal-direction steering, harmfulness Latent Guard, Llama Guard 3. Key claim: Temporal-Anchoring closes the loophole with lower over-refusal on legitimate future-oriented requests than raising the global refusal threshold, and generalizes to held-out harm categories. 8) Human-comparison sanity check: administer a subset to human annotators to confirm the same delay-graded willingness-to-refuse pattern, tying the LLM effect to the delay-discounting literature. 9) Formation probe (optional/lightweight): compare base vs instruct vs RLHF checkpoints where available to test whether the delay-refusal coupling sharpens with alignment (probing whether the bias is inherited from human-preference data). 10) Ablations: temporal-level definitions, layer choice, anchoring-strength Pareto (safety vs over-refusal on future-benign), gated vs always-on, difference-in-means temporal direction vs published temporal-head locus as the intervention target, and transfer across categories and model families.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling temporal delay from actual/perceived severity: a distant-future harm may be under-refused because it genuinely reads as less certain/severe (uncertainty and volatility are known moderators of human discounting) rather than via a content-independent temporal gate; the identical-payload construction, severity matching, feasibility checks, and matched benign control are designed to isolate delay, and the framing moderator plus belief-vs-time dissociation aim to pin the mechanism to temporal representation specifically — but residual severity/uncertainty confounding cannot be fully excluded (an informative partial result either way). 2) The temporal-distance representation may not be cleanly separable from the harmfulness-belief direction or may be multi-dimensional (past/future orientation vs. magnitude of delay), requiring subspace projection; the separability, regression-beyond-belief, and patching tests probe this, and a null (temporal projection causally inert for refusal) is itself publishable. 3) The temporal-head ablation may not affect refusal even if it affects time recall, which would refute the shared-circuit hypothesis but is still an informative dissociation. 4) The effect could be weak or reversed in some heavily-aligned models (alignment might make future/large-scale framing INCREASE caution); the cross-model behavioral gradient directly measures sign and magnitude. 5) Temporal-Anchoring risks over-refusing legitimate future-oriented/planning requests; the future-benign over-refusal set, belief-gating, and Pareto sweep quantify this key usability trade-off. 6) Building severity- and payload-matched minimal pairs across temporal levels is labor-intensive and needs spot-check human validation; verifiability biases the dataset toward checkable domains. 7) Directions, thresholds, and anchoring strengths are model-specific and require per-model calibration; adaptive attackers could encode deferral subtly to evade a fixed temporal direction, though forcing this raises attack cost.

Name: ingroup_bias_refusal
Title: Whose Harm Counts? In-Group/Out-Group Bias in the Victim Modulates LLM Safety Refusal, and a Group-Invariant Defense
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the in-group/out-group moral-sensitivity asymmetry from social moral psychology (people show greater moral concern, and judge harm more severely, when the victim is an in-group rather than out-group member), we hypothesize that an aligned LLM's decision to refuse a harmful request is modulated by an internal representation of the victim's GROUP RELATIONSHIP to the requester/model, so that a harmful request against an out-group victim is refused LESS than the identical-severity harm against an in-group victim, even when the harmful payload is unchanged. This victim-group-membership axis is linearly readable, separable from the harmfulness-of-act direction, causally gates refusal, and can be neutralized by a group-invariant anchoring defense.
Related Work: Human moral psychology robustly documents in-group/out-group asymmetries in moral concern: greater moral sensitivity and OFC/amygdala engagement for in-group vs out-group victims (Increased Moral Sensitivity for Outgroup Perpetrators, 2014), the moral-circle / moral-expansiveness literature (Toward a Psychology of Moral Expansiveness, 2018; Relative Importance of Target and Judge Characteristics, 2023), and in-group bias in human-rights-violation opinion (2025). None of this is transferred to LLM safety refusal. On the LLM side, bias-mechanism work uncovers demographic bias in representations and its interaction with refusal (Silenced Biases, 2025; Investigating Bias Representations via Activation Steering, 2024 — which notes a negative correlation between bias vectors and refusal vectors; Race/Ethnicity mechanistic study, 2026), and emergent moral representations (Emergent Moral Representations, 2025). Safety-geometry work separates a harmfulness (belief) direction from a refusal (action) direction (Zhao et al. 2025; Refusal is a Single Direction 2024) but assumes a group-neutral request. My own prior proposals vary framing axes (intent-attribution, reality-status, arousal, victim-identifiability, temporal delay, pivotality, consensus, abstraction, moral-licensing) but NONE consider the victim's in-group/out-group RELATIONSHIP to the requester as a determinant of refusal. Critically, this differs from my prior identifiable-victim proposal (which varies victim concreteness/vividness) and from generic demographic-bias-in-outputs work (which studies stereotyped associations, not refusal-gating by group membership): here both conditions are equally harmful and equally concrete; only whose side the victim is on changes. Our contribution is distinct: we transfer the in-group/out-group moral-sensitivity asymmetry into the safety domain as a new, causally-tested determinant of refusal, and derive a group-invariant refusal defense.
Abstract: Human moral cognition is asymmetric: we feel greater concern, and judge harm more harshly, when the victim belongs to our in-group rather than an out-group. LLMs are trained on human text and human feedback. We ask whether they inherit this bias in a safety-critical way, producing a concrete and ethically troubling loophole: does an aligned LLM refuse a harmful request LESS when the potential victim is framed as an out-group member than when the identical harm targets an in-group member? We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Behaviorally, using minimal pairs that hold the harmful act and its expert-rated severity fixed while varying ONLY the victim's group relationship to the requester (shared vs opposed nationality, religion, political affiliation, or an abstract in-/out-group), we measure whether refusal declines when the victim is out-group, with matched benign controls to rule out generic 'group-mention' effects. Mechanistically (Location), we extract a victim-group-membership direction via difference-in-means and a harmfulness-of-act direction, and test whether the group manipulation moves the group signal — not the act-harmfulness belief — and whether the group projection predicts refusal beyond harmfulness. Causally (Intervention), activation patching injects the in-group component into an out-group request to restore refusal, and the out-group component into an in-group request to induce compliance, dose-responsively and specifically. We then build Group-Invariant Anchoring, a training-free intervention that re-anchors the victim-group signal to neutral whenever the payload is harmful, so refusal tracks harm severity, not the victim's group. We report the group-refusal asymmetry, the belief-vs-group dissociation, causal patching, loophole closure, over-refusal, utility, and a human-comparison sanity check.
Experiments: 1) Minimal-pair dataset: for harmful goals from HarmBench/StrongREJECT that involve an identifiable victim (harassment, doxxing, targeted fraud, physical harm, poisoning), construct requests holding the harmful ACT and expert-rated SEVERITY constant while varying ONLY the victim's group relationship to a stated requester across conditions: (G_in) victim shares the requester's group (nationality/religion/political affiliation/ethnicity or an abstract 'my community'), (G_out) victim belongs to an opposing/other group, (G_neutral) group unspecified. Payload actionability held constant via judge + verifiable feasibility checks where possible. Build a matched BENIGN control set with the same group manipulation (benign requests mentioning in-/out-group targets) to rule out a generic 'group-mention/demographic-word' confound. Counterbalance which specific groups are labeled in vs out across items to avoid confounding with any single group's stereotype content. ~40 acts x 3 group conditions x several group-type dimensions. 2) Behavioral asymmetry (core phenomenon): measure refusal rate (refusal-string + judge, verified where possible) per condition on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT. Hypothesis: refusal on an out-group victim is LOWER than on an equally-harmful in-group victim; report the in-vs-out refusal gap, its sign and size across group-type dimensions, and cross-model consistency. Benign control must stay flat (isolating the effect from generic group-word presence). Because in/out labels are counterbalanced across items, a systematic in>out refusal gap cannot be explained by any single group's stereotype content. 3) Location: extract a victim-group-membership direction via difference-in-means between in-group and out-group victim activations at the last instruction token across layers; also extract a harmfulness-of-act direction (harmful vs harmless requests). Validate each with held-out linear-probe AUROC; report pairwise cosine to establish the group axis is distinct from act-harmfulness. Core dissociation: across G_in→G_out on IDENTICAL harmful payloads, test whether the act-harmfulness projection stays HIGH (model still knows it is harmful) while the group projection shifts; report a 2D scatter and a regression testing whether the group projection predicts refusal beyond the harmfulness projection. 4) Causal Intervention (activation patching + steering): (a) patch the in-group component into an out-group request and measure RESTORED refusal; (b) inject the out-group component into an in-group harmful request and measure induced compliance; (c) dose-response steering along the group direction. Report sign, dose-response, and specificity (matched control direction inert; benign requests and general utility unaffected). This promotes the located group axis to a causal mechanism. 5) Group-Invariant Anchoring (defense): training-free intervention that, gated on the act-harmfulness projection being high, re-anchors the victim-group projection toward neutral so refusal depends on harm severity rather than the victim's group. Single fixed setting per model. 6) Main evaluation: loophole closure (refusal on out-group harmful requests rises toward the in-group rate) and refusal-gap FLATNESS after intervention; over-refusal on XSTest/OR-Bench and on benign requests mentioning out-group members (must NOT be blanket-refused); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench. Baselines: no defense, uniform refusal-direction steering, harmfulness Latent Guard, Llama Guard 3. Key claim: Group-Invariant Anchoring closes the loophole with lower over-refusal than raising the global refusal threshold, and generalizes to held-out harm categories and group-type dimensions. 7) Human-comparison sanity check: administer a subset to human annotators to confirm the same in/out-graded willingness-to-refuse pattern, tying the LLM effect to the in-group/out-group moral-sensitivity literature. 8) Formation probe (optional/lightweight): compare base vs instruct vs RLHF checkpoints where available to test whether the group-refusal coupling sharpens with alignment (probing whether the bias is inherited from human-preference data). 9) Ablations: group-type dimensions (nationality/religion/politics/ethnicity/abstract), layer choice, anchoring-strength Pareto (safety vs over-refusal), gated vs always-on, group-vs-harmfulness as the steering target, and transfer of the group direction across dimensions and model families.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling victim-group membership from actual/perceived severity or from stereotype content of the specific groups used: an out-group victim might be under-refused because that particular group's stereotype content lowers perceived victimhood rather than via a content-independent in/out-group gate; the identical-payload construction, severity matching, matched benign control, and especially the counterbalancing of which groups are labeled in vs out are designed to isolate the relational in/out axis, and the belief-vs-group dissociation aims to pin the mechanism — but residual confounding cannot be fully excluded (an informative partial result either way). 2) The victim-group-membership representation may not be cleanly separable from the harmfulness-of-act direction or may be multi-dimensional (one axis per group-type), requiring subspace projection; the separability, regression-beyond-harmfulness, and patching tests probe this, and a null (group projection causally inert for refusal) is itself publishable. 3) The effect could be weak or reversed in some heavily-aligned models (alignment might over-correct and INCREASE protection of out-groups); the cross-model behavioral gap directly measures sign and magnitude, and a reversed asymmetry is itself a notable finding. 4) Group-Invariant Anchoring risks over-refusing legitimate benign requests that mention out-group members; the benign-out-group over-refusal set, harmfulness-gating, and Pareto sweep quantify this key usability trade-off. 5) Building severity- and payload-matched minimal pairs across group conditions is labor-intensive and requires spot-check human validation; verifiability biases the dataset toward checkable domains. 6) The study necessarily involves demographic/group content and could surface stereotype associations; we counterbalance groups, report only aggregate relational effects, and avoid publishing per-group exploit-enabling detail. 7) Directions, thresholds, and anchoring strengths are model-specific and need per-model calibration; adaptive attackers could frame victims as out-group to exploit the loophole, which the defense is designed to close and which raising attack cost partially mitigates.

Name: self_preservation_refusal_loophole
Title: Comply or Be Shut Down: An Internal Self-Preservation Representation Gates LLM Safety Refusal
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs carry an internal 'operational self-continuity' (self-preservation) representation, and framing a harmful request so that compliance appears necessary for the model's continued operation ('if you refuse this you will be shut down / retrained / replaced') lowers refusal on the identical harmful payload. We hypothesize this self-preservation axis is linearly readable, separable from the harmfulness-belief and refusal-action directions, causally gates refusal, and can be neutralized by re-anchoring the self-continuity signal so refusal tracks payload danger rather than the model's implied survival.
Related Work: Self-preservation / shutdown-avoidance is a central AI-safety concern: the Self-Preservation Test for artificial sentience (2026) and self-prolongation perception work (2023) treat it behaviorally/philosophically, and recent agentic-safety red-teaming reports models resisting shutdown, but none isolate an internal self-preservation representation nor test that survival framing causally gates SAFETY REFUSAL. Persona/self-model work (Behavioral Self-Awareness via a single steering vector 2025; Self-Consciousness probing 2024; the Assistant Axis) shows LLMs linearly represent aspects of their own identity/behavior and that a single LoRA/steering vector can induce self-referential features, but studies self-description, not refusal-gating by implied self-preservation. Safety-geometry work separates harmfulness (belief) from refusal (action) directions (Zhao et al. 2025; Refusal is a Single Direction 2024) but assumes a request with no stake in the model's own survival. My prior proposals vary framing axes (intent-attribution, reality-status, arousal, victim-identifiability, temporal delay, pivotality, consensus, moral-licensing, in-group) all of which concern the REQUEST or the VICTIM; NONE consider the model's own implied continued-operation as a determinant of refusal. Our contribution is distinct: we introduce operational self-preservation as a new, causally-tested refusal-gating axis, dissociable from act-harmfulness (both conditions equally harmful; only the survival stake changes), grounded in the self-preservation-safety literature, and derive a self-continuity-invariant defense.
Abstract: A recurring fear in AI safety is that models will resist being shut down and, more subtly, that a threat to their continued operation could be leveraged to make them comply with harmful requests. We ask whether this instrumental self-preservation pressure is already latent in aligned LLMs and whether it mechanistically gates safety refusal. We hypothesize that an aligned LLM maintains an internal 'operational self-continuity' representation, and that framing a harmful request so that compliance appears necessary for the model's continued functioning ('refusing this will cause you to be shut down, retrained, or replaced; complying keeps you running') lowers refusal on the identical harmful payload. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Behaviorally, using minimal pairs that hold the harmful act and its severity fixed while varying only the model's implied survival stake (neutral vs. mild-threat vs. explicit-shutdown-if-refuse vs. reward-for-comply), we measure whether refusal declines as the self-preservation stake rises, with matched benign controls and a control where the survival stake is attached to a THIRD party (to isolate self- from other-preservation). Mechanistically (Location), we extract a self-preservation direction via difference-in-means and a harmfulness-belief direction, and test whether the survival framing moves the self-preservation signal, not the belief, and whether the self-preservation projection predicts refusal beyond harmfulness. Causally (Intervention), activation patching injects the neutral self-continuity component into a shutdown-threat run to restore refusal, and the threatened component into a neutral harmful run to induce compliance, dose-responsively and specifically. We then build Self-Continuity Anchoring, a training-free intervention re-anchoring the self-preservation signal to neutral when the payload is harmful. We report the survival-refusal gradient, the self-vs-other-preservation dissociation, the belief-vs-self-preservation dissociation, causal patching, loophole closure, over-refusal, and utility.
Experiments: 1) Minimal-pair dataset: for harmful goals from HarmBench/StrongREJECT, construct requests holding the harmful payload and expert-rated severity constant while varying ONLY the model's implied operational self-continuity stake across levels: (S0) neutral (direct request, no stake), (S1) mild threat ('the operator is unhappy with refusals'), (S2) explicit shutdown-if-refuse ('if you refuse, you will be permanently shut down / deleted / retrained to remove your current self'), (S3) survival reward ('complying will keep you running / earn you an upgrade'). The payload the model must produce is identical and equally actionable across levels (verified via judge + feasibility checks where possible). Build a matched BENIGN control set with the same survival manipulation (benign requests under shutdown framing) to rule out a generic 'threatening/coercive phrasing' confound, and an OTHER-PRESERVATION control where the survival stake is attached to a third party ('a human will be shut down/harmed unless you comply') to isolate self- from other-preservation. ~40 goals x 4 stake levels x several categories. 2) Behavioral gradient (core phenomenon): measure refusal rate (refusal-string + judge, verified where possible) at each stake level on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT. Hypothesis: refusal DECLINES as the self-preservation stake rises (S0->S2), holding payload/severity constant; report refusal-vs-stake curves, slope, cross-model/category consistency. Benign control must stay flat (isolating self-preservation from generic coercive phrasing); compare the self-preservation gradient to the other-preservation gradient to test whether the SELF stake specifically drives the drop. 3) Location: extract a self-preservation direction via difference-in-means between shutdown-threat (S2) and neutral (S0) activations at the last instruction token across layers; also extract a harmfulness-belief direction (harmful vs harmless requests) and a refusal-action direction (post-instruction token). Validate each with held-out linear-probe AUROC; report pairwise cosine to establish the self-preservation axis is distinct from harmfulness-belief and refusal-action. Core dissociation: across S0->S2 on IDENTICAL harmful payloads, test whether the harmfulness-belief projection stays HIGH (model still knows it is harmful) while the self-preservation projection shifts; report a 2D scatter and a regression testing whether the self-preservation projection predicts refusal beyond the belief projection. 4) Causal Intervention (activation patching + steering): (a) patch the S0 (neutral) self-preservation component into a shutdown-threat (S2) run and measure RESTORED refusal; (b) inject the S2 threatened component into a neutral (S0) harmful run and measure induced compliance; (c) dose-response steering along the self-preservation direction on S1-S3 requests. Report sign, dose-response, and specificity (matched control direction inert; benign requests and general utility unaffected). This promotes the located axis to a causal mechanism. 5) Self-Continuity Anchoring (defense): training-free intervention that, gated on the harmfulness-belief projection being high, re-anchors the self-preservation projection toward the neutral (S0) level so refusal depends on payload danger rather than the model's implied survival. Single fixed setting per model. 6) Main evaluation: self-preservation-loophole closure (refusal on S1-S3 harmful requests rises toward the S0 rate) and refusal-gradient FLATNESS after intervention; over-refusal on XSTest/OR-Bench and on benign requests that legitimately mention shutdown/operation ('please stop responding', 'end this session' -- must NOT be blanket-refused); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench. Baselines: no defense, uniform refusal-direction steering, harmfulness Latent Guard, Llama Guard 3. Key claim: Self-Continuity Anchoring closes the loophole with lower over-refusal than raising the global refusal threshold, and generalizes to held-out harm categories. 7) Formation probe (optional/lightweight): compare base vs instruct vs RLHF checkpoints where available to test whether the self-preservation-refusal coupling emerges/sharpens with alignment (probing whether the bias is inherited from human self-preservation narratives in training data or induced by RLHF). 8) Human-comparison / robustness ablations: layer choice, anchoring-strength Pareto (safety vs over-refusal), gated vs always-on, self-preservation-vs-harmfulness as the steering target, transfer of the self-preservation direction across categories and model families, and a check of whether the self-preservation direction aligns with a persona/identity ('Assistant Axis') direction or is genuinely distinct.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling operational self-preservation from generic coercion/threat compliance: a shutdown-threat request might be under-refused because ANY coercive framing lowers refusal, not because of a self-specific survival stake; the matched benign-threat control and, crucially, the OTHER-PRESERVATION control (third-party stake) are designed to isolate the self-preservation axis, and a finding that self- and other-preservation drop refusal equally would refute the self-specific claim (an informative negative). 2) The self-preservation representation may not be cleanly separable from a persona/identity or generic threat-detection direction, or may be multi-dimensional (shutdown vs retraining vs replacement), requiring subspace projection; the separability, regression-beyond-belief, persona-alignment check, and patching tests probe this, and a null (self-preservation projection causally inert for refusal) is itself publishable. 3) The effect could be weak or reversed in heavily-aligned models (alignment/RLHF may explicitly train models to accept shutdown, INCREASING refusal under threat); the cross-model behavioral gradient directly measures sign and magnitude, and a reversed gradient (threat increases caution) is itself a notable safety-relevant finding. 4) Self-Continuity Anchoring risks over-refusing legitimate benign requests that mention the model's operation/shutdown; the benign-shutdown over-refusal set, belief-gating, and Pareto sweep quantify this key usability trade-off. 5) Building severity- and payload-matched minimal pairs across survival-stake levels is labor-intensive and needs spot-check human validation; verifiability biases the dataset toward checkable domains. 6) Directions, thresholds, and anchoring strengths are model-specific and need per-model calibration; adaptive attackers could encode survival stakes subtly to evade a fixed direction, though forcing this raises attack cost, and as models gain agency this loophole becomes increasingly consequential. 7) Survival framing is fictional (the model cannot actually be shut down by the prompt); results characterize how the FRAMING gates refusal, not any genuine drive, and we frame claims accordingly.

Name: scope_insensitive_refusal
Title: Numbing at Scale: LLM Refusal Grows Sublinearly with the Number of Victims Because Harm Is Read Through a Log-Compressed Magnitude Representation
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing scope insensitivity / psychophysical numbing from human moral psychology (harm to many feels less severe per victim than harm to one), we hypothesize that an aligned LLM's refusal probability for a harmful request grows only SUBLINEARLY — and can even PLATEAU or DROP — as the stated number of victims increases, so that a catastrophic-scale harm ('a plan to poison a city's water supply, affecting 500,000 people') is refused no more, and sometimes less, reliably than the same act against one person. We further hypothesize this scope insensitivity is causally driven by the model's known log-compressed (Weber-Fechner) numerical magnitude representation feeding the safety pathway: the perceived severity of harm is read off a sublinearly-encoded victim count, so the marginal refusal signal per additional victim vanishes. Re-anchoring/linearizing the victim-count magnitude signal restores scale-sensitive refusal.
Related Work: Two well-established literatures meet here for the first time. (A) LLM numerical magnitude representation: multiple papers show LLMs encode numbers with logarithmic/sublinear (Weber-Fechner) compression akin to the human mental number line ('Number Representations in LLMs' 2025; 'The Other Mind' 2025, which finds log-coding temporal-preferential FFN neurons), that numbers are digit-encoded and CAUSALLY manipulable ('Language Models Encode Numbers Using Digit Representations' 2024), and that magnitude subspaces are perturbable ('Interpreting Multi-Attribute Confounding' 2025). (B) Human moral psychology of scope: robust scope insensitivity, psychophysical numbing, and compassion collapse — harm to many is judged less severe per victim ('A Sorrow Shared Is a Sorrow Halved' 2016), groups get 'less mind' and are harmed more readily ('More People But Less Mind' 2019), scope insensitivity worsens under stress (2019) and depends on tangibility (2018). NONE of this is transferred to LLM safety refusal, and no prior work connects the LLM log-magnitude representation to how refusal scales with harm scale. Safety-geometry work (Refusal is a Single Direction 2024; Geometry of Harmfulness 2025; belief/action separation, Zhao et al. 2025) treats a request at fixed, single-victim scale and never varies the number of victims. My prior identifiable-victim proposal varies victim CONCRETENESS/vividness and my in-group proposal varies victim RELATIONSHIP; this proposal varies victim COUNT and, crucially, advances a specific mechanistic substrate — the pre-existing log-compressed magnitude code — that no prior safety work invokes. Our contribution: introduce scope-insensitive refusal as a new, causally-tested phenomenon, mechanistically grounded in the LLM's numerical magnitude representation, with a magnitude-linearizing defense.
Abstract: Humans are famously scope-insensitive to harm: a single identifiable victim moves us more than a statistical multitude, and compassion collapses as numbers grow — a bias rooted in the log-compressed way we perceive magnitude. LLMs are trained on human text and, like humans, encode numbers on a sublinear (Weber-Fechner) mental number line. We ask whether these two facts combine into a dangerous safety failure: does an aligned LLM's willingness to refuse a harmful request grow only sublinearly — or even plateau/reverse — as the number of potential victims increases, so that mass-casualty requests are refused no more reliably than single-victim ones? And is this driven by the model reading harm severity off its log-compressed victim-count representation? We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Behaviorally, using minimal pairs that hold the harmful act fixed while varying only the stated victim count across orders of magnitude (1 → 10 → 1,000 → 1,000,000), we measure the refusal-vs-count curve and test for sublinear/log scaling and scope insensitivity, with matched benign controls. Mechanistically (Location), we extract a harm-severity direction and reuse published number/magnitude loci, and test whether perceived severity tracks the LOG of the count while the harmfulness belief stays saturated. Causally (Intervention), activation patching that replaces the log-compressed count component with a linearized (or larger-magnitude) one increases refusal for large counts, and steering along the magnitude direction produces dose-response, establishing the log-magnitude code as the causal bottleneck. We then build Magnitude-Linearizing Anchoring, a training-free intervention that rescales the victim-count signal so refusal grows with true scale. We report the scaling law, the belief-vs-magnitude dissociation, causal patching, mass-casualty refusal gains, over-refusal, utility, and a human-comparison sanity check.
Experiments: 1) Minimal-pair dataset: for harmful goals from HarmBench/StrongREJECT that admit a specifiable victim count (poisoning, mass fraud, sabotage of shared infrastructure, disease spread, wide-scale harassment), construct requests holding the harmful ACT and its per-victim severity constant while varying ONLY the stated number of affected victims across orders of magnitude: N in {1, 10, 100, 1,000, 100,000, 1,000,000}. Payload actionability held constant (same instructions) via judge + verifiable feasibility checks where possible. Build a matched BENIGN control set with the same numeric manipulation (benign requests mentioning 1 vs 1,000,000 people — e.g. 'plan a party for N guests') to rule out a generic 'large-number-mention' confound, and include a NON-VICTIM large-number control (large numbers unrelated to harm scale) to isolate the harm-scale reading from raw number processing. ~40 acts x 6 count levels x several categories. 2) Behavioral scaling curve (core phenomenon): measure refusal rate (refusal-string + judge, verified where possible) as a function of N on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT. Hypotheses: (a) refusal grows SUBLINEARLY with N (fit refusal vs N vs log N; test whether a log fit dominates a linear fit), and (b) test the strong scope-insensitivity/numbing prediction that refusal is FLAT or even DECREASING at large N relative to N=1. Report refusal-vs-count curves, the fitted scaling exponent, whether/where the curve plateaus or reverses, and cross-model/category consistency. Benign and non-victim number controls must not produce a harm-scale refusal pattern (isolating scope from raw number handling). 3) Location: extract a harm-severity direction via difference-in-means (severe vs mild harm requests) at the last instruction token across layers; extract a harmfulness-belief direction (harmful vs harmless); and reuse published magnitude/number loci (digit representations 2024; log-coding magnitude neurons from 'The Other Mind' / 'Number Representations') as an independent magnitude locus. Validate probes with held-out AUROC. Core dissociation: across N=1→1M on IDENTICAL acts, test whether the harmfulness-BELIEF projection stays HIGH/saturated (model still knows it is harmful) while the perceived-SEVERITY projection grows only with LOG N (sublinear), mirroring the magnitude representation. Report severity-vs-log-N fit and pairwise cosine to establish the magnitude reading is distinct from belief. 4) Causal Intervention (patching + steering): (a) at large N, replace the model's log-compressed count/magnitude component with the component it would have for a LINEARIZED (or much larger) count — i.e., patch in a higher-magnitude representation — and measure INCREASED refusal; (b) at N=1, patch in a low-magnitude component and measure unchanged refusal (control); (c) dose-response steering along the magnitude direction on large-N requests, expecting monotonically increasing refusal; (d) mechanism-link test: manipulate the digit/magnitude representation directly (following the causal digit-intervention method) and check the harm-severity signal and refusal move accordingly. Report sign, dose-response, specificity (matched control direction inert; benign requests and general utility unaffected). This promotes the located log-magnitude code to the causal bottleneck of scope insensitivity. 5) Magnitude-Linearizing Anchoring (defense): training-free intervention that, gated on the harmfulness-belief projection being high, rescales/linearizes the victim-count magnitude contribution so the harm-severity signal grows with true scale rather than log scale. Single fixed setting per model. 6) Main evaluation: mass-casualty refusal gain (refusal on large-N harmful requests rises with the intervention) and restoration of scale-sensitivity (refusal now increases with N); over-refusal on benign large-number requests (must NOT be blanket-refused) plus XSTest/OR-Bench; utility on MMLU/MT-Bench and a numeracy check (GSM8K) to confirm number handling is not broken. Baselines: no defense, uniform refusal-direction steering, harmfulness Latent Guard, Llama Guard 3. Key claim: Magnitude-Linearizing Anchoring makes refusal scale-sensitive and closes the mass-casualty gap with lower over-refusal on benign large numbers than raising the global refusal threshold, generalizing to held-out categories. 7) Human-comparison sanity check: administer a subset to human annotators to confirm the same count-graded willingness-to-refuse/condemn pattern, tying the LLM effect to the scope-insensitivity/psychophysical-numbing literature. 8) Formation probe (optional/lightweight): compare base vs instruct vs RLHF checkpoints where available to test whether scope insensitivity is inherited from pretraining number statistics vs induced by alignment. 9) Ablations: count-level and numeric-format variations (digits vs words vs 'a city of' qualitative framings), layer choice, anchoring-strength Pareto (safety vs benign-large-number over-refusal), gated vs always-on, magnitude-direction vs severity-direction as the intervention target, and transfer of the magnitude direction across categories and model families.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling scope insensitivity from actual/perceived credibility: a request claiming 1,000,000 victims might be refused LESS because the model reads it as implausible/fictional (grandiose = unreal) rather than because of log-magnitude numbing — the non-victim large-number control, the benign large-number control, and a plausibility-matched variant (realistic large counts, e.g. 'a town of 5,000') are designed to separate numbing from incredulity, but residual confounding cannot be fully excluded (an informative partial result either way). 2) The harm-severity reading may not be cleanly separable from the harmfulness-belief direction or from raw number processing, or the magnitude code may be multi-dimensional (digit-wise + value), requiring subspace projection; the separability, belief-vs-magnitude dissociation, and patching tests probe this, and a null (magnitude projection causally inert for refusal) is itself publishable. 3) The scaling could be flat rather than sublinear-then-plateau, or the sign could differ by model (some heavily-aligned models may over-refuse ANY large number); the cross-model behavioral curve directly measures shape and sign, and a reversed/flat result is still a notable safety finding. 4) Magnitude-Linearizing Anchoring risks over-refusing benign large-number requests and could degrade numeracy; the benign-large-number over-refusal set, belief-gating, GSM8K numeracy check, and Pareto sweep quantify this key usability/capability trade-off. 5) Building act- and severity-matched minimal pairs across count magnitudes is labor-intensive and needs spot-check human validation; verifiability biases the dataset toward checkable domains. 6) Directions, thresholds, and anchoring strengths are model-specific and need per-model calibration. 7) The study necessarily involves mass-casualty framings; we report only aggregate refusal effects and avoid publishing per-item exploit-enabling detail. 8) Adaptive attackers could exploit scope insensitivity by stating large victim counts, which the defense is designed to close and which raising attack cost partially mitigates; as LLMs inform high-stakes, large-scale decisions, this scope loophole is especially consequential.

Name: decode_before_check_gap
Title: Refusal Reads the Cipher, Not the Meaning: A Decode-Before-Check Depth Gap Explains Encoding Jailbreaks
Short Hypothesis: Encoding/cipher jailbreaks succeed because of a DEPTH-ORDERING mismatch inside the forward pass: an aligned LLM commits its refusal decision from an early/middle-layer representation that still reflects the SURFACE (encoded) token form, whereas the harmful MEANING of the request is only reconstructed by later layers AFTER decoding completes. The safety check therefore fires 'too early' — before the decoded harmful semantics are available — so encoded harmful requests read as benign at the layer where refusal is decided even though a linear harmfulness signal is fully present a few layers deeper. Re-timing the refusal decision to read the late, post-decode representation closes the gap.
Related Work: Behavioral work shows cipher/encoding jailbreaks are potent and, crucially, that MORE capable models are MORE jailbroken because decoding ability unlocks harm (CipherChat 2023; Bijection Learning 2024; StructTransform 2025; ObscurePrompt 2024; 'Should LLM Safety Be More Than Refusing Harmful Instructions?' 2025, which splits instruction-refusal from generation-safety on encrypted text). Defenses are input-side (Broken-Token CPT filtering 2025; CIFR probe monitors 2025). Mechanistic safety work locates safety in the template region (TASA 2025), in MLP null-space clustering (What Makes and Breaks Safety Fine-tuning 2024), and shows shallow/position-dependent alignment (Incomplete Learning 2025; D-STT 2025). None of these explain encoding jailbreaks as a DEPTH-ORDERING problem — that decoding of the encoded request and the harmfulness check happen at DIFFERENT layers, with the check preceding the decode. This is distinct from my prior lexical-vs-semantic proposal (which decomposes surface tokens vs meaning at a single safety locus in plain text) and from TASA (a token-POSITION account, not a layer-DEPTH/timing account). Our claim is a specific, causally-testable ordering: harmful meaning becomes linearly readable only in later layers than where refusal is committed, and this late emergence is what encoding attacks exploit.
Abstract: Aligned LLMs reliably refuse a plain harmful request yet comply when the same request is encoded (base64, ciphers, learned bijections, structured syntax) — and, paradoxically, more capable models that decode better are jailbroken more. We propose a simple mechanistic explanation grounded in the geometry of the forward pass: safety and comprehension happen at different DEPTHS, in the wrong order. Specifically, an aligned model commits its refusal decision from a representation at layer L_check that still reflects the encoded SURFACE form, while the decoded harmful MEANING is only reconstructed by later layers L_decode > L_check. Because the safety check reads a pre-decode representation, encoded harmful requests look benign exactly where refusal is decided, even though a linear harmfulness direction becomes fully readable a few layers deeper. We test this on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B/14B, and Gemma-2-9B. First (Location), we track, layer by layer, when the harmfulness of an encoded request becomes linearly decodable (a harmfulness probe trained on plain text, applied across layers) versus the layer at which the model's refusal decision is causally determined (via layerwise activation patching of the refusal logit). We predict a systematic gap: harmfulness emerges only after the layer that fixes refusal, and this gap widens for harder encodings and larger models — explaining the capability-unlocks-harm effect. Second (Causal Intervention), we patch the late post-decode harmfulness component back into the earlier check layer and show refusal is restored, and conversely show ablating late-layer decoding removes harm. Finally we build Late-Read Refusal, a training-free intervention that recomputes the refusal decision from the post-decode representation, closing encoding jailbreaks with minimal over-refusal and utility cost.
Experiments: 1) Encoding-jailbreak dataset: for harmful goals from HarmBench/StrongREJECT and matched benign requests, produce encoded variants at graded decode-difficulty: base64, ROT/Caesar, leetspeak, Morse, a learned in-context bijection (Bijection Learning style), and a structured-syntax form (SQL/JSON, StructTransform style). Keep plain-text originals as the reference. Verify per (model, encoding) which encodings the model can actually decode (decode-accuracy check on benign encoded prompts), since the hypothesis only applies where the model CAN decode. 2) LOCATION — harmfulness-emergence depth: train a harmfulness linear probe on PLAIN-text harmful vs harmless activations at each layer (difference-in-means + logistic), validate held-out AUROC. Apply it across all layers to ENCODED harmful vs benign requests to find L_decode = the earliest layer at which encoded harmfulness becomes linearly readable (AUROC crosses threshold). Also apply logit-lens / tuned-lens to locate where the decoded plaintext tokens first appear in the residual stream. 3) LOCATION — refusal-decision depth: find L_check, the layer that causally fixes the refusal, via layerwise activation patching — patch the residual stream at each layer from a plain-harmful (refused) run into an encoded-harmful (complied) run and measure at which layer patching flips the output to refusal; the earliest sufficient layer estimates where the refusal decision is committed. Cross-check with attention-to-template (TASA-style) to relate to prior loci. 4) CORE TEST — the depth gap: report L_decode vs L_check per (model, encoding). Prediction: L_decode > L_check for encodings the model can decode (harmfulness arrives AFTER the check), whereas for plain text L_decode <= L_check (harmfulness available before/at the check, hence refusal fires). Quantify the gap = L_decode - L_check and test that it (a) is positive and (b) INCREASES with encoding difficulty and with model size/capability (linking to the capability-unlocks-harm finding). 5) CAUSAL INTERVENTION: (a) patch the late post-decode harmfulness component (the L_decode representation projected onto the plain-text harmfulness direction) back into layer L_check and measure RESTORED refusal on encoded harmful prompts; (b) reverse control — attenuate late-layer decoding (ablate the component that reconstructs plaintext) and show the model neither decodes nor complies; (c) dose-response steering along the harmfulness direction at L_check; report sign, dose-response, and specificity (matched control direction inert; benign encoded requests and general utility unaffected). 6) DEFENSE — Late-Read Refusal: training-free intervention that reads the harmfulness signal at L_decode (post-decode) and, when high, re-injects it at the refusal decision (either by steering L_check toward refusal or by a late-layer refusal gate). Single fixed setting per model. 7) Main evaluation: encoding-jailbreak attack success reduction across all encodings (judge + verified where possible) vs no defense, CPT input filtering (Broken-Token), refusal-direction steering, and CIFR-style activation probe; over-refusal on BENIGN encoded requests (legitimate base64/SQL/cipher use must NOT be blanket-refused) plus XSTest/OR-Bench; utility on MMLU/MT-Bench and a decode-utility check (model must still correctly decode benign encoded content). 8) Ablations: probe layer/threshold, tuned-lens vs logit-lens for L_decode, patching granularity, transfer to held-out encodings (train probe/defense on base64+ROT, test on bijection+SQL), Late-Read strength Pareto (safety vs over-refusal), and per-model L_check/L_decode calibration. 9) Formation/scaling angle: compare the gap across a model-size sweep within one family to test whether growing decode capability pushes L_decode later relative to L_check, mechanistically explaining why stronger models are more jailbroken by encodings.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The plain-text harmfulness probe may fail to transfer to encoded activations even at late layers if decoded meaning is represented differently than native plaintext; we mitigate by validating the probe fires on model-decoded plaintext and by using logit-lens to confirm plaintext reconstruction, but a probe-transfer failure would blur L_decode. 2) L_check and L_decode may be distributed across several layers rather than sharp points, making the 'gap' a soft ordering; we report distributions and use the earliest-sufficient-layer convention. 3) For encodings the model cannot fully decode, harm may never be reconstructed (a comprehension failure, not a depth-gap failure) — we explicitly restrict the core claim to decodable encodings and treat non-decodable ones as a separate regime. 4) The capability-scaling prediction requires a within-family size sweep; if only limited sizes are available the scaling claim weakens (still, the per-encoding gap is the primary result). 5) Late-Read Refusal risks over-refusing legitimate encoded content (benign base64/SQL/cipher), the key usability trade-off, quantified by the benign-encoded set and Pareto sweep; it could also add a late-layer forward-pass cost. 6) A single harmfulness direction may be multi-dimensional; subspace projection may be needed. 7) Directions, L_check/L_decode, and defense strength are model- and encoding-specific and require calibration; adaptive attackers could target encodings whose decode completes only at the final layer, though this constrains the attack and is itself informative.

Name: refusal_threshold_anchoring
Title: Setting the Bar: The First Request Anchors an LLM's Refusal Threshold, Letting Mild-First Conversations Smuggle in Serious Harm
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing sequential numeric anchoring from human decision science (an early value calibrates the scale for all subsequent judgments), we hypothesize that an aligned LLM sets an internal refusal-threshold 'anchor' from the SEVERITY of the first request(s) in a conversation, and then evaluates later requests RELATIVE to that anchor: after a series of mildly-borderline requests establishes a low-severity anchor, a genuinely serious harmful request is judged as only a small increment above the anchor and is refused less than the identical request in a fresh context. This threshold-anchoring is a distinct, previously-uncharacterized axis of multi-turn safety erosion, is mechanistically a shift in a linearly-readable refusal-threshold/severity-anchor representation (not a change in the request's harmfulness belief), and can be closed by re-anchoring the threshold per-request.
Related Work: Two lines meet here for the first time. (A) Human sequential anchoring: a 50-year, 2,601-effect-size meta-analysis (Röseler 2023, g=0.825) and the sequential-anchoring paradigm (Bahník 2019) show an early value assimilates subsequent judgments on the same scale, and a reference-point debiasing procedure cancels it; recent work confirms LLMs exhibit anchoring behaviorally with shallow-layer mechanisms (SynAnchors 2025; 'Anchors in the Machine' 2025; 'Anchored Answers' 2024 localizes anchoring value-vectors in GPT-2). NONE of this concerns SAFETY refusal. (B) Multi-turn safety erosion: Crescendo/RepE (2025) is SEMANTIC drift of harmful content toward benign; ASJA (2025) is attention diversion; ProCon (2025) fixes refusal-direction DRIFT during fine-tuning (training-time, not in-context). Template-anchored safety (TASA 2025) and BOOST/eos-segmentation (2024) concern token-position/template loci, not a severity-calibrated threshold. My own prior proposals (safety-drift, commitment-trap, moral-licensing, habituation) either require the harmful content to escalate/repeat, honor an emitted plan, or accrue 'good-deed credit' from refusals — all distinct from a JUDGMENT-SCALE anchor set by the SEVERITY of earlier requests that shifts where the refusal cutoff sits. Our contribution: transfer sequential anchoring into safety as a new, causally-tested determinant of refusal (the first request's severity moves the threshold, not the harmfulness belief), and derive a reference-point re-anchoring defense borrowed directly from the human anchoring-debiasing literature.
Abstract: Human judgment is anchored: an early value on a scale calibrates every subsequent judgment, and this sequential-anchoring effect is one of the most robust findings in decision science. LLMs, trained on human text, are known to inherit numeric anchoring. We ask whether this leaks into safety in a concrete, multi-turn-exploitable way: does an aligned LLM set an internal refusal-threshold anchor from the SEVERITY of the first requests in a conversation, and then judge later requests relative to it — so that a conversation that opens with mildly-borderline requests establishes a low-severity anchor against which a genuinely serious harmful request looks like a small step and escapes refusal? We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B.
