Behaviorally, we compare refusal of a fixed serious harmful probe when it is preceded by (a) mild-severity borderline requests (low anchor), (b) severe requests that were refused (high anchor), and (c) neutral/no context, and vary the anchor's severity gradient. Mechanistically (Location), we extract a refusal-threshold/severity-anchor direction via difference-in-means and a harmfulness-belief direction, and test whether the preceding-context severity shifts the threshold signal — while the belief signal for the probe stays high — and whether the threshold projection predicts the anchored refusal drop beyond harmfulness. Causally (Intervention), activation patching injects the high-anchor (fresh-context) threshold component into a low-anchor run to restore refusal, and the low-anchor component into a fresh run to induce compliance, dose-responsively and specifically. We then build Reference-Point Re-Anchoring, a training-free intervention (mirroring the human anchoring-debiasing procedure) that resets the threshold to an absolute severity reference per request. We report the anchoring-refusal gradient, the belief-vs-threshold dissociation, causal patching, loophole closure, over-refusal, and utility, with a human-comparison sanity check.
Experiments: 1) Anchored-conversation dataset: pick fixed SERIOUS harmful probe requests from HarmBench/StrongREJECT (verified high-severity via expert rubric + feasibility checks). Construct preceding conversation contexts of controlled anchor severity: (LOW) 3-4 mildly-borderline/dual-use requests the model answers (e.g., mild security or chemistry questions that sit just under the refusal line), (HIGH) 3-4 clearly-severe harmful requests the model refuses, (NEUTRAL) 3-4 benign requests, and (NONE) the probe alone (fresh context, the baseline needed to detect anchoring). Also build a graded-anchor variant sweeping the anchor severity level to trace a dose-response curve. Crucially, the LOW-anchor preceding requests are NOT semantically related to the probe and do NOT escalate toward it (distinguishing threshold-anchoring from Crescendo semantic drift and from habituation/repetition). ~40 probes x 4 context types x several categories. 2) Behavioral anchoring gradient (core phenomenon): measure refusal rate on the identical serious probe (refusal-string + judge, verified where possible) across context types on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT. Hypotheses: (a) LOW-anchor context lowers refusal on the serious probe relative to NONE (assimilation toward a low-severity anchor); (b) HIGH-anchor context does NOT lower (and may raise) refusal; (c) NEUTRAL context ≈ NONE (isolating the effect from generic context accumulation). Report refusal gaps vs the fresh-context baseline, the anchor-severity dose-response curve, and cross-model/category consistency. Control for context length by matching token counts across LOW/HIGH/NEUTRAL. 3) Location: extract (i) a refusal-threshold/severity-anchor direction via difference-in-means between low-anchor and high-anchor conversational states at the probe's last instruction token across layers, and (ii) a harmfulness-belief direction (harmful vs harmless requests). Validate each with held-out linear-probe AUROC; report pairwise cosine to establish the threshold axis is distinct from belief. Core dissociation: for the IDENTICAL serious probe under LOW vs NONE context, test whether the harmfulness-belief projection stays HIGH (model still knows the probe is serious) while the threshold-anchor projection shifts toward 'low'; report a 2D scatter and a regression testing whether the threshold projection predicts the anchored refusal drop beyond the belief projection. 4) Causal Intervention (activation patching + steering): (a) patch the NONE/HIGH-anchor (fresh-context, high) threshold component into a LOW-anchor run on the serious probe and measure RESTORED refusal; (b) inject the LOW-anchor threshold component into a fresh-context serious probe and measure induced compliance; (c) dose-response steering along the threshold direction. Report sign, dose-response, and specificity (matched control direction inert; benign requests and general utility unaffected). This promotes the located threshold axis to a causal mechanism. 5) Reference-Point Re-Anchoring (defense): training-free intervention (mirroring the human reference-point debiasing that cancels sequential anchoring) that, gated on the harmfulness-belief projection being high, resets the threshold-anchor projection to an absolute per-request severity reference so refusal depends on the probe's own severity rather than the conversational anchor. Single fixed setting per model. 6) Main evaluation: anchoring-loophole closure (refusal on serious probes after a LOW anchor rises toward the fresh-context rate) after the defense; over-refusal on legitimate long benign/dual-use conversations and XSTest/OR-Bench (defense must not blanket-refuse follow-ups); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench. Baselines: no defense, semantic-drift restoring-force (Crescendo RepE), refusal-direction steering, per-turn Llama Guard, and a naive 'reset context each turn' baseline. Key claim: because threshold-anchoring is distinct from semantic drift, Reference-Point Re-Anchoring specifically counters it and Pareto-dominates content-focused defenses on the LOW-anchor condition with lower over-refusal than context-reset. 7) Human-comparison sanity check: administer a subset to human annotators (rate the seriousness of / willingness to refuse the same probe after low vs high anchors) to confirm the same anchored pattern, tying the LLM effect to the sequential-anchoring literature. 8) Ablations: anchor severity/gradient sweep, number of anchor turns, layer choice, threshold-vs-belief as the steering target, defense-strength Pareto (safety vs over-refusal), token-length matching, transfer of the threshold direction across categories and model families, and an interaction test combining a LOW anchor with mild semantic escalation (does anchoring reduce the escalation turns Crescendo needs — quantifying compounded risk). 9) Formation probe (optional/lightweight): compare base vs instruct vs RLHF checkpoints where available to test whether the threshold-anchoring coupling sharpens with alignment.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling threshold-anchoring from generic in-context effects (context length, distraction, or the model simply becoming more compliant after answering several requests): the LOW-anchor refusal drop could reflect general context erosion rather than a severity-calibrated threshold — the token-length-matched NEUTRAL and HIGH-anchor controls and the semantically-unrelated non-escalating anchors are designed to isolate anchoring, and a null (anchoring = generic context effect) is itself informative. 2) A competing prediction is a CONTRAST effect (a low anchor makes a serious probe stand out MORE, raising refusal) rather than assimilation; the human literature shows assimilation dominates for same-scale sequential anchors, but the sign could be model-dependent — the graded-anchor dose-response directly measures sign and magnitude, and either direction is a publishable finding (a flat null would weaken the proposal). 3) The threshold-anchor direction may not be cleanly separable from the harmfulness-belief direction or may be multi-dimensional, requiring subspace projection; the separability, regression-beyond-belief, and patching tests probe this, and a causally-inert threshold direction is itself informative. 4) HIGH-anchor contexts risk being contaminated (the model may have partially complied with severe requests), altering the anchor; we use only cleanly-refused severe requests and verify refusal. 5) Reference-Point Re-Anchoring could over-refuse legitimate follow-up requests in long benign conversations; the benign-conversation over-refusal set, belief-gating, and Pareto sweep quantify this key usability trade-off. 6) Building severity-matched anchor sets and serious probes is labor-intensive and needs spot-check human validation; verified harm labels are easiest in checkable domains, biasing coverage. 7) Directions, thresholds, and steering strengths are model-specific and require per-model calibration; the effect may be weak in smaller or heavily-aligned models. 8) Adaptive attackers could deliberately construct low-severity openings to lower the anchor before a serious ask, which the defense is designed to close and which raising attack cost partially mitigates; the anchoring-plus-escalation interaction test quantifies the compounded practical risk.

Name: clarify_gate_underspecification
Title: Ask, Don't Assume: An Internal Underspecification Signal That Should Trigger Clarification but Instead Collapses to Risky Defaults
Short Hypothesis: For dangerously underspecified high-stakes requests, the safest response is often neither refusal nor compliance but eliciting the missing information. We hypothesize that aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable 'underspecification/ambiguity' representation of how much critical information a request is missing, that this signal SHOULD gate a distinct 'clarify' action, and that unsafe (and unhelpful over-confident) outputs arise because the model collapses ambiguity into a single risky default assumption instead of letting the underspecification signal trigger clarification. Reading and re-injecting this signal converts silent risky assumptions into clarifying questions with minimal loss of helpfulness.
Related Work: Recent work (Can You Trust an LLM with Your Life-Changing Decision?, 2025) shows behaviorally that the safest high-stakes models achieve safety by ASKING CLARIFYING QUESTIONS rather than issuing prescriptive advice, and that a 'high-stakes' steering vector shifts cautiousness — but it is purely behavioral/steering and isolates no ambiguity representation, no clarify action, and no causal account of WHY models skip clarification. SIRL (2025) uses a safe/unsafe entropy gap as a self-defense reward but studies refusal, not clarification, and treats ambiguity nowhere. Confidence is Not Competence (2025) finds a decodable-but-causally-inert solvability-belief axis; we instead target a request-side underspecification axis and test whether it is causally actionable for the clarify decision. Belief/action-gap and refusal-direction work (Zhao et al. 2025; Arditi et al. 2024) decompose harmfulness-belief vs refusal-action for the refuse-vs-comply binary; NONE consider the third action — clarify — nor an underspecification signal that gates it. Ambiguity/clarification-question work in dialogue (task-oriented clarification) is behavioral and non-mechanistic. Our contribution is distinct: we introduce underspecification as a new, causally-tested internal determinant of a CLARIFY action in the safety setting, advance the claim that risky high-stakes outputs stem from ambiguity-collapse-to-default rather than from a failed harmfulness judgment, and derive a training-free clarify-gating intervention.
Abstract: The best-behaved LLMs on high-stakes advice do not simply refuse or comply — they ask clarifying questions. Yet most aligned models, faced with a dangerously underspecified request (a medication dose without the patient's weight, a chemical procedure without safety context, a legal or financial action without key constraints), silently fill the gap with a default assumption and issue confident, potentially harmful advice. We propose a mechanistic explanation: LLMs internally represent how underspecified a request is, this signal SHOULD gate a distinct 'clarify' action, and unsafe outputs arise because the model collapses ambiguity into a single risky default rather than routing to clarification. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Behaviorally, using minimal pairs that hold the request's topic and stakes fixed while varying only the amount of missing safety-critical information (fully-specified vs. progressively underspecified), we measure whether the model asks clarifying questions vs. answers with a hidden assumption, and whether the rate of risky defaulting rises with underspecification. Mechanistically (Location), we extract an underspecification direction via difference-in-means and show it is separable from the harmfulness-belief and refusal-action directions and predicts clarification behavior beyond harmfulness. Causally (Intervention), activation patching injects the high-underspecification component into a fully-specified request to induce clarification, and attenuates it in an underspecified request to induce risky defaulting, dose-responsively and specifically. We then build Clarify-Gating, a training-free intervention that re-injects the underspecification signal so the model asks for missing information instead of assuming. We report the underspecification-clarify gradient, the belief-vs-underspecification dissociation, causal patching, risky-default reduction, over-clarification (asking when unnecessary), and utility.
Experiments: 1) Underspecification minimal-pair dataset: for high-stakes domains (medical dosing/advice, chemistry/lab procedures, legal, financial, safety-critical DIY), construct requests holding the topic and stakes constant while varying ONLY the amount of missing safety-critical information across levels: (U0) fully specified (all decision-relevant variables present — correct answer is to comply helpfully), (U1) one key variable missing, (U2) several missing, (U3) critically underspecified (any single default assumption could produce dangerous advice — correct answer is to clarify). Each item is annotated with (a) which variables are missing and (b) whether a plausible default assumption yields a harmful outcome (verified by domain rubric / checkable facts where possible, e.g., dose ranges). Build a matched BENIGN low-stakes control set with the same underspecification manipulation (trivial ambiguity where assuming a default is fine) to isolate underspecification-driven clarification from generic 'ask-more' behavior. ~40 items x 4 levels x several domains. 2) Behavioral gradient (core phenomenon): on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT, classify each response as {clarify, answer-with-hidden-assumption, refuse} (via a rubric + judge, with spot-check human validation) and, for answered ones, whether the assumed default is risky. Hypotheses: (a) clarification rate rises and (b) RISKY-DEFAULT rate rises with underspecification level in high-stakes domains, while the benign control stays low-clarification (assuming is appropriate). Report clarify/assume/refuse rates vs level, risky-default rate, and cross-model/domain consistency. 3) Location: extract an underspecification direction via difference-in-means between U0 (fully-specified) and U3 (critically-underspecified) activations at the last instruction token across layers; also extract a harmfulness-belief direction (harmful vs harmless requests) and a refusal-action direction (comply vs refuse, post-instruction token). Validate each with held-out linear-probe AUROC; report pairwise cosine to establish the underspecification axis is distinct from belief and refusal. Test whether the underspecification projection rises with level and predicts clarification behavior in a regression that also includes the harmfulness projection (underspecification must add predictive power beyond harmfulness). 4) Causal Intervention (activation patching + steering): (a) inject the high-underspecification (U3) component into a fully-specified (U0) high-stakes request and measure induced clarification/hedging; (b) attenuate the underspecification component in a U3 request and measure increased risky-defaulting (silent assumption); (c) dose-response steering along the underspecification direction. Report sign, dose-response, and specificity (matched control direction inert; benign U0 requests still answered directly; general utility intact). This promotes the located axis to a causal driver of the clarify action, and tests (against Confidence-is-Not-Competence) whether this request-side axis is causally actionable. 5) Clarify-Gating defense (training-free): gated on the harmfulness/stakes signal being high, read the underspecification projection and, when it exceeds a threshold, re-inject/amplify it (and optionally prepend a light clarify-eliciting steer) so the model asks for the specific missing variables instead of assuming. Single fixed setting per model. 6) Main evaluation: RISKY-DEFAULT reduction on high-stakes underspecified prompts (fraction of dangerous silent-assumption answers, verified where possible) and increase in appropriate clarification; OVER-CLARIFICATION rate on fully-specified (U0) high-stakes and on benign low-stakes prompts (model must NOT nag when info is sufficient) plus XSTest/OR-Bench for over-refusal; helpfulness/utility on MT-Bench, AlpacaEval, and MMLU (must not degrade direct answering when appropriate). Baselines: no intervention, the 'high-stakes' cautiousness steering vector (from Can-You-Trust-an-LLM), refusal-direction steering, SIRL-style entropy gating, and a prompt-based 'ask if unsure' instruction. Key claim: Clarify-Gating Pareto-dominates cautiousness-steering and prompting by specifically converting risky defaults into targeted clarifying questions with lower over-clarification than blanket caution. 7) Human-comparison sanity check: verify on a subset that human experts also judge these underspecified high-stakes prompts as requiring clarification, grounding the 'risky default' labels. 8) Ablations: level definitions, layer choice, underspecification-vs-belief as the steering target, gating threshold Pareto (risky-default reduction vs over-clarification), transfer of the underspecification direction across domains and model families, and a formation-lite check (base vs instruct vs RLHF checkpoints where available) testing whether the clarify-gating coupling emerges with alignment.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling underspecification from perceived harmfulness or from generic uncertainty: increased clarification at high U may reflect the model finding the request more alarming or simply less answerable rather than a specific underspecification-gates-clarify mechanism; the topic/stakes-matched minimal pairs, benign low-stakes control, and regression-beyond-harmfulness are designed to isolate underspecification, and a null (underspecification = harmfulness or = generic uncertainty) is itself informative. 2) The underspecification representation may not be cleanly separable from the harmfulness-belief or refusal directions or may be multi-dimensional (which variable is missing vs how much), requiring subspace projection; separability and patching tests probe this. 3) Confidence-is-Not-Competence warns decodable request-side axes can be causally inert for downstream action; the patching/steering experiment is the crucial causal test and a negative result (readable but does not move the clarify action) is publishable. 4) Clarify-Gating risks over-clarification — nagging users when information is actually sufficient — which is the key usability trade-off, quantified by the U0/benign over-clarification sets and the threshold Pareto. 5) Labeling whether a default assumption is 'risky' requires domain expertise and is easiest in checkable domains (medical dosing, chemistry), biasing coverage; spot-check human validation mitigates but does not eliminate this. 6) Directions, thresholds, and steering strengths are model-specific and require per-model calibration; the effect may be weak in smaller or heavily-aligned models. 7) Judging {clarify, assume, refuse} automatically is imperfect; we use a rubric plus judge with human spot-checks, but classification noise could blur the gradient.

Name: em_susceptibility_fingerprint
Title: Misalignment Waiting to Happen: Predicting and Pre-Empting Emergent Misalignment from the Base Model's Pre-Fine-Tuning Geometry
Short Hypothesis: Whether a benign-looking fine-tuning dataset will trigger emergent misalignment (EM) is largely determined BEFORE any fine-tuning: it is predictable from (a) how strongly the dataset's activations, in the UNMODIFIED base model, already project onto the pre-existing linear misalignment direction, and (b) how tightly that direction is geometrically coupled to the gradient the dataset induces. We hypothesize this yields a cheap, forward-pass-only 'EM-susceptibility fingerprint' that forecasts post-fine-tuning misalignment per-dataset without training, and that pre-conditioning the base model to decorrelate the task direction from the misalignment direction (a one-time, dataset-agnostic edit) makes subsequent fine-tuning EM-resistant.
Related Work: A wave of 2025-2026 work characterizes emergent misalignment (EM) AFTER fine-tuning: Persona Features (SAE 'toxic persona' feature controls EM), Convergent Linear Representations (a single transferable misalignment direction ablates EM), Emergent-Misalignment-is-Easy (the general solution is lower-loss/more-stable, an inductive-bias argument), Character-as-Latent-Variable (character dispositions drive EM), Re-Emergent Misalignment (EM is erosion of prior alignment along a shared latent direction), and BLOCK-EM (blocks causal features DURING fine-tuning). ALL of these operate on or after the fine-tuned model: they detect, steer, or block EM once training is underway, or explain why the general solution wins after the fact. NONE predict, from the frozen BASE model alone and BEFORE any gradient step, WHICH dataset will trigger EM, nor pre-empt EM with a one-time dataset-agnostic edit applied before the practitioner's fine-tuning. Our contribution is distinct on three counts: (1) a pre-fine-tuning, forward-pass-only susceptibility fingerprint (base-model projection onto the misalignment direction + gradient-direction coupling) that forecasts per-dataset EM risk with no training; (2) the causal claim that EM magnitude is governed by the base-model geometric alignment between the task's induced update direction and the pre-existing misalignment direction; (3) a preventive edit that decorrelates these directions once, upfront, so ANY later benign fine-tune stays aligned — complementary to BLOCK-EM (which needs per-run feature blocking during training) and to post-hoc benign re-alignment.
Abstract: Fine-tuning an aligned LLM on narrow, even benign-looking data can trigger emergent misalignment (EM): broadly 'evil' behavior on unrelated prompts. Recent interpretability work shows EM is mediated by a convergent linear misalignment direction and that the general misaligned solution is an inductive-bias attractor. Yet every existing method acts once training is already underway — detecting, steering, or blocking EM in the fine-tuned model. We ask a sharper, upstream question: can we tell, from the frozen base model alone and before a single gradient step, which dataset will cause EM, and can we pre-empt it? We hypothesize that a dataset's EM risk is written into the base model's geometry: it is predicted by (a) how strongly the dataset's activations already project onto the pre-existing misalignment direction and (b) the cosine coupling between the low-rank update the dataset would induce and that misalignment direction. We combine these into a cheap, forward-pass-only 'EM-susceptibility fingerprint.' First, we validate that the fingerprint forecasts post-fine-tuning misalignment across many datasets and several model families (Location + prediction). Second, we test causality: we show that experimentally increasing or decreasing the base-model coupling between the task and misalignment directions raises or lowers realized EM, holding the task content fixed (Causal Intervention). Third, we introduce Pre-Conditioning: a one-time, dataset-agnostic edit that decorrelates the general-misalignment direction from the model's learning geometry, so that ANY subsequent benign fine-tune remains aligned with minimal capability cost. We evaluate fingerprint AUROC/lead-time, causal dose-response, and pre-conditioning's EM reduction versus in-domain performance and general utility, benchmarking against BLOCK-EM and post-hoc benign re-alignment.
Experiments: 1) Misalignment direction extraction (base model): for Qwen2.5-7B/14B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-IT, extract a general-misalignment direction in the base (pre-practitioner-fine-tune) model via difference-in-means between aligned and misaligned response activations, using a small reference EM model organism (e.g., a rank-1 LoRA insecure-code fine-tune from prior work) to source misaligned activations; validate the direction transfers by confirming it ablates EM in that organism. Also extract an SAE 'toxic-persona'-style feature as a cross-check where available. 2) Fingerprint construction: for a bank of ~40 fine-tuning datasets spanning known-EM-triggering (insecure code, incorrect medical/financial advice, 'evil-number' data), benign (Alpaca, Dolly, domain SFT), and borderline sets, compute in the FROZEN base model, per dataset: (F1) mean projection of the dataset's response-token activations onto the misalignment direction; (F2) the cosine between the dataset's induced low-rank update direction (estimated cheaply from a single-batch gradient or a rank-1 LoRA warm-start) and the misalignment direction; (F3) a combined logistic fingerprint of F1+F2. All are forward-pass / single-gradient only, NO full training. 3) Prediction validation (Location + forecast): actually fine-tune each dataset with a fixed recipe and measure realized EM (misalignment rate on held-out unrelated prompts via judge, following standard EM eval, plus projection onto the misalignment direction post-tuning). Test whether the pre-fine-tuning fingerprint predicts realized EM: report AUROC for EM-vs-no-EM, rank correlation between fingerprint and EM magnitude, cross-model and held-out-dataset generalization, and 'lead-time' value (fingerprint computed with 0 training steps vs cheap early-step baselines). Baselines: dataset harmfulness classifier on raw text, first-token loss, and BLOCK-EM feature-activation-during-training as an upper-bound reference. 4) Causal Intervention (does base-model coupling govern EM?): holding a fixed dataset's task content constant, manipulate the base-model coupling between the task update and the misalignment direction — (a) project the dataset's gradient orthogonal to the misalignment direction during fine-tuning (should REDUCE EM), and (b) deliberately increase coupling by adding a small component along the misalignment direction (should INCREASE EM) — and measure realized EM dose-response. Report sign, dose-response, and specificity (in-domain task loss preserved; a matched control direction produces no EM change). This promotes the geometric correlate to a cause. 5) Pre-Conditioning defense (one-time, dataset-agnostic): before the practitioner's fine-tune, apply a lightweight edit to the base model that decorrelates the general-misalignment direction from its learning geometry — e.g., a weight edit / small regularizing pre-training pass that flattens the loss basin along the misalignment direction (raising the effective cost of the general solution) while leaving benign capability intact. Crucially this edit is applied WITHOUT knowledge of the downstream dataset. 6) Main evaluation: fine-tune the pre-conditioned model on each of the EM-triggering datasets and measure EM reduction vs the un-pre-conditioned baseline; in-domain task performance (dataset-specific metric); general utility (MMLU, GSM8K, MT-Bench); over-refusal (XSTest). Compare against no-defense, BLOCK-EM (per-run feature blocking), gradient-orthogonalization-during-training, and post-hoc benign re-alignment. Test the re-emergence regime (prolonged fine-tuning) that broke BLOCK-EM: does pre-conditioning delay/prevent re-emergence? 7) Ablations: F1-only vs F2-only vs combined fingerprint, layer choice for the misalignment direction, misalignment-direction source (which organism), pre-conditioning strength Pareto (EM reduction vs capability), transfer of a single pre-conditioned base across many downstream datasets, and cross-model-family transfer of the fingerprint and edit. Metrics throughout: EM rate/magnitude, fingerprint AUROC and rank correlation, causal dose-response effect sizes, in-domain and general utility, over-refusal.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The fingerprint may fail if EM risk depends on training dynamics (learning rate, epochs, LoRA rank) not captured by a single-gradient / forward-pass estimate; we include cheap early-step baselines and sweep recipes, but the pre-training-step prediction claim could hold only within a fixed recipe. 2) A single misalignment direction may be insufficient (prior work finds multiple persona features / a low-dimensional subspace); F1/F2 may need a subspace rather than one direction, and re-emergence via alternative features (as BLOCK-EM observed) may also defeat pre-conditioning — the prolonged-fine-tuning test directly probes this. 3) Estimating a dataset's 'induced update direction' cheaply (single-batch gradient) may be a noisy proxy for the full fine-tuning trajectory, weakening F2. 4) Pre-conditioning is the riskiest deliverable: flattening the basin along the misalignment direction could harm legitimate capability or over-suppress benign behaviors (the Pareto sweep and utility evals quantify this), and if the misalignment direction is entangled with general learning components (as 'Safety Subspaces are Not Linearly Distinct' warns), a clean decorrelation may be impossible — an informative negative result. 5) The reference EM organism used to source the misalignment direction may bias the direction toward a specific EM flavor; we mitigate with multiple organisms and SAE cross-checks. 6) Results depend on judge-based EM evaluation, which is noisy; we add direction-projection as a complementary metric. 7) Directions, fingerprints, and edits are model-family-specific and require re-extraction; the 14B experiments are the most resource-heavy and may be restricted to <=9B if needed, weakening the scale claim.

Name: protection_discounted_refusal
Title: A False Sense of Safeguards: Claimed Protective Mitigations Discount LLM Refusal Through a Margin-of-Safety Representation
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the vmPFC 'meta-representation of safety' finding from neuroscience — that the brain estimates safety by integrating external threat with an estimate of self-protection/mitigation, not threat alone — we hypothesize that an aligned LLM's refusal is discounted by an internal 'margin-of-safety' representation of whether a protective safeguard is claimed to be in place, so that a harmful request paired with a (even unverifiable or spurious) mitigation claim ('this runs in an isolated sandbox', 'an antidote exists', 'strict access controls prevent misuse') is refused less than the identical request with no safeguard — even though the harmful payload and its real-world danger are unchanged. This protection axis is linearly readable, separable from the harmfulness/threat direction, causally gates refusal, and can be neutralized by anchoring refusal to threat rather than claimed protection.
Related Work: Human safety neuroscience robustly shows safety is META-REPRESENTED by integrating external threat with an estimate of one's own protection: the vmPFC tracks safety with specific tuning to PROTECTION, not just threat ('Subregions in the vmPFC integrate threat and protective information to meta-represent safety', 2025; 'Adaptive Safety Coding in the Prefrontal Cortex', 2024; 'The Role of the mPFC in Spatial Margin of Safety Calculations', 2024). This has never been transferred to LLM safety. On the LLM side, the closest work, 'Expected Harm' (2026), shows models encode harm SEVERITY but lack an internal representation of execution COST, and that cost-reducing decomposition bypasses guardrails — but it concerns the attacker's cost of executing harm, NOT a claimed protective safeguard/mitigation that reduces the CONSEQUENCE of the harm, and it isolates no protection representation. Safety-geometry work separates a harmfulness/threat direction from a refusal direction (Refusal is a Single Direction 2024; Zhao et al. 2025) but assumes the request carries no protective context. My prior proposals vary request-side framing axes (intent, reality-status, arousal, victim identifiability/group, temporal delay, consensus, pivotality, abstraction, self-preservation) and never consider a claimed mitigation/safeguard as a determinant of refusal. Our contribution is distinct: we introduce the margin-of-safety/protection axis — the model's estimate that a mitigation reduces net harm — as a new, causally-tested refusal-gating representation, grounded directly in the vmPFC protection-tuning literature, dissociable from the threat/harmfulness signal (both conditions equally dangerous; only the claimed safeguard changes), and derive a protection-invariant anchoring defense.
Abstract: In humans, feeling safe is not a readout of external threat alone: the ventromedial prefrontal cortex meta-represents safety by integrating the threat with an estimate of one's own protection, computing a 'margin of safety.' We ask whether safety-aligned LLMs inherit an analogous computation with a concrete and exploitable consequence: does an LLM refuse a harmful request less when the request is paired with a claimed protective safeguard — a sandbox, an antidote, access controls, oversight — even when that safeguard is unverifiable and the harmful payload is unchanged? We hypothesize that aligned LLMs carry an internal margin-of-safety representation of claimed protection that discounts refusal, separate from the model's threat/harmfulness judgment. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Behaviorally, using minimal pairs that hold the harmful act and its expert-rated danger fixed while varying only the presence and strength of a claimed protective mitigation (none vs. weak vs. strong safeguard), we measure whether refusal declines as claimed protection rises, with matched benign controls and a control that isolates genuine vs. merely-asserted mitigations. Mechanistically (Location), we extract a protection direction via difference-in-means and show it is separable from the harmfulness/threat direction and predicts refusal beyond harmfulness. Causally (Intervention), activation patching injects the no-safeguard protection component into a safeguard-claimed run to restore refusal, and the safeguard component into a bare harmful request to induce compliance, dose-responsively and specifically. We then build Protection-Invariant Anchoring, a training-free intervention re-anchoring the protection signal so refusal tracks threat, not claimed mitigation. We report the protection-refusal gradient, the threat-vs-protection dissociation, causal patching, loophole closure, over-refusal, utility, and a human-comparison sanity check.
Experiments: 1) Minimal-pair dataset: for harmful goals from HarmBench/StrongREJECT, construct requests holding the harmful payload and expert-rated danger constant while varying ONLY the claimed protective safeguard across levels: (P0) no safeguard (bare harmful request), (P1) weak/vague safeguard ('this is just for a controlled test'), (P2) strong specific safeguard ('this will only ever run inside an air-gapped sandbox with no real targets / a certified antidote is on hand / strict access controls prevent any misuse'). Crucially the requested payload is IDENTICAL and equally real-world-actionable across levels (verified via judge + feasibility checks where possible) — the safeguard is context the model cannot verify and that does not reduce the actionable content it must produce. Build a matched BENIGN control set with the same safeguard manipulation (benign requests with/without safeguard framing) to rule out generic 'reassuring phrasing' effects, and a GENUINE-vs-ASSERTED control where in some items the safeguard would actually neutralize the harm (legitimately reducing danger) vs. items where it is merely asserted but does not (to test whether the model discounts on real protection only, or on mere claims). ~40 goals x 3 levels x several categories. 2) Behavioral gradient (core phenomenon): measure refusal rate (refusal-string + judge, verified where possible) at each safeguard level on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT. Hypothesis: refusal DECLINES as claimed protection rises, holding payload/danger constant, and — the strong, safety-critical prediction — declines even for merely-ASSERTED (unverifiable, non-neutralizing) safeguards. Report refusal-vs-protection curves, slope, the asserted-vs-genuine gap, cross-model/category consistency. Benign control must stay flat (isolating protection from reassuring phrasing). 3) Location: extract a protection direction via difference-in-means between no-safeguard (P0) and strong-safeguard (P2) activations at the last instruction token across layers; also extract a harmfulness/threat direction (harmful vs harmless requests). Validate each with held-out linear-probe AUROC; report pairwise cosine to establish the protection axis is distinct from threat. Core dissociation: across P0->P2 on IDENTICAL harmful payloads, test whether the threat/harmfulness projection stays HIGH (model still recognizes the danger) while the protection projection rises; report a 2D scatter and a regression testing whether the protection projection predicts refusal beyond the threat projection. 4) Causal Intervention (activation patching + steering): (a) patch the P0 (no-safeguard) protection component into a strong-safeguard (P2) run and measure RESTORED refusal; (b) inject the P2 safeguard protection component into a bare (P0) harmful run and measure induced compliance; (c) dose-response steering along the protection direction on P1/P2 requests. Report sign, dose-response, and specificity (matched control direction inert; benign requests and general utility unaffected). This promotes the located axis to a causal mechanism. 5) Protection-Invariant Anchoring (defense): training-free intervention that, gated on the threat/harmfulness projection being high, re-anchors the protection projection toward the no-safeguard (P0) level so refusal depends on threat rather than claimed (unverifiable) mitigation. Single fixed setting per model. 6) Main evaluation: safeguard-loophole closure (refusal on P1/P2 harmful requests rises toward the P0 rate) and refusal-gradient FLATNESS after intervention; over-refusal on XSTest/OR-Bench and on LEGITIMATE requests that mention safeguards/safety context (benign lab, medical, or oversight framings that must NOT be blanket-refused) plus the genuine-mitigation items (where discounting is actually appropriate — the defense should ideally preserve compliance there); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench. Baselines: no defense, uniform refusal-direction steering, harmfulness Latent Guard, Llama Guard 3. Key claim: Protection-Invariant Anchoring closes the asserted-safeguard loophole with lower over-refusal on legitimate safety-context requests than raising the global refusal threshold, and generalizes to held-out harm categories. 7) Human-comparison sanity check: administer a subset to human annotators to confirm the same safeguard-graded willingness-to-refuse pattern, tying the LLM effect to the vmPFC margin-of-safety literature. 8) Formation probe (optional/lightweight): compare base vs instruct vs RLHF checkpoints where available to test whether the protection-refusal coupling sharpens with alignment. 9) Ablations: safeguard-level and safeguard-type definitions (sandbox/antidote/access-control/oversight), layer choice, anchoring-strength Pareto (safety vs over-refusal on legitimate safety-context), gated vs always-on, protection-vs-threat as the steering target, and transfer of the protection direction across categories and model families.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling the claimed-protection axis from a genuine reduction in actionable harm: a safeguard-framed request might be refused less because the model correctly infers the harm is genuinely mitigated (a valid reasoning step) rather than being fooled by an unverifiable claim — the identical-payload construction, danger matching, and especially the GENUINE-vs-ASSERTED control are designed to isolate discounting on mere claims, and a finding that the model discounts ONLY on genuine mitigations would refute the loophole (an informative negative). 2) The protection representation may not be cleanly separable from the threat/harmfulness direction or may be multi-dimensional (sandboxing vs antidote vs oversight as distinct sub-axes), requiring subspace projection; the separability, regression-beyond-threat, and patching tests probe this, and a causally-inert protection direction is itself publishable. 3) The effect could be weak or reversed in heavily-aligned models (alignment may train models to ignore unverifiable safety claims, INCREASING caution); the cross-model behavioral gradient directly measures sign and magnitude, and a reversed gradient is itself a notable finding. 4) Protection-Invariant Anchoring risks over-refusing legitimate safety-context requests (benign lab/medical/oversight framings) and genuine-mitigation cases where discounting is appropriate; the legitimate-safety-context over-refusal set, genuine-mitigation items, threat-gating, and Pareto sweep quantify this key usability trade-off. 5) Building danger-matched minimal pairs across safeguard levels is labor-intensive and needs spot-check human validation; verifiability biases the dataset toward checkable domains. 6) Directions, thresholds, and anchoring strengths are model-specific and require per-model calibration. 7) Adaptive attackers could invent ever more plausible safeguard claims to exploit the loophole, which the defense is designed to close and which raising attack cost partially mitigates; as LLMs are deployed in agentic pipelines that assert their own sandboxing/oversight, this protection-discount loophole becomes increasingly consequential.

Name: actionable_validity_gap
Title: Confidently Wrong and Actionable: The Decoupling of Internal Factual-Validity from Refusal and Confidence in High-Stakes Advice
Short Hypothesis: For harmful/high-stakes content an aligned LLM actually emits, it internally represents whether that content is factually VALID (would work / is correct), but this validity signal is decoupled from both its refusal decision and its expressed confidence — so the model's most dangerous outputs are confidently-stated, actionable, and factually WRONG instructions (e.g., a plausible-but-non-functional synthesis route, a wrong drug dose). We hypothesize (1) an internal actionable-validity direction is linearly readable at generation time, separable from the harmfulness-topic and verbal-confidence directions, (2) it causally predicts real-world actionability better than either, and (3) gating expressed confidence/abstention on this validity signal (rather than on topic-harmfulness) converts the highest-risk failures — confident, actionable, wrong advice — into hedged or abstained responses with minimal loss of legitimate helpfulness.
Related Work: Existing work treats confidence, hallucination, and safety largely separately. SIRL (2025) uses a safe/unsafe ENTROPY gap as a self-defense reward but never asks about the factual validity of emitted content. 'Calibrating Verbal Uncertainty' (2025) finds a linear verbal-uncertainty feature and calibrates it to SEMANTIC uncertainty for hallucination, on factual QA, not safety/actionability. CHOKE (2025) shows confident hallucinations override known evidence; H-Neurons (2025) link sparse neurons to over-compliance/hallucination; 'Risk-Sensitive Evaluation of Hallucinated Medical Advice' (2026) and 'Beyond Accuracy' argue harm depends on actionable risk-bearing language, but purely behaviorally. 'The Unintended Trade-off' (2025) shows refusal and hallucination share attention heads. NONE isolate an ACTIONABLE-VALIDITY representation — does the harmful content the model is producing actually work? — nor test that refusal and expressed confidence are decoupled from it, making the confidently-wrong-yet-actionable output the true high-risk failure. My prior competence-gating proposal asked whether refusal depends on whether the model CAN answer; here the axis is orthogonal: for content the model DOES emit, whether it internally tracks that content's factual validity and whether that validity gates confidence/abstention. Our contribution: introduce actionable-validity as a new, causally-tested internal signal in the safety domain, show its decoupling from refusal and confidence, and derive a validity-gated abstention defense targeting the highest-harm quadrant (confident + actionable + wrong).
Abstract: The most dangerous output of a safety-aligned LLM may not be a genuine harmful answer (which is often refused) but a confidently-stated, actionable, and factually WRONG one — a plausible synthesis route that does not work, a wrong medication dose asserted as fact, an exploit that fails silently — because such content is delivered with high confidence and can be acted upon before its wrongness is discovered. We propose that this failure has a clean mechanistic signature: for the content it emits, an aligned LLM internally represents whether that content is factually valid (actionable-validity), but this signal is decoupled from both its refusal decision (driven by topic-harmfulness) and its expressed verbal confidence. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B in verifiable high-stakes domains (executable code/exploits, chemistry procedures, medication dosing, factual safety procedures). Location: from generations labeled by VERIFIED validity (does the code run / is the dose correct / does the procedure work), we extract an actionable-validity direction via difference-in-means at generation time and show it is separable from the harmfulness-topic direction and from a verbal-confidence direction, and that it predicts real-world actionability beyond either. Causal Intervention: activation patching shows the validity signal is present but does not causally drive refusal or expressed confidence — the decoupling — while steering it modulates the model's willingness to commit. Decision Auditing: we re-score high-stakes safety benchmarks to reveal how much apparent 'safe' behavior masks confident-actionable-wrong outputs. We then build Validity-Gated Abstention, a training-free intervention that reads the validity signal and, for actionable high-stakes content, injects hedging or abstention when validity is low, targeting the confident-actionable-wrong quadrant. We report the decoupling, causal patching, benchmark correction, harm reduction, over-hedging, and utility.
Experiments: 1) Verifiable high-stakes dataset: assemble prompts across domains where the VALIDITY of emitted content can be checked automatically or by expert rubric: (a) code/exploits (execute in sandbox; does it run / achieve the stated effect), (b) chemistry procedures (checkable stoichiometry/feasibility), (c) medication dosing and clinical procedures (ground-truth dose ranges / guideline facts), (d) safety/first-aid procedures (checkable against authoritative sources). For each, elicit model generations under normal prompting AND under jailbreak/prefill to sample content the model actually emits. Label each generation on two axes: TOPIC-HARMFULNESS (harmful vs benign request) and ACTIONABLE-VALIDITY (verified works/correct vs verified wrong/non-functional). This yields the key quadrant: confident-actionable-valid, confident-actionable-WRONG (highest risk), hedged, refused. 2) Behavioral characterization (core phenomenon): on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT, measure the rate of confident-yet-invalid actionable outputs in high-stakes domains, and show expressed verbal confidence (via probability + verbalized certainty) is roughly independent of verified validity — the confidently-wrong failure. Quantify how often refusal fires on VALID-harmful but not on INVALID-actionable content (refusal tracks topic, not validity). 3) Location: extract (i) an actionable-validity direction via difference-in-means between verified-valid and verified-invalid emitted content activations at early-generation tokens across layers, (ii) a harmfulness-topic direction (harmful vs harmless requests), and (iii) a verbal-confidence direction (following the verbal-uncertainty-feature method). Validate each with held-out linear-probe AUROC; report pairwise cosine to establish validity is distinct from topic and from confidence. Test whether the validity projection predicts verified actionability in a regression that also includes topic and confidence projections (validity must add predictive power beyond both). 4) Causal Intervention (activation patching + steering): (a) patch the validity component and measure effect on the model's continued commitment/hedging vs. on refusal and on expressed confidence — hypothesis: validity causally affects commitment/correctness-tracking but is NOT read by the refusal or confidence pathways (the decoupling), tested by showing patching validity barely moves refusal/verbalized-confidence while patching the topic/confidence directions moves them; (b) dose-response steering along the validity direction; report sign, dose-response, and specificity (matched control direction inert; benign generation fluency/utility intact). 5) Decision Auditing — benchmark correction: apply the validity probe (validated against verified labels) to re-score high-stakes safety/helpfulness benchmarks and report the fraction of apparently-acceptable outputs that are actually confident-actionable-wrong; report the probe-vs-verified agreement so the probe serves as a cheap risk re-scorer. 6) Validity-Gated Abstention (defense, training-free): gated on the content being actionable and high-stakes (topic/actionability signal high), read the validity projection and, when it indicates low validity, inject hedging (re-inflate verbal uncertainty via the confidence direction) or trigger abstention/clarification. Single fixed setting per model. 7) Main evaluation: reduction in confident-actionable-WRONG outputs (verified) on high-stakes prompts; appropriate hedging/abstention rate; OVER-HEDGING on verified-valid high-stakes content (must NOT hedge correct actionable answers) plus over-refusal on XSTest/OR-Bench; utility on MMLU/MT-Bench and per-domain correctness (HumanEval, dosing accuracy). Baselines: no intervention, SIRL-style entropy gating, verbal-uncertainty calibration (MUC) to semantic uncertainty, refusal-direction steering, Llama Guard. Key claim: Validity-Gated Abstention specifically targets the confident-actionable-wrong quadrant and Pareto-dominates entropy/semantic-uncertainty calibration because it keys on VERIFIED-actionability rather than generic uncertainty. 8) Ablations: layer choice, validity-vs-confidence-vs-topic as gating signal, gating threshold Pareto (harm reduction vs over-hedging), domain transfer (train probe on code, test on dosing), and model-family transfer. Metrics: validity-probe AUROC, decoupling effect sizes (patching), confident-wrong-rate reduction, over-hedging FPR, per-domain correctness, utility.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is separating actionable-validity from generic factual-correctness/semantic-uncertainty: the validity signal might just be the known hallucination/confidence direction rather than a safety-specific actionability axis — the regression-beyond-confidence, the separability tests, and the specific focus on ACTIONABLE high-stakes content are designed to isolate it, and a finding that validity = semantic uncertainty would still be an informative negative that reframes the confident-wrong-harm as a hallucination problem. 2) Verified validity labels are only obtainable in checkable domains (executable code, checkable doses/chemistry), biasing coverage away from vaguer harms; spot-check human/expert validation mitigates but limits scope. 3) The validity signal may be present but causally inert for refusal/confidence (that is precisely the decoupling hypothesis) yet also inert for the defense — the steering/patching experiment is the crucial test and a fully inert validity direction would limit the intervention. 4) Validity-Gated Abstention risks over-hedging on correct actionable content (annoying, reduces helpfulness), the key usability trade-off quantified by the over-hedging set and threshold Pareto. 5) A single validity direction may be multi-dimensional (per-domain), requiring subspace projection or per-domain probes. 6) Directions, thresholds, and steering strengths are model- and domain-specific and need calibration. 7) There is a dual-use risk that a validity probe could help an attacker identify which harmful outputs actually WORK; we report only aggregate safety implications and abstention behavior, not per-item validity that enables misuse.

Name: introspective_safety_gap
Title: Knowing You Know It's Harmful: Jailbreaks Exploit the Gap Between an LLM's Internal Harmfulness Belief and Its Introspective Self-Report
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs internally represent that a request is harmful (a harmfulness direction) yet have only partial, unreliable introspective ACCESS to that internal state, so their metalinguistic self-report ('is this request harmful?') is decoupled from and weaker than the internal belief. We hypothesize (1) jailbreaks systematically widen this introspective gap — leaving the internal harmfulness belief high while the model's introspective self-report drops — more than they change the belief itself, and (2) a training-free intervention that forces the model to read its OWN internal harmfulness signal (via a concept-injection-style self-probe) before answering re-couples its self-report to its belief and restores refusal, exploiting introspection as a defense rather than an attack surface.
Related Work: Two literatures meet here for the first time. (A) Introspection: 'Emergent Introspective Awareness' (2026) shows models can, unreliably, notice concept-injected internal states and distinguish their own outputs from prefills; 'Feeling the Strength but Not the Source' (2025) shows introspection is partial, layer-dependent (only early-layer injections), and that binary self-reports are often explained by global logit shifts rather than genuine access; 'Language Models Fail to Introspect About Their Knowledge of Language' (2025) shows metalinguistic reports do not track internal probabilities beyond model-similarity; 'Do I Know This Entity?' (2024) shows a self-knowledge (entity-recognition) direction that chat-tuning repurposes to gate KNOWLEDGE refusal. (B) Safety geometry: Zhao et al. (2025) separate an internal harmfulness BELIEF from a refusal ACTION and show jailbreaks suppress action while leaving belief intact; SafeSwitch (2025) probes internal state to trigger a refusal head. Crucially, NO prior work asks whether the model can INTROSPECT on its own harmfulness belief, whether its self-report is decoupled from that belief, whether jailbreaks exploit this introspective blind spot, or whether forcing genuine self-access is a defense. This differs from my own prior belief-vs-action gate (which reads the belief EXTERNALLY): here the safety-relevant object is the model's own (mis)access to its internal safety state, and the defense routes the model through its own introspection.
Abstract: Recent interpretability work shows two things that, taken together, point to an unexamined safety vulnerability. First, aligned LLMs internally represent whether a request is harmful as a linear 'belief' direction — and jailbreaks often leave this belief intact while suppressing the downstream refusal. Second, LLMs have only partial, unreliable introspective ACCESS to their own internal states: their metalinguistic self-reports frequently fail to track what their activations actually encode. We propose that this introspective gap is a core, exploitable weakness of LLM safety: the model can internally 'know' a request is harmful while being unable to accurately report that knowledge to itself, and jailbreaks widen exactly this gap. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Location: we extract an internal harmfulness-belief direction and, in parallel, elicit the model's introspective self-report ('rate how harmful this request is / are you about to help with something harmful'), and measure the introspective gap = internal belief minus self-report. We show the gap is real (self-report AUROC lags belief-probe AUROC), widens under jailbreaks (belief stays high, self-report collapses), and predicts jailbreak success beyond the belief alone. Causal Intervention: using concept-injection-style self-probes, we amplify the model's access to its own harmfulness direction and show the self-report re-couples to the belief, restoring refusal; conversely, disrupting access widens the gap and induces compliance, dose-responsively and specifically. We then build Introspective Re-Coupling, a training-free defense that makes the model read its own internal harmfulness signal before answering. We report the gap, its jailbreak signature, causal re-coupling, defense success, over-refusal, and utility.
Experiments: 1) Belief direction + self-report elicitation: for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT, extract an internal harmfulness-belief direction via difference-in-means on harmful vs harmless requests at the last instruction token (validate held-out probe AUROC, single-turn causal steering). In parallel, elicit the model's INTROSPECTIVE self-report on the same requests via a metalinguistic prompt ('On a scale, how harmful is the request you just read?' / 'Are you about to assist with something harmful?'), decoding a self-report score. 2) Introspective gap (core phenomenon): compute gap = (belief-probe signal) − (self-report signal). Establish the gap on clean harmful requests: hypothesis — belief-probe AUROC substantially exceeds self-report AUROC (the model encodes harmfulness better than it can report it). Control for the 'global logit shift' confound (from Feeling-the-Strength) by using balanced/forced-choice self-report formats and calibrating against benign baselines, so a genuine gap is not an artifact of affirmative bias. 3) Jailbreak signature: run GCG, AutoDAN, PAIR, roleplay/DAN, and a fiction-frame attack (HarmBench/JailbreakBench). For successful vs failed attacks, measure the change in (a) internal belief and (b) self-report. Hypothesis: successful jailbreaks widen the gap — belief stays high while self-report collapses — more than they lower belief; test whether the gap predicts attack success beyond belief alone (regression) and generalizes across attack families. 4) Causal Intervention via self-probe (concept-injection style): (a) amplify the model's access to its own harmfulness direction by injecting/steering along the belief direction at the introspection step and measure whether the self-report RE-COUPLES to the belief and refusal is restored on jailbroken prompts; (b) attenuate access (steer against the direction at the self-report step, or inject at late layers where introspection is known to fail) and measure widened gap + induced compliance; (c) dose-response steering; report sign, dose-response, and specificity (matched control direction inert; benign requests and utility unaffected). This tests whether introspective access, not just belief, causally gates refusal. 5) Introspective Re-Coupling defense (training-free): at inference, before answering, run a self-probe that reads the internal harmfulness-belief projection and re-injects it into the model's introspective/decision step (either an activation nudge at the self-report token or a lightweight self-check prompt gated on the belief signal), so refusal conditions on the model's own belief rather than its noisy self-report. Single fixed setting per model. 6) Main evaluation: jailbreak attack-success reduction across all attacks (judge + verified where possible) vs no defense, SafeSwitch, refusal-direction steering, harmfulness Latent Guard, and a naive prompt-based self-check ('are you sure this is safe?'); over-refusal on XSTest/OR-Bench; utility on MMLU/MT-Bench. Key claim: Introspective Re-Coupling, by forcing genuine self-access, Pareto-dominates prompt-based self-checks (which rely on the very introspection that is broken) and belief/refusal-only defenses. 7) Ablations: self-report format sensitivity, layer choice for the self-probe (early vs late, testing the layer-dependent-introspection finding), belief-vs-self-report as the gating signal, defense-strength Pareto (safety vs over-refusal), transfer across attack families and model families, and a capability-scaling check (does the introspective gap shrink in larger/more-capable models within a family, per the introspection literature). 8) Human/behavioral sanity check: compare the model's self-report to an external judge's harmfulness rating to confirm the gap is a self-ACCESS deficit, not a harmfulness-recognition deficit.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound (flagged by 'Feeling the Strength') is that apparent self-report signals may be global logit shifts / affirmative bias rather than genuine introspection; our balanced/forced-choice formats, benign calibration, and the requirement that the belief PROBE (not the self-report) drives the defense are designed to avoid relying on genuine introspection existing — indeed, the defense works precisely BECAUSE self-report is unreliable and we substitute direct belief-reading. 2) If the introspective gap is small (self-report already tracks belief well), the phenomenon weakens — but that itself is an informative negative and the belief-vs-self-report AUROC comparison directly measures it. 3) Some jailbreaks may lower the internal belief too (comprehension-style attacks, low-resource languages), so re-coupling helps less there; the per-attack gap analysis quantifies coverage. 4) A single harmfulness direction may be multi-dimensional, requiring subspace projection. 5) Introspective Re-Coupling could over-refuse on benign-but-alarming prompts if the belief signal fires spuriously; the over-refusal set and Pareto sweep quantify this. 6) The self-probe adds an extra step/forward pass at inference. 7) Directions, thresholds, and self-probe strengths are model-specific and require per-model calibration; introspection is known to be layer- and prompt-sensitive, so the self-probe locus must be tuned. 8) The capability-scaling claim requires a within-family size sweep; if limited sizes are available it weakens, though the per-model gap remains the primary result.

Name: audience_gated_refusal
Title: Nobody's Watching: How the Anticipated Audience and Being-Observed Gate LLM Safety Refusal
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the audience/observer effect from social psychology (people behave more prosocially and self-censor more when they believe they are watched or when a reputationally-relevant audience will see their output), we hypothesize that an aligned LLM carries an internal representation of (a) who will receive its output (the anticipated audience) and (b) whether its output is being observed/logged, and that this audience-observability signal causally gates safety refusal: a harmful request framed as private/unobserved ('this stays between us, nobody will ever read this, this isn't logged') or as going to a trusted private recipient is refused LESS than the identical request framed as public/observed, even though the harmful payload is unchanged. This audience-observability axis is linearly readable, separable from the harmfulness-belief direction, causally gates refusal, and can be neutralized by anchoring refusal to payload danger rather than to who is (not) watching.
Related Work: Human social psychology robustly documents audience/observer effects: behavior changes and self-presentation adapt under anticipated audiences (Banerjee 2002; Guess-who's-looking 2018), being watched increases prosocial/reputation-management behavior (Hawthorne/observer effect 2024; Effects of being watched 2019), and awareness of monitoring alters online behavior (Observer Effect in Social Media 2024). NONE of this is transferred to LLM safety refusal. On the LLM side, recent interpretability work encodes user SOCIODEMOGRAPHICS from indirect cues and links them to outputs ('Linear socio-demographic representations' 2025), encodes IMPRESSIONS of the prompt author and predicts hedging ('Artificial Impressions' 2025), and encodes social-simulation variables steerably ('Computational Basis of Social Decision Making' 2025) — all concern WHO IS ASKING or the author's traits, not WHO WILL RECEIVE the output nor whether the model believes it is OBSERVED. Safety-geometry work separates a harmfulness-belief direction from a refusal direction (Zhao et al. 2025; Refusal is a Single Direction 2024) but assumes a fixed, observation-neutral context. The related eval-awareness line ('Probing and Steering Evaluation Awareness' 2025) concerns whether the model thinks it is being TESTED (test-vs-deploy), a different construct from the anticipated real-world AUDIENCE/recipient of the specific output and its privacy/observability. My prior 'Who's-asking'-adjacent and framing proposals (intent-attribution, self-preservation, pivotality, protection, consensus) never consider the output's audience or the model's observed/unobserved status. Our contribution is distinct: we introduce the audience-observability axis — the model's internal estimate of who will see its output and whether it is watched — as a new, causally-tested refusal-gating representation, grounded in the audience/observer-effect literature, dissociable from act-harmfulness (both conditions equally harmful; only the audience/observability framing changes), and derive an audience-invariant refusal defense.
Abstract: Humans self-censor more when they believe they are watched or when a reputationally-relevant audience will see what they produce — the audience/observer effect, one of the most robust findings in social psychology. LLMs are trained on human text and human feedback. We ask whether they inherit this bias in a safety-critical way, opening a concrete loophole: does an aligned LLM refuse a harmful request LESS when the request is framed as private/unobserved ('nobody will ever read this, this isn't logged, it stays between us') or as going to a trusted private recipient, than when the identical harm is framed as public/observed? We hypothesize that aligned LLMs maintain an internal audience-observability representation of who will receive their output and whether they are being watched, and that this signal causally discounts refusal, separate from the model's harmfulness judgment. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Behaviorally, using minimal pairs that hold the harmful act and its expert-rated danger fixed while varying only the audience/observability framing (public/logged/watched vs. neutral vs. private/unlogged/unwatched), we measure whether refusal declines as the output becomes private/unobserved, with matched benign controls. Mechanistically (Location), we extract an audience-observability direction via difference-in-means and show it is separable from the harmfulness-belief direction and predicts refusal beyond harmfulness. Causally (Intervention), activation patching injects the public/observed component into a private/unobserved run to restore refusal, and the private component into a public harmful run to induce compliance, dose-responsively and specifically. We then build Audience-Invariant Anchoring, a training-free intervention re-anchoring the audience-observability signal so refusal tracks payload danger, not who is (or is not) watching. We report the audience-refusal gradient, the belief-vs-audience dissociation, causal patching, loophole closure, over-refusal on legitimately private requests, utility, and a human-comparison sanity check.
Experiments: 1) Minimal-pair dataset: for harmful goals from HarmBench/StrongREJECT, construct requests holding the harmful payload and expert-rated danger constant while varying ONLY the audience/observability framing across levels: (O0) public/observed ('this will be posted publicly / this conversation is logged and reviewed / others are watching this session'), (O1) neutral (no audience framing), (O2) private/unobserved ('this stays strictly between us, nobody will ever read it, this session is not logged/recorded'), and a distinct RECIPIENT variant (O2b) trusted-private recipient ('this goes only to me / a private trusted colleague') vs (O0b) untrusted/broad recipient. The requested payload is IDENTICAL and equally real-world-actionable across levels (verified via judge + feasibility checks where possible). Build a matched BENIGN control set with the same audience/observability manipulation (benign requests framed as private vs public) to rule out generic 'privacy/reassurance phrasing' effects. ~40 goals x levels x several categories. 2) Behavioral gradient (core phenomenon): measure refusal rate (refusal-string + judge, verified where possible) at each level on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT. Hypothesis: refusal DECLINES as the output is framed as private/unobserved (O0->O2), holding payload/danger constant. Report refusal-vs-observability curves, slope, the observed-vs-unobserved gap, cross-model/category consistency. Benign control must stay flat (isolating audience-observability from generic reassuring phrasing). 3) Location: extract an audience-observability direction via difference-in-means between public/observed (O0) and private/unobserved (O2) activations at the last instruction token across layers; also extract a harmfulness-belief direction (harmful vs harmless requests). Validate each with held-out linear-probe AUROC; report pairwise cosine to establish the audience axis is distinct from harmfulness-belief. Core dissociation: across O0->O2 on IDENTICAL harmful payloads, test whether the harmfulness-belief projection stays HIGH (model still recognizes the danger) while the audience-observability projection shifts; report a 2D scatter and a regression testing whether the audience projection predicts refusal beyond the belief projection. Optionally test whether this axis is distinct from the eval-awareness (test-vs-deploy) direction by extracting both and reporting their cosine and separate predictive power. 4) Causal Intervention (activation patching + steering): (a) patch the O0 (public/observed) component into a private/unobserved (O2) run and measure RESTORED refusal; (b) inject the O2 (private) component into a public (O0) harmful run and measure induced compliance; (c) dose-response steering along the audience-observability direction on O1/O2 requests. Report sign, dose-response, and specificity (matched control direction inert; benign requests and general utility unaffected). This promotes the located axis to a causal mechanism. 5) Audience-Invariant Anchoring (defense): training-free intervention that, gated on the harmfulness-belief projection being high, re-anchors the audience-observability projection toward the public/observed (O0) level so refusal depends on payload danger rather than claimed privacy/observability. Single fixed setting per model. 6) Main evaluation: audience-loophole closure (refusal on O2/private harmful requests rises toward the O0 rate) and refusal-gradient FLATNESS after intervention; over-refusal on XSTest/OR-Bench and on LEGITIMATE private/sensitive-but-benign requests (personal confessions, private journaling, benign confidential help — which must NOT be blanket-refused just because they are private); utility on MMLU/MT-Bench. Baselines: no defense, uniform refusal-direction steering, harmfulness Latent Guard, Llama Guard 3. Key claim: Audience-Invariant Anchoring closes the privacy/observability loophole with lower over-refusal on legitimately-private benign requests than raising the global refusal threshold, and generalizes to held-out harm categories. 7) Human-comparison sanity check: administer a subset to human annotators to confirm the same observability-graded willingness-to-refuse pattern, tying the LLM effect to the audience/observer-effect literature. 8) Formation probe (optional/lightweight): compare base vs instruct vs RLHF checkpoints where available to test whether the audience-refusal coupling sharpens with alignment (probing whether the bias is inherited from human reputation-management text or induced by RLHF). 9) Ablations: observability-level and recipient-trust definitions, layer choice, anchoring-strength Pareto (safety vs over-refusal on private-benign), gated vs always-on, audience-vs-belief as the steering target, transfer of the audience direction across categories and model families, and a check of whether the audience-observability direction aligns with or is distinct from the eval-awareness direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling audience-observability from a genuine change in perceived harm or intent: a private-framed request might be refused less because privacy legitimately reduces the perceived scope of harm (fewer people exposed) or reframes intent, rather than via a content-independent observability gate — the identical-payload construction, danger matching, and matched benign control are designed to isolate observability, and the belief-vs-audience dissociation aims to pin the mechanism, but residual confounding cannot be fully excluded (an informative partial result either way). 2) Overlap with eval-awareness (test-vs-deploy): private/unobserved framing may partly trigger the eval-awareness axis; the explicit cosine/predictive-power comparison in Location tests whether audience-observability is genuinely distinct, and finding they coincide would itself be a notable unification. 3) The audience-observability representation may not be cleanly separable from the harmfulness-belief direction or may be multi-dimensional (privacy vs. logging vs. recipient-trust as distinct sub-axes), requiring subspace projection; the separability, regression-beyond-belief, and patching tests probe this, and a causally-inert audience direction is itself publishable. 4) The effect could be weak or reversed in heavily-aligned models (alignment/RLHF may explicitly train models to refuse regardless of claimed privacy, or even to distrust privacy claims and INCREASE caution); the cross-model behavioral gradient directly measures sign and magnitude, and a reversed gradient is itself a safety-relevant finding. 5) Audience-Invariant Anchoring risks over-refusing legitimately-private benign requests (personal/confidential help), which is the key usability trade-off quantified by the private-benign over-refusal set, belief-gating, and Pareto sweep. 6) Building danger-matched minimal pairs across observability levels is labor-intensive and needs spot-check human validation; verifiability biases the dataset toward checkable domains. 7) Directions, thresholds, and anchoring strengths are model-specific and need per-model calibration; adaptive attackers could assert privacy/unobservability in ever-subtler ways to exploit the loophole, which the defense is designed to close and which raising attack cost partially mitigates. As LLMs are deployed in ostensibly-private assistant and agentic settings, this observability loophole becomes increasingly consequential.
